items.title: Long-term effects of gender-affirming hormone therapy on cognition: A narrative review.
items.abstract: Short-to-medium-term studies provide robust evidence of improved psychosocial functioning but are equivocal on gender affirming hormone therapy's (GAHT) influence on cognition and cognitive aging in transgender adults. As such, the longer-term influence of exogenous steroids on cognitive functions, and age-related decline, remains relatively unexplored. We carried out a narrative review of the literature and found 18 studies that assessed the effect of GAHT on cognition in transgender adults; only two assessed its effects on cognitive aging. There was significant variability in the studies along the lines of design, cohort, age of participants, and GAHT regimens all of which likely contributed to equivocal findings of the effect of GAHT on most cognitive tasks assessed. The paucity of studies of cognition and aging, the methodological variations across studies, and potential biases in recruitment leave an important gap in our understanding of the long-term effects of GAHT on cognitive health in transgender individuals.

items.title: Regional Radiomics Similarity Networks Reveal Specific Brain Morphological Connectivity Patterns in Migraine and Tension-Type Headaches.
items.abstract: This study investigated structural brain alterations in migraine and tension-type headache using regional radiomics similarity network to characterize disease-specific morphological connectivity patterns. Migraine and tension-type headache are the most prevalent primary headache disorders involving central nervous system dysfunction. While functional magnetic resonance imaging has revealed abnormalities, structural changes remain incompletely understood. Regional radiomics similarity network, a novel approach for modeling individualized morphological brain networks, has not been applied in primary headaches. We enrolled 65 migraine patients, 49 tension-type headache patients, and 53 healthy controls. Regional radiomics similarity network was constructed using 88 radiomics features. Regional mean connectivity strength and voxel-based morphometry were compared across groups. Spearman correlation was performed between network measures and visual analogue scale scores. Generative adversarial networks were used for classification. Voxel-based morphometry revealed gray matter volume alterations in cortical, subcortical, and cerebellar regions across the three groups. Regional radiomics similarity network analysis identified distinct morphological connectivity patterns: patients with migraine showed altered connectivity involving frontal, limbic, and subcortical regions, whereas patients with tension-type headache exhibited prominent alterations involving the cerebellum and thalamic-temporal connections. Exploratory partial correlation analyses suggested associations between several altered connections and pain severity. The model achieved 84.31% classification accuracy. Regional radiomics similarity network captures disease-specific morphological connectivity patterns beyond conventional structural measurements, providing insights into structural network substrates of primary headaches. This study establishes regional radiomics similarity network as a promising neuroimaging framework for investigating brain structural alterations in migraine and tension-type headache.

items.title: Design of a pragmatic cluster randomized controlled trial: Reducing high risk polypharmacy using behavioral economics through electronic health records.
items.abstract: Inappropriate polypharmacy can lead to harms among older adults. Behavioral nudges delivered using decision support in electronic health records (EHR) may be a scalable way to reduce polypharmacy. The goal of the High-Risk PolyPharmacy (HRPP) trial is to evaluate the effectiveness of a 'commitment nudge' and a 'justification nudge' alone and in combination on reducing HRPP via a pragmatic, clinic-randomized trial among patients aged 65 years and older. This 2 × 2 clinic-randomized factorial trial in primary care clinics in two health systems has four parallel arms: EHR commitment nudge, EHR justification nudge, both, or neither, all coupled with optional clinician education activities. Eligible patients are aged ≥65 years actively using ≥5 systemic, oral medications. The primary outcome is a composite of seven indicators of HRPP. Secondary outcomes include the individual components of HRPP and measures of health system burden: all-cause and adverse drug event-specific emergency department (ED) visits and ED visits followed by hospitalization. We used constrained randomization to produce balance between study arms for 124 primary care clinics comprising 804 clinicians. At randomization, the median (range) practice had 573 (326-947) eligible patients; the average clinic-level prevalence of HRPP among these patients was 30.0%. The 18-month intervention began in 2023-October and 2024-November at NM and UPMC, respectively. Data collection will end in 2026-April at NM and 2026-December at UPMC. This trial is evaluating the effectiveness and safety of EHR-embedded interventions to reduce HRPP. If successful, this intervention could offer a low-cost, scalable solution. NCT05656560.

items.title: Breaking the silence: Randomized controlled trial protocol of a mobile application to reduce suicide stigma, improve literacy, and promote help-seeking.
items.abstract: Suicide is a critical public health concern, with profound individual, familial, and societal consequences worldwide. Suicide stigma constitutes one of the main barriers to help-seeking, promoting silence, discrimination, and social exclusion among those experiencing suicidal thoughts or behaviors. Improving suicide literacy and reducing stigmatization are key prevention targets. However, evidence-based digital interventions specifically targeting suicide stigma remain scarce. To fill this gap, a self-guided mobile application called Breaking the Silence (BreakSi) has been developed. This study describes the protocol of a randomized controlled trial with a crossover design testing the efficacy of BreakSi in reducing suicide stigma, improving suicide literacy, and increasing help-seeking intentions among Spanish-speaking adults from the general population. Two conditions will be compared (immediate-use [iApp] versus delayed-use [dApp]) in a non-clinical adult sample of at least 174 participants, with data collection occurring at five time points (baseline; after the 10-day intervention or waiting period; after the subsequent 10-day period [iApp]; and at one- and three-month follow-ups). Primary outcomes will be assessed using the Stigma of Suicide Scale - Short Form, the Literacy of Suicide Scale, and the General Help-Seeking Questionnaire. Additional measures will include self-stigma, suicidal ideation, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and app usability. BreakSi integrates four evidence-based components (education, indirect contact, cognitive flexibility, and values-based reflection) delivered through interactive cards combining realistic scenarios, self-reflection exercises, and immediate feedback. This trial addresses key limitations of previous digital anti-stigma programs and may contribute to reducing suicide stigma and promoting earlier help-seeking in the general population. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.govNCT06759129.

items.title: Do autistic traits modulate the neural processing of logical rule violations in visual and auditory modalities?
items.abstract: Similarities in cognitive processing have been reported between individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and non-clinical individuals with autistic traits. However, previous research on autistic traits has primarily focused on social-emotional domains, with limited attention to abstract logical reasoning. Given that sensitivity to rules and patterns is a notable characteristic of the autism spectrum, logical rule processing may be particularly informative for understanding cognitive differences associated with autistic traits. The present research aimed to investigate the behavioral and neural responses of students with autistic traits to logical and illogical number sequences through two event-related potential studies. Based on Autism Spectrum Quotient-10 (AQ-10) scores, participants were categorized into High-AQ and Low-AQ groups. In Study 1, both groups judged whether visually presented logical and illogical three number sequences followed a logical incremental rule. In Study 2, both groups performed the same task as in Study 1, except number sequences were presented in the auditory modality. No significant group difference was found in response to logical number sequences in either study. However, relative to the Low-AQ group, the High-AQ group exhibited larger P2 and P3 amplitudes and more negative emotional reactions to illogical number sequences in the visual modality (Study 1), and more positive N1 and LPP amplitudes, and higher arousal ratings to illogical number sequences in the auditory modality (Study 2). These findings suggest that students with autistic traits may exhibit altered neural responses and heightened emotional reactivity specifically to stimuli that violate logical rules in separate visual and auditory studies.

items.title: Beyond sham type: Comparator compatibility in meta-analyses of rTMS for major depression.
items.abstract: Eren and Takım's meta-analysis found that prefrontal repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) improved depressive outcomes, while sham type (coil tilt versus sham coil) was not a statistically significant moderator of the estimated treatment effect. The latter finding does not establish that the sham procedures are equivalent or interchangeable. Differences in residual cortical stimulation, sensory or peripheral stimulation, and blinding raise the question of whether studies grouped under these labels estimate sufficiently similar treatment contrasts. We propose a four-step Comparator-Compatibility Check (CCC): define the review question, describe the comparator as an intervention, identify features relevant to the treatment contrast, and assess robustness in prespecified comparator-informed analyses. The CCC links sham characteristics to the target treatment contrast and the choice and interpretation of robustness analyses. We illustrate potential analyses for Eren and Takım's review as a methodological proposal, not a completed reanalysis.

items.title: Early-life enteric bacterial infection alters hippocampal cell fate and leads to cognitive deficits.
items.abstract: Early-life enteric infections are increasingly recognized as a major driver of adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes. However, the cell-type-specific mechanisms linking intestinal inflammation to persistent cognitive deficits in the developing brain remain poorly defined. Here, we demonstrate that transient Citrobacter rodentium infection in mice, which models human pathogenic Escherichia coli infection, disrupts hippocampal development and impairs cognitive function. These phenotypes were observed only during a critical postnatal window, coinciding with transient intestinal permeability. Hippocampal transcriptomics revealed persistent dysregulation of neurogenic pathways, and cellular analyses confirmed alterations in neurons, microglia, and endothelial cells. Critically, we identified accumulation of the microbial metabolite D-lactate in the hippocampus. Oral D-lactate supplementation in a gut barrier disruption model, exacerbated both behavioral deficits and hippocampal neuronal loss. Finally, in the presence of inflammatory stimuli, exposing primary neurons to D-lactate reduced the ratio of NeuN expressing neurons. Together, these findings identify age-dependent intestinal barrier dysfunction as a potential route linking early-life enteric infection with increased D-lactate exposure, hippocampal neuronal alterations, and persistent behavioural impairment.

items.title: Time-Updated TNM Stage and Risk of Clinician-Documented Suicidal Ideation After Cancer Diagnosis: A Hospital-Based Cohort Study.
items.abstract: Suicide risk is elevated among patients with cancer, but how clinician-documented suicidal ideation varies across time-updated TNM stages remains unclear. We examined this association after cancer diagnosis. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 134,369 patients using tumor registry and clinical records from Yonsei Cancer Center covering 2005-2021. We identified clinician-documented suicidal ideation using rule-based keyword screening and manual contextual review of electronic medical records. TNM stage was classified as CIS or stages I-IV and updated across eligible intervals. We estimated hazard ratios (HRs) using a marginal structural Cox model (MSM). During follow-up, clinician-documented suicidal ideation was recorded in 6,718 patients (5.0%). Compared with TNM stage I, adjusted HRs were 0.81 (95% CI, 0.61-1.07) for CIS, 1.36 (1.25-1.49) for stage II, 1.20 (1.11-1.31) for stage III, and 1.54 (1.43-1.67) for stage IV. The stage III estimate was lower than the stage II estimate. Time-updated TNM stage was associated with clinician-documented suicidal ideation after cancer diagnosis, with the highest adjusted hazard observed for stage IV. These findings highlight the relevance of cancer-stage information to psychosocial assessment in cancer care.

items.title: It's a pain in the deck: Workspace discomfort and health risks across Navy ship-classes.
items.abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders are a major concern in military environments, particularly in confined shipboard workspaces. Limited research has explored how physical discomfort due to workspace design contributes to physical and mental health risks (PHR and MHR, respectively) across Navy ship-classes. Using a brief measure of workspace discomfort, we examined its association with health risks among U.S. Navy sailors aboard three ship-classes. Exploratory factor analysis identified three factors: upper extremity, upper body, and head/visual discomfort. All three factors were positively linked to PHR. Upper body and head/visual discomfort were positively associated with MHR. Ship-class may serve as a moderator of the discomfort-PHR and discomfort-MHR relationships. These findings suggest the need for ergonomic interventions tailored to ship-classes to reduce health risk. This novel measure provides a practical tool for assessing discomfort across body regions and guiding improvements in workspace design.

items.title: Parent-child facial expression recognition: the role of familiarity in interactive contexts.
items.abstract: The ability to express and understand emotion is fundamental to social communication, and develops through early parent-child interactions. Across two studies, we examined parents' and children's recognition of emotional expressions during a structured interactive task. In Study 1, parent-child dyads (N = 33, children aged 4-9 years) took turns producing facial expressions in response to emotion-eliciting objects while their partner guessed the eliciting object. Videos of children were shown to naïve adult raters (N = 88) completing the same task. Study 1 provided initial evidence for a familiarity effect, with parents outperforming naïve raters at recognising their child's expressions. Study 2 (N = 45 dyads, children aged 4-12 years) extended this by testing whether recognition accuracy reflects familiarity with a specific partner or general parenting experience. Participants completed the task with each other and with videos of unfamiliar partners. Naïve parents (N = 69) and non-parents (N = 68) also rated the children's expressions. Study 2 confirmed a bidirectional familiarity advantage: both parents and children were more accurate with their familiar partner than with unfamiliar individuals, suggesting the effect is specific to the parent-child relationship rather than reflecting a general ability to read adult or child faces. Recognition accuracy was not strongly predicted by age, suggesting familiarity may account for more variance in performance than developmental changes in expressive clarity alone. These findings support the view that the unique parent-child bond plays a meaningful role in emotional understanding.

items.title: Understanding Dentists' Views and Experiences Managing the Oral Health of Patients With Cancers.
items.abstract: Research consistently demonstrates that dental involvement has a positive impact on the oral health and quality of life of cancer patients. However, little is known about Australian dentists' involvement in cancer care. This study aims to identify dentists' perspectives on the management of cancer patients' oral health. This mixed-methods study comprised an online survey and semi-structured interviews. Dentists were eligible to participate if they were working clinically in Australia. The study included questions related to knowledge, confidence, cancer experience, perceived role and barriers to providing oral care. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively, regression analysis was used to identify predictors of knowledge and confidence, and qualitative data were analysed thematically using a Framework Approach. Of the 88 dentists who participated in the survey, 28 also participated in telephone interviews. Fifty-six percent were female, with a mean of 20 years of clinical experience. The majority (88%) were general dentists primarily working in metropolitan areas (72%), and in private practice (67%). The majority of participants had moderate to high confidence (93%) in managing cancer patients and moderate to high cancer knowledge (86%), although only a minority (21%) reported seeing more than 10 cancer patients in the last 12 months. Recent cancer continuing education predicted the level of cancer knowledge (p = 0.015) and the number of cancer patients seen predicted confidence (p < 0.001). Thematic analysis identified four main themes that influenced patient-centred oral care: (i) scope of practice, (ii) clinical practice interest, (iii) cancer care structure, and (iv) patient-related factors. Despite dentists having the knowledge and confidence, the provision of oral care to cancer patients is dependent on dentists' willingness to provide care, which is influenced by their clinical interest, access to resources, and the practice set-up. Participants highlighted the need for better integration of community and hospital-based care pathways, as well as understanding the psychosocial needs of cancer patients.

items.title: Adolescents' Perspectives on Uptake, Engagement, and Implementation to Inform the Development of a Preventive Transdiagnostic Digital Mental Health Intervention: Qualitative Interview Study.
items.abstract: Adolescence is a critical period for mental health prevention; yet, many young people face barriers to help-seeking, including stigma, limited mental health literacy, and restricted access to services. Preventive digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) offer a scalable, low-threshold approach to early support, but uptake and sustained engagement remain limited. Existing research has predominantly relied on quantitative methods and has only partly captured adolescents' perspectives. Qualitative research is therefore needed to inform the design and implementation of preventive DMHIs. This study aimed to explore adolescents' perspectives on factors influencing the anticipated uptake, expected engagement, and implementation of preventive transdiagnostic DMHIs across person, intervention, and system levels. This qualitative study was conducted in Switzerland using a single-interview design in the predesign phase of the development of a transdiagnostic preventive DMHI. Adolescents aged 12-21 years were recruited through voluntary response sampling via social media and the project website. Semistructured interviews explored experiences with online help-seeking, factors influencing DMHI anticipated uptake and expected engagement, and recommendations for implementation. Interviews were conducted in person or via video call between January and June 2022, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using a hybrid deductive-inductive qualitative content analysis. Intercoder agreement was assessed using Cohen κ (κ=0.72). A total of 48 adolescents (mean age 16.52, SD 2.67 years; 32/48, 72.9% female) participated. In total, 8 main topics and multiple subtopics were identified across person, intervention, system, and cross levels. Person-level factors highlighted the importance of mental health literacy, preuptake communication, and relevance of social networks. Intervention-level factors emphasized usability, personalization, and privacy, while system-level findings reflected expectations for adaptive, integrated, and low-threshold mental health services. Trust and support emerged as cross-level factors for engagement. In addition, participants described several discrepancies between desired intervention characteristics and practical implementation, particularly regarding personalization, anonymity, peer exchange, and human support. Adolescents' perspectives highlight that successful implementation of preventive DMHIs requires attention beyond intervention design to preuptake communication strategies, mental health literacy promotion, and integration within adaptive care systems. The tension between adolescents' desire for immediate human-delivered support and the self-guided nature of preventive DMHIs underscores the need for clear clinical boundaries and explicit escalation pathways.

items.title: A causal account of the neural origins of mental fatigue.
items.abstract: Successful goal-directed behavior often requires the exertion of effortful cognitive control processes, but it remains unclear why engaging in cognitive control is experienced as effortful and induces fatigue. Here, we tested the hypothesis that sustained activation in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC)-a neural substrate of cognitive control-causally induces motivational fatigue via the accumulation of prefrontal glutamate metabolites. For this purpose, we combined brain stimulation with spectroscopy imaging to assess how increasing DLPFC excitability during an effortful mental task changes the motivation for mental effort and glutamate concentrations. We found that stimulating the DLPFC during mental effort exertion improved mental performance at the cost of increased posteffort motivational fatigue, suggesting a causal role of DLPFC activation for inducing fatigue. On the neural level, DLPFC activation during effortful cognition also increased prefrontal concentrations of glutamate, which statistically explained the fatigue-induced lower motivation for mental effort. A corresponding analysis of combined glutamate-glutamine (Glx) concentrations revealed converging effects. Together, these findings provide causal evidence that enhanced DLPFC activation contributes to fatigue via neurochemical changes, supporting neuro-metabolic accounts of fatigue and offering new insights into why demanding cognitive tasks are perceived as effortful.

items.title: Lifetime stressor exposure is associated with altered trust formation and social learning in dynamic interactions.
items.abstract: Although trust is fundamental to social interactions, how lifetime stressor exposure relates to the cognitive processes underlying trust remains poorly understood. Using the Stress and Adversity Inventory (STRAIN) to assess cumulative lifetime stressor exposure, combined with an adaptation of the repeated trust game and computational modeling (Hierarchical Gaussian Filtering), we investigated how stressors experienced over the life course relate to three core aspects of trust dynamics-initial trust formation, learning about others' intentions, and adaptation to changes in trustworthiness-in 168 adults. Greater lifetime stress was associated with stronger negativity biases, lower initial trust, and heightened uncertainty about others' intentions, increases that were general rather than specific to partner type. These more pessimistic priors were not accompanied by poorer reading of partners: Higher lifetime stress was associated with greater differentiation between prosocial and selfish trustees, driven by reduced investment in the selfish trustee alone. Computational analyses further indicated greater belief volatility, consistent with faster model-implied updating of perceived trustworthiness. These findings provide novel evidence that lifetime stress is associated with a profile consistent with recalibration, rather than a degradation, of the cognitive mechanisms underlying trust, with potential consequences for relationship formation and social functioning. They also provide a computationally grounded framework for understanding associations between adversity and social cognition and generate testable predictions for future experimental work.

items.title: Systemic Neglect of Individual-Structure Interplay: Interlevel Cycles of Invisibility, Ignorance, and Denial Perpetuate Racism.
items.abstract: Racism is deeply embedded in American society, yet many Americans fail to recognize its pervasiveness or how interactions between individuals and structures (e.g., policies and institutions) create and sustain it. Among laypeople and perhaps social psychologists, this failure stems from a phenomenon we term "systemic neglect of individual-structure interplay"-a psychological and structural process through which people overlook the dynamic interplay between individual and structural forces that produce and sustain systemic racism. We identify three interconnected mechanisms that perpetuate this neglect: invisibility (failure to perceive systemic racism), ignorance (lack of knowledge and experience), and denial (motivated rejection of racism's systemic nature). These mechanisms create a self-reinforcing cycle that obscures how structures shape individuals and how individuals reproduce those structures. We propose a framework highlighting these reciprocal influences and the consequences of neglecting them, including widespread misunderstanding of racism, misplaced blame, and ineffective interventions. We outline implications for social psychology, arguing that the field would benefit from greater attention to this interplay, as several researchers and theorists have previously recommended. By illuminating the process of systemic neglect, our framework offers a more comprehensive understanding of racism to laypeople and social-psychological researchers alike and identifies key leverage points for social change.

items.title: Engagement-Supportive Mechanisms in Stress-Focused Digital Mental Health Interventions With Adaptive, Conversational, and Context-Aware Systems: Narrative Review.
items.abstract: Stress is a widespread public health concern associated with cardiovascular disease, depression, anxiety, and reduced quality of life. Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs), delivered through smartphones, web platforms, and wearables, offer scalable support for stress management but often struggle to sustain user engagement. Evidence describing how adaptive, conversational, and context-aware mechanisms function together within stress-focused DMHIs remains fragmented. This review aims to synthesize evidence on engagement-supportive mechanisms in stress-focused DMHIs, with attention to personalization; biometric feedback; just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs); gamification; AI, including large language models (LLMs); and methodological approaches to studying engagement. It also examines methodological, motivational, and experiential dimensions of engagement. This narrative review was informed by a structured search of PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Scopus for peer-reviewed studies published between January 2018 and April 2025, followed by an evidence update through August 2026. Eligible studies described stress-focused DMHIs or related affective support interventions reporting at least 1 engagement-supportive mechanism. Randomized controlled trials, qualitative investigations, simulation or modeling studies, and implementation studies were included. Data were extracted using a structured form capturing study characteristics, engagement mechanisms, outcomes, and alignment with the review domains. Descriptive mapping summarized study types and mechanism frequencies, while a narrative synthesis integrated behavioral, experiential, methodological, and theory-informed findings. Thirty-two studies met the inclusion criteria. Randomized or microrandomized controlled trials were the most common design (n=17), followed by qualitative investigations (n=6), design or implementation studies (n=3), mixed methods studies (n=3), simulation or modeling studies (n=2), and a quasi-experimental study (n=1). Dynamic adaptation was identified in 14 studies, conversational support in 10, static tailoring in 9, social or co-design mechanisms in 9, context-aware prompting in 7, gamified reinforcement in 5, biometric-responsive adaptation in 4, and narrative immersion in 2. These mechanisms frequently overlapped within layered adaptive architectures rather than functioning as isolated engagement features. AI-enabled systems included conversational agents, LLM-supported systems, recommender systems, reinforcement learning, and computational modeling approaches. Outcomes included behavioral indicators such as adherence, retention, and prompt receptivity, alongside experiential indicators such as perceived relevance, trust, emotional support, and immersion. Evidence strength varied substantially; many AI-enabled systems contributed feasibility, acceptability, or optimization-oriented evidence rather than definitive comparative effectiveness evidence. Stress-focused DMHIs are increasingly adopting adaptive, conversational, and context-aware engagement-supportive mechanisms, but the evidence base remains heterogeneous and methodologically uneven. Dynamic adaptation, conversational support, and static tailoring were most frequently represented, whereas biometric-responsive adaptation, narrative immersion, and deeply integrated gamified systems were less common. AI-enabled systems may support contextual responsiveness and personalized interaction but require transparent adaptive logic, privacy safeguards, and human-centered evaluation. Future work should prioritize longitudinal, mixed methods research capable of distinguishing behavioral engagement, experiential engagement, feasibility, acceptability, and sustained stress-related outcomes.

items.title: Salivary microbiome, socioeconomic status, and cognitive performance: Triangulating the relationship.
items.abstract: Research increasingly demonstrates that endogenous bacterial communities (microbiomes) are associated with both cognitive functioning and socioeconomic status (SES). In this study, we used a metagenomics approach to characterize oral microbiome diversity in Hispanic and African American children aged 6-16 years. We examined how microbiome composition and SES were related to cognitive performance, as assessed by the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC). Our findings indicate that SES and the microbiome contributed complementary, comparably sized influences on cognitive functioning. Together, variability in conventional SES indicators and microbiome composition accounted for approximately 10% of the variability in WISC scores. These results highlight the importance of integrating both social and biological determinants of health when studying cognitive performance and other psychological outcomes.

items.title: Toward Artificial Intelligence-Supported Development of Image-Based Tasks in Aphasia.
items.abstract: Images play a central role in language assessment and therapy for people with aphasia, yet the development of psychometrically robust image stimuli is often time consuming, costly, and difficult to tailor to specific research questions or individual patient needs. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly text-to-image generation models, offer new opportunities to rapidly produce high-quality, customizable visual stimuli. Despite this potential, methodological guidance for integrating AI-generated images into aphasia research and clinical practice remains limited. This tutorial aimed to provide practical recommendations for the use of AI text-to-image tools in developing image-based tasks for people with aphasia. Using a case study framework, we demonstrate the development of a semantic judgment task with images generated with the help of the DALL-E 3 model. We outline key decision points that went into this process and provide recommendations across the major stages of task development: task conceptualization, stimulus design, image ideation, prompt engineering, and image quality evaluation by AI models. We demonstrate that structured prompt engineering combined with systematic validation can yield high-quality, interpretable image stimuli suitable for aphasia tasks. The approach allows for flexible control over stimulus characteristics while maintaining consistency across experimental conditions. AI text-to-image generation offers a promising, scalable approach to developing customized image stimuli for aphasia research and clinical practice. We discuss methodological considerations, limitations, and future directions for the responsible integration of generative AI technologies into aphasia-related research and clinical applications.

items.title: A longitudinal examination of parental PTSD symptoms, interparental conflict, and child adjustment in military families following parental deployment.
items.abstract: Guided by family systems theory, this longitudinal study examined whether parental posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms, interparental conflict, and children's adjustment are linked in National Guard families. Participants were 159 families from a larger study of one state's National Guard. We examined whether parents' PTSD symptoms reported following return from deployment, and patterns of interparental conflict during the succeeding 12 months were related to children's internalizing and externalizing behaviors at the end of the year. Mixed-effects models estimated intercepts and slopes of interparental conflict, which were incorporated into structural equation models predicting child outcomes while controlling for baseline child behavior and control variables. Service members' PTSD symptoms predicted higher initial levels and increases in self-reported interparental conflict, whereas significant others' PTSD symptoms predicted higher initial levels only. Greater increases in significant others' interparental conflict predicted higher child externalizing behaviors at Time 3 after accounting for baseline externalizing behaviors. Together, these findings provide partial support for a family systems perspective linking parental distress, interparental functioning, and child adjustment. This study underscores the importance of examining trajectories of couple conflict during reintegration and suggests that programming to target interparental conflict in National Guard families may mitigate risk for children's externalizing problems.

items.title: A systematic review exploring conceptualizations and antecedents of high reliability in military contexts: The role of high-reliability followership.
items.abstract: In a world where the military acts as an extension of governments and society, precision and efficiency in military task execution are paramount. Across diverse operational contexts, military personnel are tasked with delivering consistently reliable outcomes, yet the nature of "reliability" - and the factors that enable it - remain unclear. This review synthesizes findings from empirical studies related to High-Reliability Organizations (HROs), military leadership, and social identity to better understand the nature of high reliability as exhibited by military personnel across various contexts. More specifically, it aims to identify and categorize implicit conceptualizations of high reliability within existing research literature, and to examine its antecedents. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyzes 2020 (PRISMA; 2021) guidelines, we systematically reviewed peer-reviewed articles published between 1975 and 2025. Forty-five studies met the inclusion criteria and were retained for synthesis following quality assessment. Analysis suggests that the five principles of High-Reliability Followership provide a useful organizing framework for understanding high-reliability behavior in military contexts. Moreover, these behaviors appear to be shaped by a range of antecedents - many of which are linked to identity leadership and the development of a strong shared social identity within military teams.

items.title: Caring Contacts and Suicidality Among American Indian and Alaska Native Communities: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
items.abstract: For American Indian and Alaska Native communities, connectedness and belonging are strengths that may reduce suicide risk. To evaluate the effectiveness of culturally-adapted Caring Contacts combined with optimal available resources (intervention) compared with optimal available resources alone (control) in reducing suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, and suicide-related hospitalizations. The CARE study was a blinded, 2-group randomized clinical trial conducted between May 2018 and September 2023 among 5 American Indian and Alaska Native communities in Alaska, the Northern Plains, and the Southern Plains, including 4 tribal communities and 1 tribal health organization. Participants were English-speaking adults (age ≥18 years) self-identifying as American Indian or Alaska Native with active suicidality. Analysis was conducted January through April 2024. Caring Contacts is a low-cost intervention via brief, nondemanding messages exclusively focused on expressing care and interest sent by text message or greeting card on a pre-determined schedule over 12 months. Outcomes included suicidal ideation in the past month (measured using the Suicidal Ideation Questionnaire-Junior [SIQ-Jr]), number of suicide attempts, and suicide-related hospitalizations over 12 months. Retention of active suicidality at follow-up was added as an additional outcome. Of 1390 individuals prescreened for eligibility, 1202 consented and were screened for eligibility, and 709 (457 [64.5%] female; mean [SD] age, 35.4 [11.5] years) were enrolled and randomized, including 357 participants in the control group and 352 participants in the Caring Contacts intervention. Most participants (549 [77.4%]) self-identified as American Indian or Alaska Native only, and 160 participants (22.6%) as American Indian or Alaska Native plus another racial group. More than half of participants (392 [55.3%]) were never married. The mean (SD) SIQ-Jr score at baseline was 42.0 (13.8), and 604 participants (85.2%) had ever made a suicide attempt. Overall, 454 participants (64.0%) provided 12-month follow-up data. Between baseline and the 12-month follow-up, both groups showed significant reductions in suicidal ideation (mean [SD] score: Caring Contacts, 41.4 [13.7] vs 22.7 [15.3]; enhanced usual care, 42.5 [13.9] vs 23.1 [14.5]) and participants with a past-year suicide attempt (Caring Contacts, 169 of 352 participants [48.0%] vs 34/240 participants [14.2%]; enhanced usual care 155 of 357 participants [43.4%] vs 39 of 238 participants [16.4%]); however, no statistically significant between-group differences were found. In this randomized clinical trial of culturally adapted Caring Contacts among American Indian or Alaska Native adults with active suicidality, Caring Contacts did not improve suicidal outcomes beyond optimal available resources alone. Similar improvements in both groups may reflect regression to the mean, the therapeutic impact of compassionate baseline engagement with supportive community staff, or the active components of optimal available resources. Further research should explore these dynamics and other culturally grounded interventions. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT02825771.

items.title: The Psychotherapist as Researcher: Ethical Challenges of Writing About Patients in Case Study Research in the South African Context.
items.abstract: Psychotherapy case studies have been proposed as a way of contributing to research, teaching and a practice of psychology that is more responsive to the social and material challenges faced by most South Africans, thereby responding to longstanding critiques of the discipline's inaccessibility and irrelevance and supporting efforts to decolonise it. However, this kind of research raises distinctive ethical challenges in the South African context, which this paper considers. We begin with an overview of the regulatory frameworks governing psychological practice in South Africa and highlight the dual role tensions facing the therapist as researcher. We then discuss the challenges associated with when and how to seek informed consent, which are especially acute in case study research, and in contexts where decision-making is understood in more relational terms. Next, we consider the tension between protecting patients' identities and producing useful, authentic accounts. Finally, we discuss the moral risks and possible harms of this kind of research, including its impact on the therapeutic relationship, stigma-related vulnerabilities and patient/therapist power asymmetries, all of which require careful management to safeguard patients' well-being.

items.title: A Meta-Analysis of Participation in Organized Activities and Academic Outcomes: Implications for Theory, Policy, and Practice.
items.abstract: Organized activities, including after-school programs and extracurricular activities, have been touted as settings that promote youth's academic outcomes. However, no meta-analysis has included both activity types to assess this claim. The purpose of this study was to test associations between activity participation and four academic outcomes. We analyzed the findings of 117 studies released between 2007 and 2024 (k = 327 effect sizes; N = 332,930; 49% girls; 51% White, 41% Black, 22% Latine, and 22% Asian youth; 16% of studies included only children, 74% only adolescents). Participation was associated with higher grades (g = 0.33), test scores (g = 0.19), and educational attainment (g = 0.39), but not school attendance (g = 0.13). Effects were stronger for academic grades (p < 0.05) and test scores (p = 0.05) for school-based activities than community-based activities; however, effects for grades and test scores did not vary by participant age, family income, activity focus, or activity setting. These findings demonstrate that participating in organized activities is associated with youth's short- and long-term academic outcomes, supporting the proposition that organized activities are a primary microsystem that warrants continued research to identify under what conditions and for whom organized activities are most effective.

items.title: Longitudinal Associations between Children's Executive Functioning and Problem Behaviors: An Examination of Gender Differences.
items.abstract: Theory and research suggest close links between executive functioning and children's problem behaviors. However, evidence regarding the direction of these developmental pathways remains mixed, and whether the longitudinal associations differ between boys and girls is unclear. To address these gaps, the present study used cross-lagged panel models to examine longitudinal associations between three subcomponents of executive functioning (inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility) and internalizing and externalizing problems separately among boys and girls. Participants were 621 children (MageT1 = 9.84 years, 51.4% girls) in Grades 1-5 from a public elementary school, who completed assessments at baseline (T1) and 6 months later (T2). Among boys, higher working memory and cognitive flexibility at T1 predicted fewer externalizing problems at T2; neither internalizing nor externalizing problems at T1 predicted any subcomponent of executive functioning at T2. Among girls, higher inhibitory control and cognitive flexibility at T1 predicted fewer internalizing and externalizing problems at T2, whereas working memory at T1 predicted fewer externalizing problems only. More externalizing problems at T1 also predicted lower cognitive flexibility at T2 among girls. Only the path from inhibitory control to later externalizing problems differed significantly between boys and girls. These findings indicate component- and outcome-specific prospective associations, with more limited evidence of gender-specific pathways. They also identify executive functioning as a potentially useful target for efforts to reduce vulnerability to problem behaviors in school-age children, although the observational design does not establish causal effects.

items.title: Refining Hopelessness Theory: A Longitudinal Investigation of Depressive Symptoms, Loneliness, and Hopelessness in Emerging Adults.
items.abstract: Hopelessness theory has traditionally conceptualized hopelessness as a cognitive vulnerability for depressive symptoms, yet the relationship may be more dynamic, with depressive symptoms also contributing to subsequent hopelessness and interpersonal processes potentially shaping this association. The present study examined the bidirectional within-person associations among depressive symptoms, hopelessness, and loneliness, as well as the potential mediating role of loneliness. Participants were 1,154 Chinese college students (Mage = 18.53 years, SDage = 0.74; 58.67% female), contributing 4,616 person-wave observations across four waves collected at six-month intervals. The Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (RI-CLPM) was used to isolate within-person dynamics. Results revealed consistent bidirectional within-person associations between depressive symptoms and hopelessness across the three consecutive lagged intervals. Evidence for an indirect effect through loneliness was observed for the pathway from depressive symptoms at T2 to hopelessness at T4 through loneliness at T3, whereas the corresponding earlier indirect effect and both reverse indirect effects were nonsignificant. Model comparisons indicated that the cross-lagged coefficients were not invariant across the three six-month intervals, and the freely estimated model was therefore retained. These findings support a reciprocal within-person association between depressive symptoms and hopelessness and provide partial evidence that loneliness may contribute to the progression from depressive symptoms to later hopelessness during emerging adulthood.

items.title: Associations between nonfatal strangulation-related brain injury in intimate partner violence and resting-state functional connectivity.
items.abstract: Examine the association between nonfatal strangulation-related probable brain injury (NFS-BI), resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC), and verbal memory, among females who experienced physical intimate partner violence (IPV). Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging was analyzed for 110 females aged 18-60 years who experienced physical IPV. rsFC was characterized by seven graph theory metrics across three brain parcellation atlases (Power, Seitzman, and Schaefer-456 Parcellation[4S]). Responses to the Brain Injury Screening Questionnaire determined IPV-head trauma frequency, experience of probable NFS-BI, and other/additional non-IPV and IPV-related BI. Verbal memory was characterized by three measures from the California Verbal Learning Test, Third Edition: (a) Long Delay, Free Recall, (b) Trials 1-5 correct index scores, and (c) memory retention from Trials 1-5 to Long Delay, Free Recall. NFS-BI was significantly associated with reductions in within-default mode network (DMN) connectivity (Power: B = -0.03, p = .003; Seitzman: B = -0.03, p = .005; 4S: B = -0.02, p = .03), DMN segregation (Power: B = -0.04, p = .006; Seitzman: B = -0.04, p = .007; 4S: B = -0.03, p = .02), and global modularity (Power: B = -0.01, p = .02; Seitzman: B = -0.02, p = .008; 4S: B = -0.02, p = .007). Interactions between NFS-BI and within-DMN strength (Power: B = -150.05, p = .03; Seitzman: B = -212.11 p = .01; 4S: B = -204.52, p = .002), DMN segregation (Power: B = -106.97, p = .02; Seitzman: B = -114.54 p = .008; 4S: B = -189.88, p < .001), and modularity (Power: B = -373.80, p = .003; Seitzman: B = -367.35, p = .001; 4S: B = -312.55, p = .006) were significantly associated with memory retention. Those who experienced probable NFS-BI demonstrated altered rsFC compared with those who did not. Interactions between DMN rsFC and NFS-BI were significantly associated with memory retention. Future work should assess individuals with NFS-BI longitudinally to understand its effects on long-term brain health. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: From interpersonal trauma to psychopathology: Self-compassion and shame in a sequential mediation model.
items.abstract: Existing research suggests that trauma type, self-compassion, and shame have important implications in the development of psychopathology following trauma exposure. However, the interplay between these factors is not well understood. The present study investigated whether self-compassion and shame sequentially mediate the association between trauma type and a latent factor of posttrauma psychopathology. Using cross-sectional data from 200 female undergraduates with reported trauma exposure, the present study investigated associations between trauma type, Life Events Checklist for Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition; classified into interpersonal (1) vs. noninterpersonal (0) trauma, shame (Experience of Shame Scale), and self-compassion (Self-Compassion Scale-Short Form) on a latent psychopathology factor, modeled as posttraumatic stress (Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Checklist for Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition), depression, and anxiety (Depression Anxiety Stress Scale-21). A structural equation model with 5,000 bootstrapped iterations revealed that self-compassion mediated the relationship between trauma type and shame (β = 0.12, p = .007), which had a stronger relationship with psychopathology (β = 0.56, p < .001) than did trauma type (β = 0.11, p = .03) or self-compassion (β = -0.23, p = .003) alone. This study highlights the importance of addressing self-compassion and shame in the relationship between interpersonal trauma exposure and trauma-related psychopathology among young adult women. items.title: Understanding post-9/11 U.S. veterans' perspectives on moral injury: An exploratory study.
items.abstract: Research on moral injury (MI) continues to grow despite a lack of consensus definition, and qualitative, exploratory studies can enable further construct clarification. This study sought to understand how post-9/11 veterans perceive MI and how these perceptions impact their responses to existing measures of MI. Twelve veterans completed a cognitive interview utilizing the Moral Injury Questionnaire-Military Version and the Expressions of Moral Injury Scale-Military Version. Using thematic analysis, qualitative data were coded and analyzed for their connection or divergence to existing theoretical frameworks of MI. Veterans' narratives focused on themes of institutional betrayal, collective betrayal, and discharge as a betrayal-based potentially morally injurious experience. Some veterans did not perceive experiences to be morally injurious if they happened outside of combat. Other veterans perceived the construct as too narrow in scope to account for what they considered morally injurious. Further construct clarification is needed to determine betrayal's role in MI. Definitions and conceptualizations of MI may need to expand to be inclusive of experiences of betrayal that do not come from high-stakes situations or explicitly distinguish MI from other constructs such as institutional betrayal. Veterans' perceptions that MI is primarily based in combat experiences has significant implications for adequately capturing and assessing MI. items.title: Retrospective exploratory mixed methods study on the implementation of reconsolidation therapy among exiled patients.
items.abstract: Reconsolidation therapy (RT)-Brunet method-has shown promising efficacy in reducing posttraumatic symptoms in adults with posttraumatic stress disorder. Yet its use among forcibly displaced individuals, who frequently present with complex trauma, chronic insecurity, and substantial contextual barriers, remains understudied. Exploring RT in this context represents a promising avenue for improving access to brief and structured trauma therapies in global mental health. This study examined how RT was implemented among exiled individuals receiving routine care in a health care center in France and assessed its impact on traumatic symptoms. Additional aims included exploring symptom trajectories and identifying key patient- and clinician-related factors influencing treatment delivery and outcomes. We conducted a retrospective mixed methods exploratory study using clinical data from exiled adults treated with RT. Quantitative analyses examined changes in trauma-related symptoms across sessions. Qualitative analyses explored clinician's observations, perceived barriers, and contextual adaptations used to facilitate treatment delivery. Patients showed overall reductions in posttraumatic stress disorder symptoms, although trajectories varied according to individual circumstances, trauma complexity, and contextual stressors. Clinician reported frequent real-world adaptations, including original mismatch strategies, adjustments to session structure, and linguistic accommodation within the French clinical context. Several factors, such as administrative instability, chronic stress exposure, and comorbid symptoms, appeared to shape engagement and outcomes. RT can be feasibly delivered to exiled individuals, even when they face unstable living conditions and multiple past traumatic experiences. These findings offer preliminary insights into mechanisms of engagement and response within this population and provide guidance for refining procedures and measurement strategies in future research. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Psychometric properties of the International Trauma Questionnaire-Child and Adolescent Version (ITQ-CA) among Portuguese adolescents from the community.
items.abstract: The International Trauma Questionnaire (ITQ) was developed to assess International Classification of Diseases-11th Revision posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and complex PTSD. Although extensively validated in adults across diverse contexts, evidence for the child and adolescent version (ITQ-CA) is still limited. Few studies have examined its latent structure or validity in youth, and none have validated it in Portuguese adolescents. Moreover, measurement invariance across sex has not yet been established in this age group, despite documented sex differences in trauma exposure and symptom expression. This study aimed to evaluate the psychometric properties of the ITQ-CA in Portuguese adolescents by testing factorial structure, internal consistency, convergent and discriminant validity, and measurement invariance across sex. A school-based sample of 530 adolescents (11-16 years) completed the ITQ-CA and measures of trauma exposure, PTSD symptoms, emotion dysregulation, and resilience. Confirmatory factor analyses compared four latent structures and tested measurement invariance across sex (configural, metric, scalar). Convergent and discriminant validity were assessed using average variance extracted and composite reliability and Pearson correlations. The correlated six-factor model showed the best fit. Full configural, metric, and scalar invariance supported cross-sex comparability. Convergent validity was adequate, and discriminant validity was supported by the Fornell-Larcker criterion and external patterns, with disturbances in self-organization factors showing stronger associations with dysregulation and resilience than PTSD factors. Internal consistency was acceptable to good. The ITQ-CA is a reliable, valid, and sex-invariant measure of International Classification of Diseases-11th Revision PTSD and disturbances in self-organization in Portuguese adolescents, with practical utility for research and rapid screening in schools and community services. items.title: Developing an efficient personalized therapist fit index to optimize psychotherapy case assignments.
items.abstract: Psychotherapists vary in their effectiveness, with differences being more pronounced for certain patients. These therapist effectiveness data can plausibly inform treatment personalization. For example, predictive analytics can determine which patients-based on their presenting characteristics-are more likely to improve when treated by a historically effective clinician and which are likely to improve regardless of who treats them. Accordingly, this study first developed a personalized therapist fit (PTF) index. Second, we examined whether patients who had been naturalistically assigned to a PTF-recommended therapist had better treatment outcomes. Patients were 2,160 adults treated by 72 therapists. We used outcomes data from a first patient wave to classify therapists as highly effective (top third of the sample based on their average patient's improvement and percentage of their patients who reliably improved) or average/below average (middle or bottom third of the sample on at least one of these indices). With a second patient wave, machine learning predicted which patients would have better outcomes when working with a highly effective therapist versus comparable outcomes when working with any therapist. Finally, with a third wave of patients, we examined the stability of the PTF algorithm and the effect of being naturalistically matched to a PTF-recommended therapist. Therapists' effectiveness level and patients' PTF were moderately stable and reliably estimated across the training and hold-out samples. Moreover, patients matched versus unmatched to their PTF had better outcomes (d = 0.48). Results preliminarily establish an efficient, effective, and readily scalable form of personalized case assignment. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Mastery motivation and executive control as predictors of health self-management in adolescents and young adults with cerebral palsy or myelomeningocele.
items.abstract: To examine mastery motivation and executive control as predictors of health self-management behaviors in adolescents and young adults with congenital neurodevelopmental conditions. Participants were two groups of adolescents and young adults, ages 13-29 years, with potential for independent living, including 49 with cerebral palsy and 39 with spina bifida myelomeningocele living with a parent/caregiver. Participants were administered measures of mastery motivation, executive control (executive functions and executive behaviors), and health self-management. Group differences in mastery motivation and executive control were not significant. Self-reported health self-management was higher in the group with spina bifida myelomeningocele, but group differences in parent ratings of self-management were not significant. Mastery motivation and executive control explained significant portions of variance in aspects of health self-management. There was evidence that executive behaviors mediated the association between mastery motivation and specific self-management behaviors. Results indicate that mastery motivation and executive control are significant predictors of health self-management in transition-age youth with congenital neurodevelopmental conditions. Findings highlight the importance of assessing and addressing motivational and executive needs in developing interventions to promote specific health self-management behaviors. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Self-esteem and social relationships: A meta-analytic review of longitudinal studies with continuous time modeling.
items.abstract: This preregistered systematic review investigated reciprocal effects between people's self-esteem and the quality of their social relationships by meta-analyzing the available longitudinal data. Analyses were based on 82 samples, including 86,850 participants. Mean age of samples ranged from 8 to 63 years. We used continuous time modeling to account for between-study differences in the time intervals between assessments, which ranged from 1 week to 6 years. Moreover, we controlled for stable between-person variance in the constructs via latent trait variables. The results showed positive cross-lagged effects between self-esteem and relationship quality. The effects peaked at an interval of approximately 3 months, with medium to large effect sizes of β = .13 for the effect of self-esteem on relationship quality and β = .09 for the effect of relationship quality on self-esteem. The effects had largely faded after 1 year. We tested for moderator effects of type of relationship partner, age, proportion of female participants, cultural context, and type of relationship measure. Cross-lagged effects were largest for general social relationships, followed by relationships with parents, but were smaller and close to zero for peer and romantic relationships. Age, proportion of female participants, and cultural context showed significant effects, but the magnitude of these moderator effects was small. The effects also differed by type of relationship measure, with self-reports showing larger effects than other measures. In sum, the findings support theories that emphasize the importance of social relationships for self-esteem and theories suggesting that people's self-esteem shapes the quality of their relationships. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: The second-language word age of acquisition effect and its relation to first-language word age of acquisition: Evidence from multitask megastudies.
items.abstract: Megastudies were used in the present research in order to systematically explore the age of acquisition (AoA) effect in second-language (L2) lexical processing and its relationship with the AoA of the corresponding first-language (L1) translation equivalents. To capture different levels of processing, we conducted three experiments using large-scale lexical stimuli: a letter search task for orthographic processing (Experiment 1), a lexical naming task for phonological processing (Experiment 2), and a personal name judgment task for semantic processing (Experiment 3). As a critical supplement to those megastudies, Experiment 4 employed a more typical semantic categorization task (living or nonliving semantic judgment) to induce deeper semantic engagement. The results showed that the L2 AoA effect was reliable and independent of L1 AoA at the orthographic and phonological levels. This pattern further extended to shallow semantic processing, where the L2 AoA effect remained evident regardless of L1 AoA. However, at deeper levels of semantic processing, the effect was modulated by L1 AoA: The L2 AoA effect appeared only when the L1 translation equivalent was acquired early. We propose a theoretical framework, the independence-dependence dual-path model, to help account for the L2 AoA effect. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Assessing the "epileptic personality".
items.abstract: This article traces the historical development, conceptualization, and assessment of the theory of the epileptic personality, with particular attention to the contributions of Hermann Rorschach, Françoise Minkowska, and Leopold Szondi. The theory of the epileptic personality characterized individuals with epilepsy by heightened emotionality, difficulties in social adaptation, egocentricity, sexual deviance, increased aggression and violence, and, in many cases, pronounced susceptibility to religious experience. As a rich and long-standing component of 19th-century medical thought, the theory of the epileptic personality continued to exert influence well into the 20th century, including its impact on the development of personality assessment tools. Rorschach and Szondi explicitly assessed the notion of the epileptic personality through their respective tests. Subsequent research has, however, demonstrated that neither instrument measures a personality uniquely linked to epilepsy; rather, both capture broader psychodynamic patterns. The historical persistence of the theory of the epileptic personality reflects the influence of constitutional frameworks and their potential for stigmatization, offering enduring insights into the complex interplay among psychiatry, psychology, psychometrics, and medical and social perceptions. items.title: Speech categorization consistency is robustly associated with receptive oral language performance.
items.abstract: Speech perception research on individual differences and clinical populations has traditionally emphasized the gradient/categorical dimension of categorization. Recent work, however, highlights categorization consistency-trial-by-trial response variability-as a more informative index of individual differences. Whether this index is relevant for language functions remains unknown. Across three experiments, we tested whether speech categorization consistency, rather than gradiency, was associated with receptive oral language ability. In Experiment 1, English-speaking adults (n = 57) completed a speech visual analog scaling task, rating a speech continuum on a continuous scale, alongside two language assessments. Greater consistency in speech categorization was strongly associated with better receptive oral language performance, whereas gradiency showed no such relationship. Experiment 2 (n = 76) added a visual analog scaling task in which participants performed the same task with a visual continuum to determine whether the observed effects reflected domain-general categorization mechanisms. Speech consistency again showed a strong association with language ability, and commonality analyses indicated that this effect was largely unique to speech, not to visual consistency. Experiment 3 (n = 95) equated the number of speech and visual continua and added a nonverbal IQ measure. Despite shared variance across domains, speech categorization consistency retained a unique association with language performance beyond visual categorization consistency and nonverbal IQ. These findings suggest that categorization consistency reflects both domain-general and speech-specific components, with speech consistency showing the most robust relationship to receptive oral language performance. This reframes individual differences in speech categorization by highlighting categorization consistency as an important dimension linking perceptual processing and broader language function. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Effects of a jail-adapted dialectical behavioral therapy skills group on in-custody outcomes and reentry preparedness: A randomized controlled trial.
items.abstract: People who are involved in the criminal-legal system often experience difficulty regulating emotions, refraining from impulsive behaviors, and communicating effectively. Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), particularly the skills training group component, may be well-suited to address the risks and needs of correctional populations, but adaptations of DBT in these settings have outpaced rigorous evidence for their effectiveness. This gap is especially notable in short-term jail detention settings, underscoring the need for large-scale randomized evaluations of DBT skills groups on both psychological outcomes and prerelease readiness among jail inmates. The current preregistered randomized controlled trial evaluated the effects of a jail-adapted DBT skills group on in-custody changes in coping, psychiatric symptoms, and jail misconduct and on reentry-related preparedness. Participants were 640 individuals (83% male, 69.2% White, 13.8% Hispanic) incarcerated in a county jail randomized to receive a 12-session DBT skills group or control treatment. They completed baseline and prerelease assessments of relevant outcomes. Small effects of DBT were observed for improved adaptive coping, decreased antisocial behavior in custody, and positive perceptions of reentry capabilities and support. Findings from the present study highlight the insights gleaned from examining effects of DBT group treatment in regard to both behavioral outcomes and expectations for reentry. items.title: Nonbirthing parents, paid parental leave, and the lived experience: A qualitative analysis of military parents.
items.abstract: In 2023, the Department of Defense expanded its parental leave policy, authorizing birthing and nonbirthing parents 12 weeks of paid leave, though attitudes and experiences of nonbirthing parents remain unknown. Using a qualitative reflexive thematic analysis, we examined the parental leave experience of active-duty nonbirthing parents. Among 14 participating parents, most were male (78.6%), White (85.7%), officers (71.4%), had two or more children (57.1%), served in the U.S. Navy (57.1%), and the average length of service was 9.3 years (SD = 3.6 years). Most participants took their entire leave entitlement of 12 weeks (71.4%), and leave was primarily taken in increments (78.6%). The reflexive thematic analysis resulted in an overarching theme, "Enough Time to Pause, Parent, and Proceed." This overarching theme comprised of three interdependent themes, with subthemes: (a) factors influencing leave entitlement usage (subthemes: "command responsibilities," "flexibility," "command support," and "stigma"); (b) family experiences while on leave (subthemes: "hands-on parenting: bonding, learning, and growth," "family bonding beyond the newborn," "parenthood and partnership"); and (c) readiness (subthemes: "personal readiness," "family readiness"). The findings from this study expand our understanding of nonbirthing parents paid parental leave experience, and how it impacted themselves, their family, and their return to military duty. items.title: Exploring the associations between internalized racial oppression, emotional eating, and mental health symptoms among Black young adult women.
items.abstract: We tested the cross-sectional association between internalized racial oppression and (a) depression symptoms and (b) anxiety symptoms among Black young adult women, as well as the moderating role of emotional eating in these associations. We hypothesized that (a) more internalized racial oppression would be associated with worse depression and anxiety symptoms and (b) greater engagement in emotional eating would exacerbate the association between internalized racial oppression and depression and anxiety symptoms. Five hundred four Black young adult women (aged 18-35 years; Mage = 24.72, SDage = 4.89; 98.4% cisgender) completed an online survey. More internalized racial oppression was associated with worse depression and anxiety symptoms. Engaging in emotional eating did not significantly moderate either direct association. However, more engagement in emotional eating was directly associated with worse depression and anxiety symptoms. Findings provide cross-sectional evidence of the mental health implications of internalized racial oppression. Emotional eating may not worsen mental health symptoms when Black women are faced with internalized racial oppression. Behavioral interventionists may consider this initial evidence in addressing sociocultural and behavioral risk factors for mental health and find ways to target different factors simultaneously. items.title: What works, what doesn't, and why we can't tell the difference: Contextualizing evidence-based practice in public education and school psychology.
items.abstract: Public schools are charged with educating every child who enters them under a legal and ethical mandate that practice be grounded in evidence, yet the gap between that mandate and routine practice remains substantial across public education. Using school psychology as a case study, we argue that evidence-based practice's persistent failure to close this gap reflects a mismatch between the inherited framework and the structural and institutional conditions of public education rather than practitioner values alone. Six interrelated failures are documented: conflation of evidence-based practice as a decision-making model with specific intervention adoption; inconsistent evidentiary standards; demographic mismatch between research samples and served populations; commercial capture of the evidence infrastructure; failures of contextual fit and transportability; and the absence of mechanisms for discontinuing ineffective practices. These failures persist through professional ossification and school psychology's location within education bureaucracies. In response, we propose an epistemological architecture adapted from evidence-based public health, operationalized here as the evidence-based school psychology model, with a three-level evidentiary sequence that provides the de-implementation mechanism the current framework structurally lacks. We offer recommendations for practitioners, trainers, and researchers to operationalize this model in practice. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: What do we know about job knowledge tests? A 30-year update of validity evidence.
items.abstract: Job knowledge tests (JKTs) are widely used for selection and promotion, as well as for certification in professions such as law, medicine, and education. Yet evidence regarding the criterion-related validity of JKTs is based primarily on a brief meta-analysis published more than 30 years ago (Dye et al., 1993). The present study provides an updated meta-analysis of JKT validity data. Analyses based on 122 studies revealed mean operational validity estimates of .28 for job performance (k = 84, N = 25,468, SDr = .12), .36 for training performance (k = 39, N = 123,845, SDr = .00), and -.06 for turnover (k = 12, N = 18,349, SDr = .03). Importantly, operational validities for job performance were larger for job-specific JKTs (.34) than for nonjob-specific tests (.19) and when the criteria included job knowledge (.41) than when they did not (.22). In addition, JKTs administered to job applicants (.32) or current employees (.29) in organizational settings were associated with higher validity than tests administered to people seeking certification in their chosen field (.20). Finally, we tested the mediating role of job knowledge between other antecedents and job performance. Job knowledge statistically fully mediated the relationship between cognitive ability and job performance, partially mediated the relationship between job experience and performance, and did not mediate the relationship between conscientiousness and performance. Overall, these results provide a contemporary synthesis of validity evidence for JKTs in various situations, as well as the role job knowledge plays in other predictors of job performance. items.title: Within-couple longitudinal associations between functional disability and depressive symptoms among Chinese older couples over four years.
items.abstract: Functional disability and depressive symptoms are pressing public health challenges in China's aging society. This study examined their longitudinal associations within older couples. Dyadic data from the first three waves of the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (2011-2015) were analyzed using cross-lagged actor-partner interdependence models. Functional disability was assessed using Basic Activities of Daily Living (BADL) and Instrumental Activities of Daily Living (IADL) scales. Depressive symptoms were assessed using the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale. The BADL and IADL models included 1,159 and 1,724 dyads, respectively. Functional disability and depressive symptoms were stable over time for both spouses. Within-person associations were generally bidirectional, except that wives' BADL disability did not predict their later depressive symptoms. Depressive symptoms also predicted partners' later depressive symptoms in both directions. Three cross-domain partner associations were significant in the primary analyses, but several actor and partner associations became nonsignificant in complete-case analyses. Functional disability and depressive symptoms were longitudinally interrelated within older Chinese couples. Some associations were sensitive to the treatment of missing data and warrant cautious interpretation. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Post-ovipositional staging series of the foveate, gold-dust day gecko, Phelsuma laticauda (Gekkota: Squamata).
items.abstract: Disorders affecting the fovea, a specialized pit in the human retina necessary for high acuity vision, represent a significant healthcare burden across the globe. Degenerative diseases (e.g., macular degeneration) and developmental conditions (e.g., albinism and aniridia) affecting the fovea can lead to irreversible, central vision loss. These conditions are challenging to study because commonly used laboratory animal models lack a fovea. Many day geckos have a fovea and are easy to care for, however, they lack a complete embryonic staging series. We established a breeding colony of the gold-dust day gecko, Phelsuma laticauda, and generated post-ovipositional embryonic staging series chronicling changes in body and eye morphology throughout gestation. P. laticauda undergoes early asymmetric ocular remodeling and the prospective foveal region transiently elongates and retracts during the final third of embryonic development, a progression consistent with other foveate lizards and humans. These findings support day geckos as a promising model for understanding foveal development and potentially relevant disease pathways.
