items.title: Changes in Demographic and Clinical Characteristics of MuSK Myasthenia Gravis.
items.abstract: Background Over the last two decades, an increasing number of late- and very-late onset myasthenia gravis cases (VLOMG) with acetylcholine receptor antibodies (AChR-MG) have been reported, whereas demographic studies on muscle-specific tyrosine kinase antibodies MG (MuSK-MG) are lacking. We investigated whether the proportion of patients with MuSK-MG with onset ≥ 50 years has increased and whether these patients show distinct clinical characteristics. Methods We retrospectively enrolled consecutive patients with MuSK-MG onset ≥ 16 years followed between 1980 and 2025 at our tertiary center. Demographic characteristics and maximum disease severity, classified according to Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America classification, were analyzed. Patients were stratified into three age-at-onset subgroups. Results Overall, 120 patients were included. A significant increase in the median age at MuSK-MG onset was observed, from 36 years (IQR, 23-45.75) in the 1980s to 47 years (IQR, 29-69) in the 2013-2025 period (p = 0.033). Patients with onset ≥ 50 years increased from 2/17 (11.8%) to 19/39 (48.7%) (p = 0.015), including 12 VLOMG cases. Males increased from 23.5% to 35.9%. Maximum MG severity decreased over time, with a remarkable reduction of respiratory crises (p = 0.004), with no significant differences across age-at-onset groups. Conclusions Demographic changes observed in AChR-MG also occur, though less prominently, in MuSK-MG.

items.title: STWO_GDSNet: Supercell Thunderstorm Wind Optimization-Based Gated Dual-Stream Convolutional Neural Network for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection.
items.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) affects social interaction and behaviour in children. Current diagnostic methods largely depend on clinical observation and standardized assessments, which can be subjective, time-intensive and influenced by the experience of evaluator. Here, STWO_GDSNet is devised for detecting ASD. Firstly, input image is sent to image pre-preparation, where image is denoised by anisotropic diffusion Kuwahara filtering (ADKF), followed by N4 bias field correction. Next, based on functional connectivity, the pivotal region is extracted by STWO that combines supercell thunderstorm algorithm (STA) and leaf in wind optimization (LiWO). After that, multiscale triangle descriptor (MTD) is extracted in descriptor computation phase. Subsequently, the input autism data are pre-prepared by normalization and standardization. Next, analysis of variance (ANOVA) method conducts attribute pruning, and extracted features as well as the pruned data are passed to gated dual-stream convolutional neural network (GDSNet) for detecting ASD. Here, GDSNet is trained by STWO that incorporates STA and LiWO. The efficacy of STWO_GDSNet is examined by considering accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, which yield maximal values of 96.24%, 95.99% and 96.61%.

items.title: COVID-19 Vaccination and the Risk of Migraine Chronification: A Comparative Cohort Study of Vaccinated and Unvaccinated Patients With Episodic Migraine.
items.abstract: Introduction Headache is among the most frequently reported adverse events after COVID-19 vaccination, and patients with migraine often fear that vaccination will worsen their disease or accelerate the transition from episodic to chronic migraine. Controlled data comparing vaccinated and unvaccinated patients with migraine are scarce. Methods We conducted a comparative prospective cohort study of 60 adults with pre-existing episodic migraine, classified at enrolment as vaccinated (n = 30) or unvaccinated (n = 30) against COVID-19, at a single neuroscience clinic in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, and followed for 6 months. Migraine status (episodic or chronic, per ICHD-3) was assessed at 3 and 6 months. Between-group chronification was compared using Fisher's exact test with odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs); patient-level transitions were also examined. No a priori sample-size calculation was performed. Results There were no statistically significant baseline differences between groups in age (30.3 ± 5.07 vs. 30.5 ± 4.46 years; p = 0.87), sex (p = 0.78), or preventive medication (p = 0.58). Provisional chronic-frequency status was recorded in 5/30 vaccinated versus 11/30 unvaccinated patients at 3 months (OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.10-1.16; p = 0.14), and chronic migraine in 3/30 versus 6/30 at 6 months (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.10-1.97; p = 0.47). All such transitions occurred by 3 months, with no new cases between 3 and 6 months; the confidence intervals were wide and included no difference. Conclusions In this small observational cohort, no statistically significant association was detected between COVID-19 vaccination and migraine chronification. The wide confidence intervals preclude firm conclusions regarding either harm or benefit, and larger, adequately powered studies are needed.

items.title: Opioid Modulation of Major Neurotransmitter Systems: Acute, Chronic, and Withdrawal Effects.
items.abstract: Opioids are widely used in clinical practice for the management of moderate-to-severe acute and chronic pain. However, their use is associated with the development of tolerance and physical dependence, often followed by a withdrawal syndrome upon discontinuation. The mechanisms underlying opioid dependence and withdrawal are highly complex and remain incompletely understood. These processes involve multiple regions of the central nervous system and are accompanied by widespread alterations in neuronal signaling pathways. Neurotransmitters, which are essential for communication between neurons, play a critical role in opioid addiction and withdrawal. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the major neurotransmitter systems, their involvement, and the changes that occur during acute and chronic opioid exposure. Particular attention is also given to the consequences of opioid discontinuation. Overall, this review summarizes current knowledge of the molecular mechanisms underlying both the acute and long-term effects of opioids on key neurotransmitter systems in the brain.

items.title: Timing Matters: Cross-Codal Integration of Bridging Event Information Happens While Viewing Picture Stories.
items.abstract: Despite the prevalence of multi-codal narratives-such as comics consisting of pictures and text-in everyday life, little is understood about how individuals integrate information across different codalities to form cohesive mental representations. In the present study, we explored when processing costs emerged during cross-codal integration of bridging event information in multi-codal narratives. Participants were presented with uni-codal (i.e., consisting only of pictures or of text) and multi-codal stories in which the bridging event information was presented in the other codality. We measured viewing times for the bridging event and end-state panels to reflect the cognitive costs associated with integration. The results showed a significant interaction between codality switch and panel position. While the presence of a codality switch increased viewing times for both panel positions, there was a much larger increase for the bridging event panel than the end-state panel. This result supports a hypothesis suggesting that during narrative understanding, information of a different codality is integrated into the mental representation of the narrative upon encountering it. Our results underscore the influence of codality on narrative integration, indicating that understanding may be affected by the format in which information is presented. Future models of event cognition should incorporate codality as a factor in narrative comprehension.

items.title: Morinda Officinalis Oligosaccharides Alleviate Post-Stroke Depression-Like Behaviors Alongside Increased Gut Microbial Diversity and Butyrate Levels and Reduced Hippocampal Pla2g4a Expression.
items.abstract: Background and purpose Post-stroke depression (PSD) represents a common and debilitating complication after cerebral ischemia, yet mechanism-based therapies remain an urgent unmet need. The microbiota-gut-brain axis has been implicated in PSD pathophysiology, but the precise molecular pathways are largely elusive. Morinda officinalis oligosaccharides (MOO), a clinically approved antidepressant in China, exhibit poor oral absorption, raising the possibility of a gut-dependent mechanism. Experimental approach Male C57BL/6J mice were subjected to transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) followed by 21 days of chronic restraint stress (CRS) to establish a PSD model. MOO (50 mg/kg/day) was administered via gavage from Day 7 to 27. Depression-like behaviors, 16S rRNA-based gut microbiota profiling, short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) quantification, intestinal and blood-brain barrier integrity assessments, and hippocampal proteomics were performed. The transferability of MOO-associated fecal effects was assessed using a donor-controlled fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) design. The butyrate-Pla2g4a relationship was further examined by sodium butyrate supplementation and AAV-mediated hippocampal Pla2g4a overexpression. Key results MOO administration altered gut microbial composition, increased the abundance of probiotics and decreased the abundance of harmful bacteria, and was accompanied by increased fecal butyrate levels. The donor-controlled FMT experiment provided preliminary evidence that fecally transferable factors from MOO-treated PSD donors may contribute to behavioral improvements in PSD recipients. MOO and sodium butyrate treatment were associated with improved indices of intestinal and blood-brain barrier integrity. Hippocampal proteomics identified Pla2g4a, a phospholipase linked to neuroinflammation, as a candidate molecule related to the observed effects. Both MOO and sodium butyrate treatment were associated with reduced hippocampal Pla2g4a expression, and Pla2g4a expression was inversely correlated with butyrate levels. Hippocampal Pla2g4a overexpression attenuated the behavioral improvements associated with sodium butyrate treatment, supporting the functional involvement of Pla2g4a in the response to sodium butyrate. Conclusions and implications MOO treatment was associated with improved depression-like behaviors in PSD mice, accompanied by gut microbial alterations, increased fecal butyrate, improved barrier integrity, and reduced hippocampal Pla2g4a expression. FMT findings provided preliminary evidence that fecally transferable factors from MOO-treated donors may contribute to behavioral improvements, while Pla2g4a overexpression attenuated the behavioral effects of sodium butyrate. These findings highlight a potential association among MOO, gut-derived butyrate, barrier integrity, and hippocampal Pla2g4a in PSD.

items.title: Emotional, Behavioural and Social Correlates in Subthreshold and Full-Syndrome ADHD.
items.abstract: Subthreshold attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ST-ADHD) describes individuals who exhibit clinically significant symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity or impulsivity without meeting full diagnostic criteria for ADHD. Despite its subclinical status, ST-ADHD may be associated with substantial emotional, behavioural and social impairment. This study aimed to compare children and adolescents with ST-ADHD and full-syndrome ADHD in terms of emotional and behavioural difficulties and psychiatric comorbidities. This cross-sectional retrospective study included 217 patients with full-syndrome ADHD and 111 with ST-ADHD. Emotional, behavioural and social functioning were assessed using the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ). Group differences were evaluated after controlling for potential confounding factors, including age, sex and education level. Interaction analyses were also performed to examine whether these differences varied by age or sex. Age distributions were comparable between the groups, although sex ratios and education levels differed. Psychiatric comorbidity was more prevalent in the ADHD group than in the ST-ADHD group (74.2% vs. 60.4%, p = 0.010). In covariate-adjusted analyses, hyperactivity/inattention scores remained significantly higher in the ADHD group, whereas emotional problems, conduct problems and peer-related difficulties did not differ significantly between the groups. Formal interaction analyses did not show significant Group × Age or Group × Sex effects. The observed functional difficulties and relatively high comorbidity rates suggest that ST-ADHD may represent a clinically relevant condition and that a dimensional assessment approach incorporating developmental and clinical characteristics may be useful. However, given the absence of a non-ADHD comparison group, these results should be interpreted cautiously. Future studies including typically developing children and psychiatric comparison groups are needed to further clarify the specificity of these difficulties.

items.title: The Glial Firestorm: Targeting Ferroptotic Microglia-Astrocyte Crosstalk in Intracerebral Hemorrhage.
items.abstract: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) causes substantial mortality and disability, with secondary injury extending beyond the initial hematoma. This narrative review examines the working hypothesis that ferroptotic microglia amplify a neurotoxic astrocyte response after ICH. In the iron-rich hemorrhagic milieu, microglial iron loading and impaired antioxidant defenses favor lipid peroxidation, whereas inflammatory astrocyte states marked by LCN2, C3, and MMP3 contribute to barrier dysfunction and neuronal injury. Findings from ICH and related experimental models suggest that oxidized lipids, extracellular vesicles, and inflammatory mediators could connect these responses. Reactive astrocytes may then reinforce myeloid oxidative stress through altered iron handling, glutamate clearance, and complement signaling. Ferroptosis must be considered alongside apoptosis, necroptosis, and pyroptosis, and resident microglia share erythrophagocytic and iron-handling functions with infiltrating monocytes/macrophages. These overlapping processes limit the attribution of mixed myeloid signals to a single lineage or death pathway. The proposed bidirectional circuit remains a framework for testing rather than an established sequence in ICH. Therapeutic interception could combine early control of iron-dependent lipid injury with later astrocyte modulation through STAT3 or PPAR-γ, provided that beneficial hematoma clearance is preserved. High-resolution spatiotemporal mapping, lineage-resolved experiments, and sex-specific analyses are needed to identify the relevant cells and treatment windows. Targeting this glial interaction may complement neuroprotection, but its therapeutic value requires direct experimental and clinical validation.

items.title: Differential Cellular Dynamics of Platelet-Derived Growth Factor Receptor β Cells and Macrophages After Complete Spinal Cord Transection in Neonatal and Juvenile Rats.
items.abstract: Lesion morphology after complete spinal cord transection (CST) varies depending on the time of injury. Following CST, the stumps are connected by fibrous tissue in adult and juvenile rats, whereas they are connected by thin meningeal tissue in neonatal rats. Here, we compared the cellular dynamics after CST in neonatal and juvenile rats to investigate factors contributing to the morphologic differences between the two groups. The intensity of PDGFRβ-positive structures associated with fibrotic scar formation at the lesion core was significantly higher in juvenile CST rats than in neonatal CST rats. In neonatal rats, the intensity gradually decreased, whereas in juvenile rats it peaked at 7 days and then decreased. Pro-inflammatory CD11c-positive macrophages were abundant in the lesion core 2 days after CST, then rapidly decreased in both neonatal and juvenile CST rats. Anti-inflammatory CD163-positive macrophages in the lesion core were significantly more abundant in neonatal CST rats than in juvenile CST rats and remained elevated until 14 days after CST. Neonatal CST rats exhibited less fibroblast accumulation and higher CD163-positive macrophage density in the lesion core compared with juvenile CST rats. These differences may be associated with morphologic differences in the lesion core between the two groups. CD163-positive macrophages in the neonatal CST rats may primarily promote meningeal remodeling rather than fibrous tissue proliferation leading to fibrous scar formation.

items.title: Inferior Frontal Gyrus Alterations in Freezing of Gait in Parkinson's Disease Without Evidence for Overall Hemispheric Lateralization: A Systematic Review and Activation Likelihood Estimation Meta-Analysis.
items.abstract: Freezing of gait (FOG) is one of the most debilitating motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD). Prior studies have suggested a potential right-hemispheric preference in the pathophysiology of FOG. Yet, there is limited evidence regarding which brain regions are most consistently associated with FOG and whether these alterations indeed show right-hemispheric lateralization. We aimed to identify brain regions associated with FOG based on multimodal neuroimaging findings and to examine their hemispheric lateralization. A systematic review across multiple neuroimaging modalities was performed, followed by an activation likelihood estimation (ALE) coordinate-based meta-analysis to assess convergent brain alterations in PD patients with FOG (freezers) versus those without FOG (nonfreezers). Hemispheric lateralization was assessed using the distribution of reported stereotactic coordinates. The systematic review included 108 articles, of which 33 were included in the primary ALE meta-analysis. We identified a significant convergent cluster in the right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) pars opercularis/dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in PD freezers compared with nonfreezers. No evidence of overall hemispheric lateralization was observed based on the distribution of reported coordinates. Our findings identify the right IFG as a consistent neural correlate of FOG, potentially reflecting heightened frontal recruitment, with no clear evidence of hemispheric lateralization. The lack of further consistency in brain regions could reflect the known heterogeneity in the pathophysiology of FOG.

items.title: A Comparative Exploratory Study of Cognitive and Functional Outcomes by Sex and Age in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus and Atrial Fibrillation.
items.abstract: Background/aim Atrial fibrillation (AF) and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) are associated with cognitive decline, but possible sex-related differences in cognitive and functional outcomes remain uncertain. Patients and methods The study included 140 patients with T2DM, AF, and a Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score Results Severe cognitive impairment was present in 32/68 men (47.06%) and 36/72 women (50.00%), with no significant difference between sexes. These exploratory findings support cognitive, cardiovascular, psychological, and functional assessment in patients with T2DM and AF.

items.title: Enacted love: Capitalization responses signal love, including toward strangers.
items.abstract: What behavior is seen as "love" and why does it matter? We theorize active-constructive responding to another's disclosure of good news is prototypical "enacted love" and test hypotheses about implications for a loving person's relationship development. We use three distinct methods-dyadic interactions between romantic couples (Study 1, N = 160), real spontaneous responses to a stranger's good news (Study 2, N = 204), and observation of others' real capitalization responses to a stranger's good news (Studies 3-5, N = 97, 105, and 402, respectively)-to assess convergent and discriminant evidence for the construct. Study 2 uses experience sampling to track the development of capitalization respondents' social lives over time. Studies 4 and 5 use within-subjects experiments to test hypotheses that loving behavior could influence others' interactions with loving people. Results have theoretical implications for close relationships and the concept of "loving one's neighbor," plus practical implications for building bridges in a divided society. items.title: Plasma Lipidomic Features of Adolescent Major Depressive Disorder and Lipid Changes After Fluoxetine Treatment.
items.abstract: Background Major depressive disorder (MDD) in adolescents is a major public health concern, yet objective biological markers and treatment-related metabolic changes remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to characterize plasma lipidomic alterations in adolescent MDD and explore lipid changes associated with fluoxetine treatment. Methods This study enrolled 75 adolescents with MDD and 75 matched healthy controls (HCs). Among the adolescents with MDD, 44 had paired baseline and week-8 plasma samples available and were included in the longitudinal analysis. Plasma lipidomic profiles were analyzed using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS). Results A total of 865 lipid species were detected. Compared with HCs, adolescents with MDD showed distinct plasma lipidomic profiles, with 82 differentially abundant lipid species identified, primarily involving triglycerides, lysophospholipids, free fatty acids, membrane phospholipids, and sphingolipids. Among the machine-learning models, logistic regression showed the highest discriminative performance, with a pooled out-of-fold AUC of 0.85 (95% CI, 0.79-0.91). Longitudinal analysis identified 21 lipid species meeting the differential criteria following fluoxetine treatment, mainly involving triglycerides and bile acid-related metabolites. Integrative pathway and target analyses suggested that fluoxetine-associated lipid changes may involve neurotransmitter signaling, inflammatory lipid metabolism, PI3K-Akt signaling, and nuclear receptor-related pathways. Conclusion This study characterizes alterations in plasma lipid metabolism in adolescent MDD and the lipidomic changes following fluoxetine treatment, providing new lipidomic evidence for candidate lipid signatures and potential treatment-associated biological pathways. items.title: Levodopa and Subthalamic Nucleus Deep Brain Stimulation Modulate Excitation/Inhibition Balance and the Neural Encoding of Isochronous Sequences in Persons With Parkinson's Disease.
items.abstract: Temporally regular auditory stimuli, as found in isochronous sound streams, metronome beats, or music, are often used in rhythmic auditory stimulation (RAS) interventions to initiate and stabilize the temporal coordination of motor plans in persons with Parkinson's disease (pwPD). Research suggests that RAS promotes the recruitment of a cerebellar-prefrontal network and recalibrates abnormal β-band synchronization in the striato-thalamo-cortical pathway. These cuing effects can resemble those observed via dopaminergic treatments (e.g., levodopa) and deep brain stimulation (DBS) targeting the subthalamic nucleus (STN). Here, we investigated the influence of both levodopa administration and STN DBS on the neural encoding of isochronous auditory sequences in pwPD. A comprehensive analysis of electroencephalography (EEG) data revealed changes in β-band event-locked neural responses, as well as event-related potentials, neural tracking of rhythm (δ-band inter-trial phase coherence), and excitation/inhibition balance (E/I) as a function of these treatments. Furthermore, we characterized the link between changes in E/I and motor symptom severity (UPDRS-III) with levodopa administration. We suggest that characterizing individual responses to specific treatments is a fundamental step in tailoring rehabilitation protocols and optimizing intervention efficacy.

items.title: Endoplasmic Reticulum Autophagy Enhancement Alleviates Synaptic Plasticity Dysfunction and Ameliorates Cognitive Impairment in SAE Mice by Relieving STING-Associated Inhibition of PKM2 Activity.
items.abstract: Background The pathogenesis of cognitive impairment in patients with sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE) remains unclear. This study investigated whether enhancing micro-endoplasmic reticulum autophagy (micro-ER-phagy) could alleviate synaptic dysfunction and improve cognitive impairment in SAE mice models by relieving stimulator of interferon gene (STING)-associated inhibition of pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2) activity. Methods Male wild-type and neuron-specific PKM2 conditional knockout mice (PKM2 fl/fl ; hSyn-Cre + ) were used. Cognitive function in SAE mice models was assessed using the Y-maze and contextual fear conditioning tests. Neuronal plasticity was examined using transmission electron microscopy and Golgi staining, whereas immunofluorescence staining and Western blotting were employed to determine the temporal and spatial expression patterns of related proteins. Results Septic mice developed cognitive impairment. Hippocampal tissues of SAE mice exhibited synaptic plasticity dysfunction and glycolysis enhancement. Meanwhile, the hippocampus showed increased PKM2 expression and an altered ratio of PKM2 tetramers and dimers. In addition, phosphorylated STING significantly increased in concentration in hippocampal neurones and its knockdown improved cognitive function. However, this cognitive rescue failed in PKM2 conditional knockout mice treated with SAE. Finally, Sec62-mediated micro-ER-phagy promoted lysosomal degradation of STING, which relieved STING-mediated inhibition of PKM2 and improved synaptic plasticity and cognitive dysfunction in SAE mice. Conclusions Elevated micro-ER-phagy may relieve the STING-associated inhibition of PKM2 activity, improve neuronal glycolysis and synaptic plasticity, and alleviate cognitive dysfunction in SAE mice.

items.title: Potential Locations for Noninvasive Brain Stimulation in Treating Poststroke Deficits: Exploration From Multimodal Neuroimaging.
items.abstract: Aims Noninvasive brain stimulation (NIBS) shows promise for poststroke deficits (PSDs), but efficacy may be limited by inconsistent stimulation sites. Methods By integrating neuroimaging meta-analysis, lesion-symptom mapping (LSM), and resting-state functional connectivity (FC) analysis, we employed three analytical pipelines to explore potential NIBS targets for alexia, aphasia, apraxia, ataxia, dysarthria, hemiplegia, paresthesia, and dysphagia. Pipeline 1 identified cortical regions directly associated with each PSD via coordinate-based meta-analysis using Neurosynth Compose. Pipeline 2 identified cortical regions exhibiting maximal functional connectivity with neurosynth-derived regions of interest (ROI). Pipeline 3 identified cortical regions functionally connected to ROIs from a prior large-scale LSM study. During Pipeline 2 and 3, ROIs were used for seed-to-voxel FC analysis using resting-state fMRI data from 100 healthy subjects. Identified cortical targets were mapped onto the scalp and referenced by the 10-20 system and continuous proportional coordinates. Results Potential cortical targets and scalp locations were identified for all eight PSDs. For instance, for hemiplegia, validated targets included primary motor and somatosensory cortices and supplementary motor area; novel targets included angular gyrus, superior frontal gyrus, inferior parietal lobule, medial prefrontal cortex, and precuneus. Conclusions This multimodal approach systematically identified precise NIBS targets, confirming established sites and revealing novel regions to broaden neuromodulation strategies for poststroke recovery.

items.title: Engineering Mosaic T7 Bacteriophages for Dual Peptide Display to Enable Cellular Targeting and Ligand-Directed Protein Capture.
items.abstract: Integrating molecular recognition, tracing, and interactome capture within a single nanoparticle could allow for probing, manipulation, and control of complex biological systems. Achieving such multifunctionality within a single well-defined nanostructure remains challenging. T7 bacteriophage-based biological nanoparticles provide a robust and genetically programmable scaffold; however, conventional T7 display systems typically accommodate only one exogenous peptide species per phage particle, limiting multifunctional and combinatorial applications. Here, we describe a mosaic phage platform that enables the simultaneous display of two peptides on separate T7 coat protein subunits. By combining genome-encoded and plasmid-driven expression of peptide-fused capsid proteins, the system provides a modular route for assembling multifunctional phage nanoparticles. We generated mosaic T7 phages co-presenting the neuropilin-1 (NRP-1)-binding peptide RPARPAR alongside either a HA-tag or a Twin-Strep (Tstrep) tag affinity handle. These engineered phages specifically target NRP-1-expressing cells and enable immunofluorescence visualization and pull-down of NRP-1 from complex lysates. Furthermore, a random peptide T7 phage library co-displaying the constant lung-homing peptide RPARPAR shows preferential pulmonary accumulation in vivo, demonstrating utility for combinatorial targeting and tissue-directed phage selection. Collectively, this dual-display approach expands phage display by enabling cell targeting, visualization, molecular interactome probing, and in vivo tissue homing within a single genetically encoded nanoparticle platform.

items.title: The Predictive Value of Infant Ultrasonic Vocalizations in a Longitudinal Study of Maternal Separation in Rats.
items.abstract: Maternal separation (MS) is a well-established rodent model of early-life stress, implicated in the development of various neuropsychiatric conditions. Infant ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) serve as key communicative signals and have been used to assess early emotional and social development. Here, we examined the long-term behavioral and neurobiological effects of MS across adolescence and adulthood, focusing on the predictive potential of separation-induced infant USVs (40-60 kHz). MS was conducted between postnatal days (PND) 2-14, followed by a maternal potentiation test on PND 15, during which USVs were recorded. Behavioral assessments included anxiety and social play in adolescence (PND 35-36); and anxiety, sociability, anhedonia, and fear memory in adulthood (PND 80-88). MS reduced USVs in the potentiation paradigm, suppressed social play, and ameliorated anxiety-like behavior in adolescence. In adulthood, MS induced anhedonia, impaired fear memory, and decreased c-Fos-immunopositive cells in the lateral amygdala. Path and regression analyses revealed that infant USVs predicted open arm duration in the elevated plus maze in adolescence. USVs were negatively correlated with stress-induced neuronal activation in the habenula in control, but not MS animals. These findings indicate that infant USVs constitute a biobehavioral marker for early-life adverse experiences and predict the development of later affective conditions.

items.title: Hippocampal Subfield Volumes and Spatial Memory Performance in Older Adults At-Risk for Type 2 Diabetes.
items.abstract: Older adults at risk for type 2 diabetes (T2D) are more likely to experience accelerated cognitive aging and neurodegeneration due to impaired metabolism in the hippocampus. However, the precise relationship between T2D risk factors, brain volumes (i.e., gray matter, white matter, hippocampus subfields), and hippocampus-dependent functions (i.e., spatial pattern separation, a component of spatial memory) remains unexplored. To investigate these relationships in this cross-sectional study, 60 older adults at risk for T2D (e.g., high BMI or elevated A1c levels) completed a touchscreen-based spatial pattern separation behavioral task-the Trial-Unique delayed Nonmatching-to-Location (TUNL) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). HippUnfold was utilized to segment the hippocampus from high-resolution, T 1 -weighted images. We found positive correlations between A1c levels and volumes of the dentate gyrus (DG) and cornu ammonis (CA) 2, indicating that higher A1c was associated with larger volumes of hippocampal subregions. Additionally, TUNL accuracy was correlated with gray matter and distinct hippocampus subfield volumes (i.e., subiculum, CA1, and CA4), with larger volumes associated with better spatial memory performance. Understanding early structural changes in T2D risk allows us to further characterize changes in brain health associated with metabolic dysfunction.

items.title: Development and evaluation of X-ray lithophanes as test objects for interventional procedure simulation.
items.abstract: Background In the growing field of interventional radiology, emerging technologies implement the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to help tackle growing demands for treatment. Due to the anatomical differences in animals, volunteers offer the most realistic training and testing scenario, however safety considerations restrict rapid prototyping of these new technologies. Simulators have been a key facilitator in the testing of new technologies among numerous medical engineering studies, but often lack the realism to reliably test AI. Purpose This proof-of-concept study presents methods to create or enhance hyper-realistic radiographic simulators that can effectively function with a medical-grade AI software. Methods Iron-filled plastic was used to three-dimensionally (3D) print a series of blocks of heights up to 30 mm. By analyzing the intensities generated by different thicknesses of plastic, anonymous fluoroscopic images were turned into height maps (lithophanes) and 3D-printed. A static scene from transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) was then 3D-printed and imaged with different presets using two different x-ray systems for mathematical analysis. Lithophanes were then used as a radiographic background to experimental and commercial interventional simulators to test Caranx Medical's TAVIPILOT AI. Finally, fluoroscopies from 5 3D-printed lithophanes were mixed with 5 real images and presented to 5 expert volunteers to establish their realism in a structured survey. Results The 3D-printed x-ray lithophanes test-plates' radiographic appearance was rated as "Adequate" to "Good" across all fields of the survey, with participants praising their realism. The test-plate was able to reliably recreate the TAVI scene in different x-ray systems, with joint-histogram correlation coefficients above 0.9, and global structural similarity above 0.8. The lithophanes were imaged as a standalone test plate and as a backing to dynamic TAVI interventional simulators; in both cases, TAVIPILOT AI responded to the simulator as if it was operating on a real anatomical image. Conclusions Lithophane plates present an easy-to-implement solution to recreate monoplane x-ray scenes, which can be deployed to test software at the point of care with minimal logistical, ethical, or safety concerns. This study opens the door for a new range of interventional simulators able to recreate human-like appearance to test AI, offering a non-exclusive alternative to patient volunteers and anonymous data.

items.title: Digital Twins in Clinical Neurology: From Concept to Clinical Application in Multiple Sclerosis.
items.abstract: Introduction Patient digital twins (DT) are emerging as a promising paradigm for personalised and predictive healthcare. In neurology, and particularly in multiple sclerosis (MS), the availability of longitudinal, multimodal data provides a strong foundation for developing patient-specific digital models, including simulation-based and mechanistic approaches. However, it remains unclear to what extent current approaches represent integrated, clinically embedded DT systems. Methods We conducted a narrative review to synthesise current concepts, modelling approaches and translational challenges of DT in neurology, using MS as an illustrative use case. Existing approaches were mapped to core DT components, including data integration, predictive modelling, dynamic updating and clinical integration. Results Current DT-related approaches in MS demonstrate substantial progress across complementary development tracks, including multimodal data integration, predictive modelling, digital biomarkers, mechanistic simulations, virtual-patient frameworks and in silico trials. These capabilities represent important building blocks of DT development but have not yet been fully integrated into continuously operating clinical systems. Core DT functionalities, including continuous bidirectional data exchange, real-time model updating and closed-loop interaction with clinical workflows, remain limited. Key challenges include data fragmentation, limited interoperability, lack of standardised validation, and regulatory, ethical and economic constraints. Conclusion MS represents a highly suitable model domain for DT development. Future progress will depend on further maturing and validating individual modelling and data-integration capabilities, as well as on their integration into continuously updating, clinically embedded systems. Robust validation, scalable infrastructures and appropriate governance frameworks will be essential to establish safe, effective and clinically actionable use in practice.

items.title: Intrinsic Activity Reductions and Cerebello-Cortical Diaschisis-Like Mechanism in Friedreich Ataxia: An fALFF Resting-State fMRI Study.
items.abstract: Background Friedreich ataxia (FA) is characterized by progressive degeneration of the cerebellum and its output pathways, particularly the dentato-thalamo-cortical system, leading to motor impairment and the cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome (CCAS). Resting-state fMRI studies in FA have focused on alterations of long-range functional connectivity, but little is known about how intrinsic regional neural activity is affected within cerebello-cortical networks. Methods Twenty-eight adults with genetically confirmed FA and 28 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent resting-state functional MRI. Intrinsic brain activity was quantified using the fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF). Whole-brain comparisons were performed between controls and patients, and between patients with definite CCAS (FA-Cog) and cognitively preserved patients (FA-NoCog). Within the FA group, voxelwise regressions assessed associations between fALFF, motor severity (Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia [SARA]), and cognitive performance (Cerebellar Cognitive Affective Syndrome Scale [CCAS-S]), adjusting for age, sex, head motion, and cerebellar gray matter volume. Results Compared with controls, patients exhibited reduced fALFF in medial and lateral prefrontal regions. Higher SARA scores were associated with lower fALFF in occipital, sensorimotor, posterior cingulate, and cerebellar regions, whereas higher CCAS-S scores correlated with higher fALFF in bilateral prefrontal and cerebellar cognitive networks. Compared with FA-NoCog, FA-Cog patients showed lower fALFF in bilateral frontal and insular regions. Conclusions Resting-state fALFF reveals downstream dysfunction of distributed cerebello-cortical networks in FA. Associations with motor severity and cognition, together with additional fronto-insular dysfunction in patients with definite CCAS, support progressive cerebello-cortical disconnection consistent with a diaschisis-like mechanism.

items.title: A Species-Dependent Spatial Patterning of FOXP1 and nNOS Protein Expression in the Adult Mammalian Subthalamic Nucleus.
items.abstract: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) is a key component of basal ganglia circuitry involved in motor, cognitive, and limbic functions. While the transcription factor FOXP1 has been implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders and basal ganglia function, its expression in the adult STN remains insufficiently characterized. Our study investigated the expression and distribution of FOXP1 protein and its colocalization with neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) and a pan-neuronal marker (HuC/HuD) in the adult STN across three mammalian species: mouse, rat, and human. Using immunofluorescent double-labeling and quantitative analysis, we examined their spatial organization and relative proportions within the neuronal population. FOXP1 was identified as a substantial neuronal subpopulation, comprising approximately 40%-45% of STN neurons across all species. In contrast, nNOS-positive neurons showed marked interspecies variation, increasing from ∼32% in mice to ∼68% in humans. Notably, the spatial distribution of these markers differed significantly between species. In rodents, FOXP1+ and nNOS+ neurons were largely segregated along the dorsoventral axis, forming visibly distinct subdomains. Conversely, in the human STN, these populations were diffusely intermixed with a higher degree of colocalization. Additionally, both markers exhibited species-specific antero-posterior gradients. These findings provide the first evidence of FOXP1 protein expression in the adult rat and human STN and highlight fundamental interspecies differences in neuronal organization. The expanded nNOS+ population and increased FOXP1/nNOS colocalization in humans suggest evolutionary divergence in the mammalian STN cytoarchitecture. Overall, the results challenge simplified models of STN subdivision in mammals, primates especially, and underscore the need for caution when extrapolating rodent data to human neurophysiology.

items.title: The Boron-Neuron Connection: The Potential of Boron-Containing Molecules for Treating Incurable Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
items.abstract: Background Boron (B), a group 13 metalloid, has emerged as a versatile element at the intersection of chemistry, biology, and medicine. Its electron-deficient nature and ability to reversibly interconvert between trigonal planar (sp 2 ) and tetrahedral (sp 3 ) geometries enable dynamic covalent interactions with biological nucleophiles, making boron-containing compounds (BCCs) attractive pharmacophores that selectively interact with reactive oxygen species (ROS) and are ROS-responsive for therapeutic development. BCCs possess antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and metal-chelating properties that make them attractive candidates for neurodegenerative diseases. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a fatal and multifactorial motor neurodegenerative disorder, is characterized by oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and metal dyshomeostasis, providing a strong rationale for exploring boron-based therapeutics. Methods This review examines current literature on B chemistry, pharmacology, and translational applications, with emphasis on mechanisms relevant to ALS pathogenesis. This review focuses on ROS-responsive B scaffolds, blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability, neuroprotective mechanisms, hormonal modulation, metal chelation, and emerging preclinical evidence supporting boron-based interventions. Conclusions BCCs represent a promising yet underexplored therapeutic platform for ALS and related neurodegenerative disorders. Their ROS-responsive, redox-modulating, and neuroprotective properties, combined with favorable CNS drug-like pharmacokinetics, offer a mechanistically distinct approach to disease modification. Emerging preclinical evidence strongly supports further translational investigation.

items.title: Anatomically Defined Motor Phenotypes Reveal Dissociated Trajectories of Progression, Neurofilament Profiles, and Survival in ALS.
items.abstract: Background Clinical heterogeneity in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) may reflect structured disease trajectories. This study investigated whether anatomically defined motor phenotypes capture reproducible patterns associated with progression, serum neurofilament light chain (NfL), and survival. Methods In a multicenter cohort of 1307 ALS patients, motor phenotypes were classified by region of onset, timing of propagation to a vertically distant body region (early ≤ 12 months vs. later), and the degree of upper (UMN) and lower motor neuron (LMN) dysfunction. Intercenter consistency was assessed using the Friedman test and Kendall's W. Associations with ALS progression rate (ALSPR), NfL, and survival were analyzed using group comparisons and Cox regression models. Results Phenotype classification was consistent across centers (Kendall's W 0.75-0.89). Onset phenotypes were significantly associated with ALSPR, NfL, and survival (p Conclusions Anatomically defined motor phenotypes identify reproducible ALS trajectories with distinct clinical and neurofilament profiles. Early propagation provides an actionable risk marker of disease aggressiveness, while combined upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction or lower motor neuron predominance is prognostically unfavorable. These findings support integrating structured phenotyping into prognostic models and clinical trial stratification.

items.title: Arcuate kisspeptin neurons display two types of calcium events: Regulation by sex, gonads, and senktide.
items.abstract: The pattern of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) release controls reproduction in vertebrates and is regulated by feedback from the gonads. Evidence is accumulating that steroid-sensitive hypothalamic arcuate kisspeptin-neurokinin B-dynorphin (KNDy) neurons drive GnRH pulses. KNDy neurons exhibit coordinated, large amplitude calcium signals in vivo that precede LH pulses; coordinated events persist in brain slice recordings of these cells. We used cre-lox to target GCaMP6f expression to KNDy neurons. Brain slice calcium imaging was done to identify putative unitary calcium events. Newly devised analyses identified two types of calcium events (fast and slow) in intact and gonadectomized male and female adult mice. Neurokinin B and the neurokinin-3 receptor agonist senktide are strong activators of action potential firing in KNDy neurons. The effect of senktide on calcium events over 5-min baseline and treatment periods was determined. Gonadectomy unexpectedly increased GCaMP6f fluorescence; illumination levels were adjusted to standardize initial levels. Senktide increased the frequency of fast and slow events; this effect was enhanced in gonadectomized mice for fast events. Senktide increased fast event amplitude only in gonadectomized mice. For slow events, in contrast, senktide increased amplitude in all groups, with the increase being larger in gonadectomized than intact mice. Differential regulation by gonadectomy and senktide modulation of fast and slow events suggests two separate mechanisms for these events, which likely also differ from the large amplitude events observed in vivo in KNDy neurons.

items.title: Combining Cognitive Training and Brain Stimulation: A Novel Approach to Address Disordered Eating and Antipsychotic-Induced Weight Gain in People With Severe Mental Illness.
items.abstract: Background Antipsychotic-induced weight gain is a distressing side effect that most often occurs within the first 3-6 months of pharmacological initiation, significantly increasing cardiometabolic risk and mortality in individuals with severe mental illness. Aims To assess the feasibility of reducing food craving and binge eating using Approach Bias Modification Training (ABMT) combined with real or sham Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (tDCS). Method In this double-blind, parallel-group, two-arm, sham-controlled trial, adults with schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder on stable doses of antipsychotics were randomly allocated to a total of five ABMT sessions together with either real or sham tDCS administered over 3 weeks. Assessments were made at baseline (T0), post-treatment (T1) and at a 2-week follow-up (T2). Feasibility outcomes included recruitment, attendance, retention, tDCS safety, acceptability, tolerability, and blinding. Secondary outcomes were changes in food craving, binge eating, approach bias to food, body mass index, and psychological symptoms. Results Twenty-eight participants were recruited (93% of target). Retention was high (T1 = 85.7% and T2 = 78.6%); blinding accuracy was 46.4%. Medium effect sizes favoured 'ABMT + real tDCS' for reducing binge eating (d = -0.6, 95% CI -1.5, 0.3), and 'ABMT + sham tDCS' for reducing food cravings (d = 0.5, 95% CI -0.4, 1.4). Within-groups, only the 'ABMT + real tDCS' arm showed reduced approach bias to food and approach-avoidance bias to food, and increased avoidance bias to food (all p Conclusion The initiation of antipsychotic therapy is a critical clinical window for early intervention to mitigate the long-term metabolic and psychiatric consequences of antipsychotic-induced weight gain. Combining ABMT + tDCS is acceptable and may help reduce binge eating in individuals on antipsychotics, with a potential synergistic effect between cognitive training and brain stimulation. A confirmatory trial is needed to assess its effectiveness and should include BED diagnosis as a stratification criterion. Trial registration ISRCTN Identifier: 13280178.

items.title: Should Coffee Consumers Not Have Their Habitual Morning Coffee Before Testing Their Cognitive Functions?
items.abstract: Objective Caffeine could improve cognitive functions, but study protocols usually prohibit drinking coffee before cognitive testing. However, regular coffee consumers may experience withdrawal effects when they cannot drink their habitual coffee, which may impair cognitive performance. Therefore, we tested the effects of overnight coffee abstinence in regular coffee consumers: once allowing to drink their coffee and once not drinking coffee. The cognitive performance was compared with non-regular coffee consumers. Methods Thirty regular coffee consumers (RCCs) and 25 non-regular consumers (N-RCCs) took part in this study. RCCs were tested after their habitual morning coffee (c-RCC) and after overnight abstinence (a-RCC); N-RCCs were tested once. A cognitive battery assessed reaction time (RT), processing speed (digit symbol substitution test), working memory, verbal learning/memory and executive function (Stroop). Sleep quality was included as a covariate. Results Compared to c-RCC, overnight coffee abstinence significantly slowed RTs but did not affect the performance in the other cognitive tasks. In the a-RCC condition, but not the c-RCC condition, the RTs were slower than those of the N-RCCs, while accuracy measures were comparable across groups. Sleep quality did not alter these findings. Conclusions Overnight coffee abstinence selectively slowed RT, and no statistical support was found for effects on memory or executive function. This suggests that overnight coffee abstinence protocols may introduce withdrawal-related RT slowing as a confound in habitual consumers, whereas other cognitive domains may not be affected. Allowing habitual consumers to maintain normal coffee intake could reduce this bias, supporting tailored rather than uniform abstinence requirements based on the specific outcomes studied.

items.title: Advanced CT Myelography for Spontaneous Cerebrospinal Fluid Leaks.
items.abstract: Spontaneous intracranial hypotension is a frequently debilitating condition that is most commonly caused by loss of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the spine. The most frequently occurring types of spontaneous spinal CSF leaks that cause spontaneous intracranial hypotension are ventral dural tears, lateral dural tears, and CSF venous fistulas, but other leak types are recognized including sacral dural tears or fistulas into vascular malformations. Localization and characterization of spinal CSF leaks with CT myelography facilitates subsequent targeted treatment. A tailored approach based on the suspected leak type as determined at MRI of the spine is necessary to maximize the likelihood of a diagnostic study. The authors focus primarily on advanced CT myelographic techniques for leaks from dural tears and CSF venous fistulas. The importance of optimal patient positioning, typical and atypical appearances of the different leak types, and artifacts that can mimic a CSF leak are considered. ©RSNA, 2026 Supplemental material is available for this article. See the invited commentary by Madhavan in this issue.

items.title: Landscape Analysis of Digital Health Technology Use for Remote Data Acquisition in CDER-Regulated Submissions, 2023-2025.
items.abstract: Digital health technologies can support remote acquisition of clinical investigation data and may facilitate more flexible clinical trial designs. In March 2023, FDA revised Forms FDA 1571 and FDA 356h to include a structured yes/no field asking whether a submission contains DHT data or a proposal to collect DHT data. This change created a mechanism for identifying submissions involving DHT-based remote data acquisition. Following implementation of these fields, the Office of Medical Policy in FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research developed and implemented a systematic process to track, identify, and adjudicate DHT-related submissions. This analytical report presents a descriptive, aggregated, de-identified analysis of submissions that were flagged through this operational process from March 2023 through December 2025. Operational inclusion criteria were applied to identify submissions involving DHTs used for remote data acquisition intended to support regulatory decision-making. Of 2318 flagged submissions, 277 (12%) were confirmed for inclusion in this analysis. Confirmed submissions were predominantly associated with investigational applications (237/277, 86%). When classified by the nature of data collected, submissions reflected a range of remote data acquisition approaches, including patient reported data and sensor-based measurements, with some submissions combining more than one modality. Electronic diary and electronic patient-reported outcomes were most common, exclusively appearing in 161 submissions (58%), followed by data captured from general objective sensors in 92 submissions (33%) and continuous glucose monitoring data in 24 submissions (9%). These findings establish a quantitative baseline for DHT-based remote data acquisition in CDER submissions and the implementation of FDA's corresponding guidance.

items.title: Outcomes of Mindful Mood Balance for Moms, online mindfulness-based cognitive therapy for perinatal depressive relapse prevention in the USA: a two-arm, single-blind, pragmatic randomised clinical trial.
items.abstract: Background Effective and accessible approaches to prevent depressive relapse and reduce symptoms are crucial for addressing the major public health problem of depression among perinatal women. We aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of Mindful Mood Balance (MMB) for Moms plus usual care (hereafter MMB for Moms)-a web-based mindfulness-based cognitive therapy programme customised for perinatal women-compared with usual care only, in reducing depressive relapse and symptoms. Methods This single-blind, randomised clinical trial was done across the USA, in euthymic pregnant women with recurrent depression who were on recent or current antidepressant medication. Recruitment occurred from March 7, 2019, to July 8, 2020 (data collection was completed Sept 12, 2021). Participants were randomly assigned to MMB for Moms, or usual care. Primary outcomes were reduction in depressive relapse risk and symptom burden, assessed using the Mini International Neuropsychiatric Interview and Patient Health Questionaire-9, respectively, across the study period. Outcomes were assessed from baseline until 6-months postpartum in three phases (intervention, end of intervention to delivery, and postpartum). The trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03623620, and is complete. Findings Participants were recruited between March 7, 2019, and July 8, 2020. Data from 500 randomly assigned participants (mean age 32 years [SD 4·5] and mean 11·5 [2·8] weeks gestation), were analysed as the intention-to-treat sample. Of the 500 participants (249 assigned to MMB for Moms and 251 assigned to usual care), 383 [77%] provided assessment data at 3 months and 389 [78%] at 6 months postpartum. MMB for Moms had significantly lower risk of depressive relapse compared with usual care during the full trial period (up to 6 months postpartum): 81 (33%) of 249 participants assigned to MMB for Moms and 111 (44%) of 251 participants in usual care had depressive relapse (hazard ratio 0·74 [95% CI 0·56-0·99]; p=0·045; adjusted false discovery rate p=0·045). MMB for Moms was also associated with a significant reduction in depression symptom burden during the 12 week intervention phase (average decrease of 0·75 [SE 0·13] in the MMB for Moms group and 0·31 [0·13] in the usual care group) but not during the full trial period (average decrease of 0·61 [SE 0·18] in the MMB for Moms group and 0·54 [0·17] in the usual care group). Interpretation MMB for Moms resulted in lower risk of relapse compared with usual care, and lower depression symptom burden during the intervention phase, potentially offering an effective non-pharmacological support option for depression relapse prevention during the perinatal period with positive implications for public health practice. Funding US National Institutes of Health and US National Institute of Mental Health.

items.title: Betaine Attenuates Cuprizone-Induced Cortical Demyelination: The Role of the WNT4/mTOR Signalling Pathway in Regulating Astrogliosis and Synaptic Integrity.
items.abstract: Cortical grey matter pathology manifests early demyelinating diseases and is a primary driver of permanent neurological impairment. Our study investigated the neuroprotective effects of betaine against cuprizone (CPZ)-induced damage to the cerebral cortex in rats, focusing on its ability to modulate the upstream WNT4/mTOR signalling pathway. Cortical tissues were collected for biochemical assessments of oxidative and inflammatory markers, real-time PCR analysis for WNT4, GFAP, and mTOR gene expressions, histopathological examination, and immunohistochemical analysis of vimentin, S100, and synaptophysin. Exposure to CPZ resulted in severe cortical damage with profound oxidative stress. This oxidative status triggered a pronounced neuroinflammatory response, leading to elevated levels of IL-17A, IL-1β, and TNF-α, which in turn caused chronic, hyper-reactive astrogliosis. This was confirmed by the upregulation of GFAP gene expression and enhanced immunohistochemical staining of vimentin and S100β, resulting in extensive loss of cortical synaptic integrity (depletion of synaptophysin). Importantly, treatment with betaine served as a molecular brake, significantly downregulating the aberrant gene expressions of WNT4 and mTOR. This targeted downregulation effectively reduced the overactive glial response, leading to a significant reduction in astrogliosis (GFAP, vimentin, and S100β), alleviated the pro-inflammatory cytokines, restored endogenous antioxidant functions, and ultimately preserved cortical synaptophysin expression and cellular structure. Overall, these results demonstrate that betaine exerts a neuroprotective effect against CPZ-induced cortical injury, which is strongly associated with the attenuation of WNT4/mTOR signalling pathway hyperactivation, suppression of astrogliosis, and preservation of synaptic density. The preservation of cortical grey matter integrity is directly associated with alleviating cognitive deficits and long-term physical disabilities in multiple sclerosis patients, emphasising the translational relevance of targetable neuroprotective therapies.

items.title: Perceived Neighborhood Disadvantage Predicts Similarity in Amygdala Representations of Negative and Neutral Images in Early Adolescents.
items.abstract: Neighborhood disadvantage encompasses multiple co-occurring adversities, including threat and deprivation, yet its underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. Applying a dimensional framework to neighborhood contexts may help clarify how distinct features of disadvantage influence brain development. Here, we used representational similarity analysis to investigate associations between adolescents' neural representations of affective valence and neighborhood disadvantage, as measured by caregiver self-report and the Area Deprivation Index (ADI). One hundred and twenty-one adolescents aged 11 to 14 (M age = 12.81 years old, 52.07% female, 28.93% White non-Hispanic) completed an emotional reactivity fMRI task. Caregiver-reported neighborhood disadvantage was associated with greater representational similarity in right amygdala between negative and neutral images, while no such effect emerged for the ADI. Follow-up analyses examined whether specific dimensions of disadvantage drove these effects. Although our measure did not map cleanly onto threat and deprivation dimensions, factor analyses revealed distinctions between social (e.g., crime, loitering) and physical (e.g., abandoned buildings, walkability) disadvantage-related items; our preliminary findings suggest that the effects of reported overall neighborhood disadvantage may be driven by characteristics of the social environment. No associations between caregiver-reported neighborhood disadvantage or ADI were observed for positive/neutral similarity. These findings provide preliminary evidence that neighborhood disadvantage may impact the amygdala's differentiation of negative and neutral stimuli during early adolescence, supporting the view that neighborhoods are a critical ecological context for development.

items.title: The Strength of Target Representations Drives Mnemonic Discrimination: Evidence From Extended Delay and Hippocampal Damage.
items.abstract: Mnemonic discrimination is critical for episodic memory and is dependent on the computational process of pattern separation, which allows the memory system to disambiguate prior memories from potentially overlapping new memories and avoid interference. Prior work with tasks such as the Mnemonic Similarity Task (MST) has demonstrated that discrimination performance is disproportionately affected by hippocampal insult. Further studies have demonstrated that the quality of initial encoding may affect subsequent discrimination performance. Taken together, these results imply that the strength of target memory representations determines discrimination performance in the MST. Here, we manipulated target memory strength by examining MST performance at delays ranging from a few minutes to seven days in three experiments with healthy young adults and a patient with hippocampal damage. Consistent with prior forgetting literature, both target recognition and lure discrimination declined with delay in controls. In the immediate delay condition, the similarity of lures to targets drove discrimination performance, with more similar lures eliciting false alarms and less similar lures eliciting correct rejections, as reflected in the lure discrimination index (LDI). This graded relationship was attenuated or absent at delays longer than one day. However, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses revealed preserved discrimination across delays and target-lure similarity levels. Similarly, the hippocampal patient was impaired relative to controls when considering LDI, but ROC-based analysis revealed intact lure discrimination for the lowest-similarity lures at immediate delays. Finally, we observed an inversion of the typical confidence-accuracy relationship for lure trials at longer delays, with low-confidence responses more likely to be correct for high-similarity lures. Together these findings demonstrate that both the strength of target representations and the degree of lure similarity interact to drive discrimination performance.

items.title: Women With Bipolar Disorder are at Increased Risk of Sarcopenia.
items.abstract: Introduction While bipolar disorder is associated with significant comorbidity, little is known about the musculoskeletal health of individuals with bipolar disorder. Thus, we aimed to investigate the association between bipolar disorder and muscle strength, mass, quality and sarcopenia. Methods Women with bipolar disorder (n = 106) were recruited from healthcare settings and age-matched to controls (n = 300), without bipolar disorder, from the Geelong Osteoporosis Study. Both groups, aged ≥ 20 years. were drawn from South-Eastern Australia. Bipolar disorder was identified using a clinical interview (SCID-I/NP). Maximum handgrip strength (HGS) was measured using a Jamar dynamometer, appendicular lean mass (ALM) using a Lunar densitometer and body mass index (BMI, kg/m 2 ) was calculated. Foundation for the National Institute of Health (FNIH) and European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People (EWGSOP2) algorithms were used to determine low HGS, ALM, probable and confirmed sarcopenia. Socioeconomic status (SES) was determined and information on lifestyle obtained via questionnaire. Results Higher proportion of women with bipolar disorder met criteria for low HGS and ALM compared to those without bipolar disorder. Using FNIH and EWGSOP2 criteria, 36 (8.9%; 34 probable and 2 confirmed) and 46 (11.4%; 43 probable and 3 confirmed) women met criteria for sarcopenia, respectively. Women with bipolar disorder were twice as likely to have sarcopenia (FNIH; OR 2.24, 95% CI: 1.11-4.55 and EWGSOP2; OR 2.78, 95% CI: 1.47-5.20), independent of age, smoking, activity, alcohol, diet and SES. Conclusion These data suggest women with bipolar disorder have an increased likelihood of sarcopenia. Replication and research into underlying mechanisms are next necessary steps.

items.title: No lysine? No problem: the surprising roles of WNK kinases in physiology and disease.
items.abstract: WNK (With No lysine K) protein kinases gained early attention because gain-of-function mutations in genes encoding two of them cause hypertension. They differ from other kinases due to the unusual location of the catalytic lysine, hence the name WNK. These kinases control many aspects of ion transport in the kidney and are essential for development and maintenance of the cardiovascular system. In the present review, we describe WNK proteins and selected substrates, in particular, the kinases oxidative stress-responsive kinase 1 and SPS1-related proline/alanine-rich kinase, and their regulation. We spotlight findings that emphasize the broad relevance of WNKs in normal physiology and disease. Our overview focuses on basic aspects of ion transport that occur in many cell types and tissues, functions in the endothelial system, interactions with insulin-dependent and metabolic pathways, the importance in the brain in part through controlling chloride ion balance, and the whirlwind of findings in cancer that reveal how WNK signaling can be repurposed. Other actions that may be of equal importance, e.g., influences on the immune system, are touched on only briefly. We also note a few genome-wide association studies that have uncovered multiple SNPs in genes encoding WNKs and downstream effectors in an array of diseases, in anticipation of more to come in the future.

items.title: Risk-adapted MRI Protocols for the Detection of Clinically Significant Prostate Cancer.
items.abstract: Purpose To compare the diagnostic performance and clinical utility of three MRI protocols for detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) according to prebiopsy risk. Materials and Methods This retrospective study included 390 male patients who underwent prostate multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) between January 2019 and April 2024 for suspected csPCa, followed by biopsy. Patients were stratified by Rotterdam Prostate Cancer Risk Calculator score into low-risk ( P ≥ .21) and greatest potential for safe biopsy avoidance (84 biopsies avoided per missed csPCa). In intermediate-risk patients, mpMRI showed higher sensitivity (83% vs 72% for unenhanced MRI and 62% for short MRI; P = .012 for mpMRI vs short MRI) and higher biopsy efficiency (1.11 vs 0.85 for mpMRI vs unenhanced MRI). In high-risk patients, protocol-related differences were minimal (all P ≥ .12). Conclusion mpMRI was associated with improved sensitivity and biopsy efficiency in intermediate-risk patients, whereas protocol differences were limited in low- and high-risk groups; these findings support risk-adapted selection of MRI protocols. Keywords: MR-Dynamic Contrast-enhanced, MR Imaging, Urinary, Prostate, Neoplasms-Primary, Efficacy Studies, Prostatic Neoplasms, MRI, Contrast Medium, Biopsy, Risk Assessment Supplemental material is available for this article. © RSNA, 2026.

items.title: Homeostatic Control of Hebbian Plasticity Exerted by Action Potential-Mediated Metaplasticity.
items.abstract: Hebbian plasticity, in particular long-term potentiation (LTP) of excitatory synapses, is a positive feed-back mechanism and has the potential to saturate its effects with negative consequences at both the single neuron and the circuit level. Metaplasticity is one of the mechanisms that can help overcome this problem. During one form of metaplasticity, a high (or low) level of neuronal activity impedes (or favors) the expression of future LTP. Although much is known about the role of synaptic activity in driving this metaplasticity effect, the specific role of postsynaptic action potential (AP) firing activity is still controversial and largely unknown. Experimentally, a high level of AP firing has resulted in either the suppression (a pro-homeostatic effect) or the enhancement (an anti-homeostatic effect) of a later induced LTP. Accordingly, we tested a wide range of AP firing frequencies generated by postsynaptic current pulses at different time intervals relative to the time of LTP induction at Schaffer collateral synapses of hippocampal CA1 neurons in Sprague-Dawley rats. We found that a wide range of AP firing frequencies, from 3 to 90 Hz, consistently inhibited the expression of future LTP at all time intervals tested, with no modulation of NMDA glutamate receptors. Moreover, the generation of APs, as opposed to the average level of somatic depolarization during priming, was necessary for triggering the metaplasticity. Our results provide solid evidence for a pro-homeostatic metaplasticity that is engaged by postsynaptic AP firing, thus impeding the saturation of Hebbian plasticity and associated hyperexcitability.

items.title: Reframing traumatic brain injury and spinal cord injury as chronic multisystem disorders: toward integrated, long-term care.
items.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) and spinal cord injury (SCI) affect more than 220 million people worldwide and are associated with cardiometabolic, endocrine, neurological, and psychiatric sequelae for years to decades after an acute injury. However, most health systems still treat neurotrauma (TBI and SCI, collectively) as a time-limited event, leaving long-term surveillance of these patients fragmented or absent, which leads to preventable mortality and avoidable readmissions. TBI and SCI in adults should be reclassified as acute-onset multisystem chronic-risk conditions. Existing cardiovascular, endocrine, and psychiatric services do not capture neurotrauma-specific risks, including trauma-induced hypopituitarism, autonomic dysregulation, accelerated ageing, and cognitive-behavioural impairment, so neurotrauma care is best framed as a missing node in chronic neurological care. We propose a risk-stratified pathway of care navigation, multisystem screening, and telehealth; convergence with adjacent stroke, cardiometabolic, memory, psychiatric, pain, and epilepsy services; and the financing, workforce, and registry reforms needed to deliver measurable reductions in 5-year mortality, avoidable rehospitalisation, and long-term disability.

items.title: GLP-1 receptor agonist initiation and risk of psychiatric hospitalisation and emergency department presentation in adults with schizophrenia and type 2 diabetes in the USA: an observational cohort study using electronic health records data.
items.abstract: Background Many individuals with schizophrenia have persistent psychotic symptoms despite antipsychotic treatment, and the disorder is associated with a disproportionately high burden of metabolic dysregulation. Whether GLP-1 receptor agonists are associated with psychiatric benefit alongside their metabolic effects remains unknown. We aimed to examine associations between GLP-1 receptor agonist initiation and psychiatric hospitalisation and emergency department presentation in adults with schizophrenia and type 2 diabetes, compared with DPP-4 inhibitor initiation, SGLT2 inhibitor initiation, and non-initiation. Methods In this observational cohort study, we used electronic health record (EHR) data from the US NeuroBlu Data repository to construct a cohort of adults (≥18 years) with documented diagnosis of schizophrenia and comorbid type 2 diabetes. The exposure was the initiation of GLP-1 receptor agonists, compared with non-initiation or initiation of DPP-4 inhibitors or SGLT2 inhibitors. The index date, from Jan 1, 2018, was defined as the date of the first recorded psychiatric visit at which both a diagnosis of schizophrenia and comorbid type 2 diabetes were present in the participant's record. Time zero (T 0 ) was the date of the first prescription of any of these agents between Jan 1, 2018, and Oct 1, 2025; for non-initiators, T 0 was the index date. Participants contributed person-time from T 0 until 2 years of follow-up, the last recorded clinical observation in the NeuroBlu Data repository, or the end of the observation period (March 24, 2026), whichever happened earliest. The main outcomes of interest included risk of psychiatric hospitalisation and psychiatric emergency department presentation. Inverse probability weighting was applied to balance demographic, clinical, and pharmacological covariates, and weighted regression models were used. Analyses were conducted using an intention-to-treat framework, whereby exposure status was defined according to the medication initiated at T 0 . Findings A total of 70 257 individuals met the inclusion criteria; mean age was 53·1 years [SD 12·32] and 33 882 [48·2%] were women. Among the 70 257 eligible individuals, 9093 (12·9%) initiated GLP-1 receptor agonists, 4968 (7·1%) initiated DPP-4 inhibitors, 5328 (7·6%) initiated SGLT2 inhibitors, and 50 868 (72·4%) were non-initiators. In weighted regression analyses, GLP-1 receptor agonist initiation was associated with a lower risk of psychiatric hospitalisation compared with non-initiation (weighted hazard ratio [HR] 0·76 [95% CI 0·71-0·82]), DPP-4 inhibitor initiation (0·82 [0·75-0·90]), and SGLT2 inhibitor initiation (0·83 [0·78-0·88]). GLP-1 receptor agonist initiation was also associated with a lower risk of emergency department presentation than non-initiation (0·71 [0·65-0·77]), DPP-4 inhibitor initiation (0·87 [0·80-0·95]), and SGLT2 inhibitor initiation (0·80 [0·73-0·88]). Interpretation GLP-1-based therapy initiation was associated with lower psychiatric acute-care use than non-initiation and initiation of DPP-4 or SGLT2 inhibitors in adults with schizophrenia and type 2 diabetes. Potential residual confounding and selection bias restrict generalisability of the results. The findings suggest that lower psychiatric acute-care use could be a favourable secondary benefit when GLP-1-based therapies are clinically indicated for metabolic management, although their use as primary psychiatric treatments require investigation in randomised and mechanistic studies. Funding Synergy for the Development of Innovative Clinical Treatments in Schizophrenia (SYNDICAT) project (GNT2035912).

items.title: Acquired Corneal Subepithelial Hypertrophy: First Ultrastructural Characterization by Transmission Electron Microscopy.
items.abstract: Abstract Acquired corneal subepithelial hypertrophy (ACSH) is a rare corneal condition whose ultrastructural features have not previously been characterized. We report the first detailed ultrastructural analysis of ACSH in a 57-year-old man with a history of penetrating keratoplasty for corneal trauma followed by Descemet stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty who presented with progressive visual decline due to a superficial corneal opacity. Clinical evaluation included slitlamp biomicroscopy, anterior segment optical coherence tomography, corneal topography, and pachymetry, which localized the lesion to the subepithelial compartment. The lesion was managed with selective surgical peeling, and the excised tissue was examined by light microscopy and transmission electron microscopy. Surgical removal led to restoration of best-corrected visual acuity with no recurrence at 1-year follow-up. Histopathological analysis demonstrated irregular epithelial thickening, complete absence of Bowman layer, and subepithelial fibrosis with myofibroblast proliferation, without evidence of inflammation or neovascularization. Ultrastructural examination revealed epithelial mitochondrial damage with mitophagy, disruption of intercellular junctions, and subepithelial myofibroblasts containing abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum, consistent with active fibrotic remodeling. These findings support ACSH as an acquired corneal fibrotic process driven by wound healing mechanisms, with clinical, epidemiological, and histopathological features distinct from other corneal degenerations and confirmed that surgical peeling of the thickened epithelial and subepithelial tissue can be curative.

items.title: Exploring a Range of Potential Factors Promoting and Constraining EF in South African Preschoolers.
items.abstract: Background Socioeconomic disadvantage is widely associated with poorer cognitive and educational outcomes. However, emerging evidence suggests that children in low-income contexts may demonstrate resilience in executive function (EF) development. This study examined the predictors of EF in South African preschoolers from disadvantaged communities to identify modifiable, context-specific influences. Methods 125 Children (aged 3-5 years) and their caregivers were recruited from 15 early childhood centers in Cape Town. Children completed three tablet-based EF tasks from the Early Years Toolbox measuring working memory, inhibition, shifting, while caregivers reported on demographic variables, household assets, child sleep, child screen time, child exposure to violence, and parenting practices. Multiple linear regressions examined predictors of child EF, with exploratory analyses on a subset (n = 22) for hair cortisol analysis. Results Older child age (β = 0.37, p Conclusions Findings highlight that modifiable proximal factors (e.g., caregiver education and child sleep) shape EF development more strongly than socioeconomic indicators. Results challenge the presumed universality of SES-EF gradients and underscore the importance of culturally grounded, contextually validated measures for understanding resilience and early cognitive development in Majority World settings.
