items.title: Comparison of Clinical Indicators for Differentiating Unipolar and Bipolar Depression.
items.abstract: Background The global prevalence of major depressive disorder and bipolar depression (BD) has increased, with BD often underdiagnosed and mismanaged. This study aims to identify key biomarkers from demographic and laboratory indicators to differentiate unipolar depression (UD) from BD, aiding early diagnosis and personalized treatment. Methods This study was conducted at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Xinxiang Medical University between January 2022 and December 2024. A total of 174 inpatients were included, with 87 diagnosed with UD and 87 with BD. Demographic and laboratory data were collected. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were conducted to identify the risk factors. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to evaluate discriminatory ability. Results BD exhibited a higher male proportion (p = 0.004) and significantly elevated total bilirubin (TBIL), creatinine, and creatine kinase (CK) levels, along with lower thyroxine (T4) levels, compared to UD (p Conclusions Key metabolic and muscular biomarkers, including TBIL, CK, PLT, and T4, were identified as potential differentiators between UD and BD. These findings demonstrated diagnostic potential and underscored the need for further validation in larger studies.

items.title: Inter-Rater Reliability in Pre-Anaesthetic Airway Assessment: A Protocol for a Systematic Review.
items.abstract: Background Pre-anaesthetic airway assessment relies on subjective clinical judgement, whether performed through direct physical examination, such as Mallampati classification or thyromental distance, or through composite scoring systems that combine several such components, including the Simplified Airway Risk Index, the El-Ganzouri Risk Index and the Wilson score. The clinical value of these assessments depends not only on their predictive accuracy but also on whether they can be applied consistently across assessors. However, evidence on the inter-rater reliability, agreement or variability of these composite tools and their individual components remains scattered across the literature and has not previously been systematically synthesised. This systematic review therefore aims to identify, assess and synthesise the available literature on inter-rater reliability, agreement or variability in composite airway assessment tools and individual airway assessment components in the context of pre-anaesthetic or preoperative assessment. Based on previous inter-observer studies of individual airway assessment components, we hypothesise that inter-rater reliability of these tools and components will predominantly range from moderate to excellent. Methods This systematic review protocol has been developed in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) and informed by the PRISMA 2020 statement and the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews. A systematic search will be conducted in MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL and CENTRAL, supplemented by reference list screening and forward citation tracking of foundational articles. Studies involving adult patients or healthy volunteers, in which two or more assessors independently evaluated a composite airway assessment tool or individual airway assessment component through physical assessment of a real participant, will be eligible for inclusion. Two reviewers will independently screen studies and extract data using a standardised, piloted form. Methodological quality will be assessed using a checklist adapted from the Guidelines for Reporting Reliability and Agreement Studies. Findings will be synthesised primarily narratively; quantitative synthesis may be considered where studies are judged sufficiently homogeneous. Conclusion This systematic review will synthesise the available literature on inter-rater reliability, agreement or variability in composite airway assessment tools and individual airway assessment components and may help clarify the consistency of these routinely used pre-anaesthetic assessments across both clinical and research populations.

items.title: A Cortical Stress Signature of Fear-Induced Walking: Mobile Electroencephalography Theta Suppression in Older Women With Fear of Falling.
items.abstract: Background Fear of falling is one of the most common and disabling stress responses of later life, yet how it is expressed in the brain during real walking is poorly understood. We examined whether walking under a naturalistic psychological threat, a fear-of-falling stressor, changes cortical oscillatory activity in older women, using mobile electroencephalography. Methods In this within-subject study, 30 community-dwelling women aged 65 years or older underwent three-dimensional gait analysis with concurrent 14-channel electroencephalography (128 Hz) during habitual walking and after introduction of a fictional disturbing factor, a psychological, nonmotor agent that elicits fear of falling without any mechanical perturbation. Relative band power and the theta/beta ratio were compared with paired t tests and Cohen's dz., with sign-flip permutation, false-discovery-rate correction and bootstrap confidence intervals; signal validity was confirmed by the eyes-closed alpha increase, and head movement and gait speed served as controls. Results Walking under threat reduced relative theta power across frontal, temporal, occipital and sensorimotor regions (p = 0.004-0.014; dz. around -0.5; confidence intervals excluding zero), confirmed by permutation and by seven electrodes surviving correction, while the frontal and central theta/beta ratio fell. The theta change was not accounted for by head movement, and in a smaller subgroup showed no detectable association with the change in gait speed, while gait became more cautious. Conclusions A naturalistic fear stressor produces a measurable cortical signature during walking, positioning fear of falling as a neurobehavioural stress response with implications for the health and mobility of older women.

items.title: Beyond Counting Words: Verbal Fluency Components and Executive Functions in Traumatic Brain Injury.
items.abstract: Background Verbal fluency (VF) tasks are consistently included in neuropsychological assessment protocols because they provide a rapid and sensitive measure of lexical retrieval and executive functioning across a wide range of neurological conditions. In addition to considering the number of words produced by the individual, examining other variables can provide highly valuable information about their cognitive performance. Aims This study examines the clinical utility of looking into specific components of VF tasks by comparing the performance of patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI) to that of healthy controls. Method and procedures Twenty-seven individuals with TBI and 29 matched controls completed a neuropsychological assessment including phonological and semantic VF tasks, along with measures of processing speed, working memory (WM) and executive functioning. Group differences were analyzed across all variables, and within-group correlations were explored between VF components (total correct responses, perseverations, mean cluster size, and number of switches) and cognitive processes. Outcomes and results Significant group differences emerged for all cognitive measures and VF components, except for mean cluster size. In the TBI group, total correct responses on both VF tasks were associated with processing speed and WM measures. Additionally, the number of switches in phonological VF correlated with cognitive flexibility measures, while mean cluster size in semantic VF was related to a measure of WM. In contrast, within the control group, total correct responses and switching in phonological VF, as well as mean cluster size in semantic VF, were associated with WM performance. Conclusions and implications These findings highlight the sensitivity of VF tasks in detecting cognitive dysfunction following TBI. Importantly, the analysis of qualitative components (such as clustering and switching) provides a more detailed understanding of the executive mechanisms underlying VF performance. Thus, beyond simple word counts, these measures enhance the diagnostic and clinical value of VF tasks as tools for assessing cognitive functioning in both research and applied settings. What this paper adds What is already known on this subject Verbal fluency (VF) tasks, in both their phonological and semantic variations, are simple neuropsychological assessment tools that are sensitive to the cognitive performance of healthy individuals as well as patients with neurological conditions. Previous studies have demonstrated the relationship between this task and cognitive processes related to language, processing speed, and components of executive functions; nevertheless, the evidence remains inconclusive. What this paper adds to the existing knowledge Patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI) and health controls showed distinct patterns of performance across cognitive measures including VF components. In controls, VF indices were mainly associated with working memory (WM), whereas in TBI, total correct responses correlated with WM and processing speed; additionally, switching in phonological VF was linked to cognitive flexibility, and clustering in semantic VF to WM. What are the potential or actual clinical implications for this work? VF tasks should be regarded as complex cognitive measures. Beyond word counts, analyzing qualitative components provides valuable insights into executive processes, thereby enhancing their clinical applicability.

items.title: Investigation of the Prolonged Impact of Severe Socioeconomic Hardship and Mother's Perceived Social Support on Neurocognitive Development in Young Children in the Rural Ecuadorian Amazon.
items.abstract: Children living in conditions of severe socioeconomic (SES) hardship are at elevated risk for neurocognitive delays, yet most developmental neuroscience research has focused on children in high-income, Western populations, limiting our understanding of diverse developmental contexts. This study examined maternal perceived social support as a potential buffer against the stressors associated with SES hardship on child neurocognitive development in a longitudinal sample of Indigenous families in the rural Ecuadorian Amazon. Twenty-eight children (M age = 28.02 months at T1; 57.6 months at T2) participated in the study completing an assessment of early cognitive ability at T1 and an inhibition task while functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) measured cortical activation at T2. A three-level linear mixed model revealed a significant interaction between early cognitive ability and maternal perceived social support on functional activation. Specifically, children of mothers with high social support showed no association between early cognitive ability and cortical activation, while those with low support exhibited atypical patterns (hyper- or hypoactivation), suggesting that increased maternal perceived social support may help buffer the risk exposure of chronic stressors associated with SES hardship. These findings underscore the importance of culturally embedded social resources in promoting resilience among children facing cumulative risk. Supporting maternal social networks may be a promising pathway for improving child neurodevelopment in underrepresented, low-resource communities and contributes to more inclusive global models of brain development.

items.title: Olanzapine for the Prevention and Treatment of ICU Delirium: Protocol for a Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis.
items.abstract: Background Intensive care unit (ICU) delirium is a multifactorial acute brain dysfunction associated with prolonged hospitalization, increased morbidity and mortality, and higher healthcare costs. Despite these substantial negative impacts of delirium, the optimal prevention and treatment strategies are unclear. Olanzapine, an atypical antipsychotic drug, is commonly used for delirium management. We will perform an updated systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the benefits and harms of olanzapine for the prevention and treatment of ICU delirium. Methods This protocol is developed in accordance with the recommendations of The Cochrane Collaboration and is reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) guidelines. We will include all randomized clinical trials (RCTs) evaluating prophylactic or therapeutic olanzapine versus any comparator, including pharmacological, non-pharmacological, placebo, or routine care/no specific delirium-directed intervention (treated as a single comparator) in ICU patients. Observational studies will be included solely to address potential harms. We will systematically search the following databases: Embase, MEDLINE, The Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CINAHL, Scopus, and PsycINFO, as well as clinical trial registries. We will perform meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis (TSA) to investigate the risk of both Type I and II errors. We will assess the risk of bias using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (RoB-2). The quality of trials will be evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations (GRADE) approach. The review is registered in the PROSPERO database (CRD420261474813). Outcomes The primary outcome is days alive and out of the hospital. The secondary outcomes include all-cause mortality at 90 days, number of CAM-ICU (Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit) negative days at 30 days, number of days without pharmacological treatment for delirium other than study drug during the intervention period and serious intervention-related harms. Discussion This protocol outlines the methodology we will use in a systematic review with meta-analysis designed to evaluate the beneficial and harmful effects of olanzapine for prevention and treatment of delirium in ICU patients. The findings of the systematic review will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication. We hope this review will inform future RCTs and improve clinical practice.

items.title: The Impact of Heterogeneity in Individual Characteristics and Motivation to Quit Heroin Use on Contingency Management and Opioid Agonist Treatment Response: A Latent Class Analysis.
items.abstract: Introduction Contingency Management (CM) involves the systematic application of positive reinforcement (financial incentives) to promote behaviour change, to improve treatment outcomes for individuals with opioid use disorder (OUD). To better understand patient heterogeneity, this study sought to identify meaningful subgroups/classes underlying the population based on characteristic groupings, followed by determining whether CM effectiveness varied between these subgroups. Methods Baseline characteristics (evidenced/theorised to impact CM effectiveness) of participants with OUD from the PRAISe trial (N = 552) were empirically examined using latent class analysis. Model selection was based on fit statistics and interpretability. Class was then evaluated as a potential moderator of CM effectiveness on abstinence from heroin using a mixed effects model (consistent with the PRAISe trial analysis). Results A four-class solution best described the population: (1) Less clinically complex/low alcohol dependence/high motivation to quit heroin (N = 115); (2) More clinically complex/low alcohol/high motivation (N = 287); (3) More clinically complex/high alcohol/high motivation (N = 73); and (4) More clinically complex/moderate alcohol/low motivation (N = 77). CM for Attendance, previously shown to increase heroin abstinence in the overall study sample, was more effective than no CM for participants in class (1) and (2) exclusively (OR = 5.21; 95% CI 1.25, 21.78 and OR = 1.87; 95% CI 1.03, 3.40, respectively). CM targeted at abstinence, previously shown to not be effective compared to no CM overall, was not effective in any class. Discussion and conclusions CM targeted at attendance is more effective for two subgroups of the OUD population characterised by either less complex clinical presentation and/or low dependence on alcohol. Individual differences may therefore inform a targeted CM treatment approach.

items.title: Motives matter: A smartphone EMA study on the association between motives to exercise, exercise engagement and mood.
items.abstract: Objective Regular exercise is vital for preventing cardiovascular disease, maintaining a healthy body weight and supporting mental well-being, yet most people exercise insufficiently often due to motivational barriers. Design This study examined two types of exercise motive-functional (divided into health/fitness and enjoyment) and appearance-and their interplay with mood and exercise engagement in daily life. Two hypotheses were tested: (H1) functional motives, compared to appearance motive, predict greater exercise engagement, and (H2) higher (more positive) mood, in interaction with exercise motives, predicts greater exercise engagement. Method Ninety-eight healthy BMI women completed a 2-week smartphone Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) protocol reporting exercise motive (baseline), exercise engagement (frequency, intensity, duration) and mood several times/day. Results Partially supporting H1, enjoyment motive predicted greater exercise frequency and duration, whereas-contrary to H1- health/fitness motive predicted shorter duration and appearance was unrelated to engagement. H2 was not supported: mood did not predict engagement and functional motives did not strengthen the mood-engagement link. Contrary to H2, the appearance motive strengthened the (same-moment) within-person association between mood and exercise intensity, such that women higher in appearance motive showed a stronger positive mood-intensity link. Multilevel temporal networks revealed that higher (more positive) mood at one assessment weakly predicted greater exercise intensity and duration at the next assessment. Conclusions Together, enjoyment emerges as central to exercise engagement, while positive mood temporally precedes exercise, informing future lifestyle interventions. Further research on the temporal dynamics linking mood and exercise is warranted.

items.title: The OPIAID Zone Tool (Version 0.5) as a Composite Outcome for Postoperative Pain Management Quality.
items.abstract: Background Managing postoperative pain while minimising opioid-related adverse drug events (ORADEs) remains a clinical challenge. The OPIAID Zone Tool is a visual scoring system designed to evaluate pain and ORADEs together. It has pain on the x-axis and ORADEs on the y-axis and categorises patients into zones of increased combined symptom burden. We aimed to evaluate the OPIAID Zone Tool, assess its association with postoperative outcomes and explore alternative versions. Methods This prospective observational cohort pilot study included 145 adult patients undergoing orthopaedic and abdominal surgery under general anaesthesia with postoperative care in the post-anaesthesia care unit at Bispebjerg Hospital, Denmark. The primary outcome was the OPIAID Zone Tool score (version 0.5). Secondary analyses assessed associations with patient-perceived health (EQ-VAS), quality of recovery (QoR-PACU) and time to discharge readiness in PACU, evaluated using R 2 , AIC and BIC. Results Distribution across OPIAID Zones was broad (Zone 0: 13.8%, Zone 1: 6.9%, Zone 2: 22.1%, Zone 3: 18.6%, Zone 4: 20.0%, Zone 5: 18.6%), without clear clustering and with a tendency towards pain-dominant profiles. The OPIAID Zone Tool score was significantly associated with EQ-VAS (R 2 = 0.39), QoR-PACU (R 2 = 0.35) and PACU discharge readiness (R 2 = 0.50), showing stronger overall associations than pain and ORADEs assessed separately. Conclusion The OPIAID Zone Tool (version 0.5) combines pain and ORADE scores into a single metric while simultaneously visualising their distribution across the population. The Zone score was associated with patient-centred outcomes and outperformed pain and ORADEs assessed separately, though a risk of overfitting cannot be ruled out. Further refinement and prospective validation are planned to optimise the tool and confirm its clinical utility. Editorial comment How high is the quality of the early postoperative analgesia that is being delivered? This study presents a model and instrument for quantifying quality of early postoperative analgesia combining treatments, pain reporting and opioid-related adverse events. The performance of the new instrument is presented with associations to recovery scores and time to post-anaesthesia unit discharge.

items.title: Temporal Interference Modulates Medial Temporal and Frontoparietal Activity During Mnemonic Discrimination: A High-Resolution Whole-Brain fMRI Investigation.
items.abstract: Mnemonic discrimination-the ability to distinguish between existing memories and similar new inputs-supports accurate memory in the face of interference (e.g., in a card game, recognizing that the card you are currently seeing, the King of Hearts, is distinct from the King of Diamonds you encountered earlier in the same hand). Although hippocampal pattern separation has been emphasized as a key mechanism for this process, recent theoretical frameworks and empirical findings suggest that surrounding medial temporal lobe and cortical regions also contribute by resolving interference. An important source of interference in everyday life is temporal interference: similar events may compete not only because they overlap perceptually, but also because they are separated by intervening experiences (e.g., distinguishing the King of Hearts you are currently holding in your hand from the King of Diamonds you encountered earlier in the game becomes increasingly difficult as additional cards are played and additional hands intervene between the two episodes). Here, we examined how temporal interference impacts mnemonic discrimination and its neural correlates using high-resolution fMRI and a continuous recognition task in which the lag between an item's first presentation and its subsequent target or similar lure was systematically manipulated (10, 60, or 140 intervening trials). Behaviorally, increasing lag impaired both mnemonic discrimination and target recognition. At the neural level, lag effects were not observed in hippocampal subfields. Instead, temporal interference modulated activity in extrahippocampal MTL regions including parahippocampal and perirhinal cortex, as well as distributed cortical regions including frontoparietal control areas. Importantly, lag-related modulation was process-specific, with partially dissociable patterns for successful mnemonic discrimination and target recognition. Together, these findings demonstrate that temporal interference engages a distributed MTL-cortical network that supports interference resolution during mnemonic discrimination.

items.title: Adolescent Ethanol Exposure Disrupts the Mature Phenotype of Surviving Neuroprogenitors in Female Mice.
items.abstract: Rodent models of human adolescent binge drinking persistently reduce adult neurogenesis and induce innate immune signaling cascades, suggesting long-lasting dysfunction in the hippocampal neurogenic niche. Nevertheless, many neuroprogenitors survive, and the impact of adolescent ethanol on the mature phenotype of these surviving neurons is unknown, resulting in an unstudied cellular population that could impact hippocampal function. To label a cohort of immature neurons, we used doublecortin-CreERT2 transgenic mice crossed with Rosa26-CAG-tdTomato reporter mice, resulting in tamoxifen-induced labeling of newborn neurons. Female offspring underwent adolescent intermittent ethanol (AIE) (5 g/kg ethanol or water by gavage, 2-day-on/2-day-off from postnatal day 29-58 ± 1), followed by a multi-month ethanol-free period. AIE increased dendritic branch width and cellular migratory distance, increased hilar axonal varicosities, reduced dendritic spine density, and shifted action potential generation with escalating current injections in tdTomato+ cells. Although tdTomato+ expression was also decreased in AIE relative to CON mice, there was no significant change in the number of tdTomato+ somata. AIE also reduced microglial territory in the polymorphic and molecular layers despite no change in cell number. Furthermore, microglia entwined in the dendritic trees of surviving adolescent neuroprogenitors exhibited increased sphericity, potentially indicative of a shift towards a more reactive morphological phenotype. Surviving neuroprogenitors exhibited no changes in labeling of the vesicular acetylcholine transporter, despite robust cholinergic innervation proximal to the mature dendritic tree that reduced rapidly with increasing distance from dendritic arbors. These results suggest that AIE causes lasting changes in the architectural and physiological phenotype of surviving adolescent neuroprogenitors, which may be related to disrupted neuronal-microglial dynamics and have critical consequences for both hippocampal circuitry and function.

items.title: Global analysis of thermal and chemical denaturation using CheMelt: Thermodynamic dissection of highly thermostable de novo designed proteins.
items.abstract: De novo protein design often produces thermostable proteins that denature above 100°C, which complicates the analysis of their stability. Thermostable proteins can be unfolded by combined chemical and thermal denaturation followed by global analysis of multiple melting curves. Here, we have developed CheMelt, a new online tool for global analysis of unfolding data via an intuitive graphical user interface. We use nanoscale differential scanning fluorimetry followed by CheMelt data analysis to dissect the combined thermal and chemical denaturation of 35 de novo designed protein binders. Thirteen present sufficient fluorescence changes to extract thermodynamic parameters of unfolding. These de novo designed proteins have systematically lower ΔC p and m-values than comparable natural proteins. We show that a high thermostability of a designed protein does not necessarily imply a high equilibrium stability, and demonstrate the potential of CheMelt in dissecting thermodynamic properties for protein design and engineering. CheMelt can be accessed at https://spc.embl-hamburg.de/app/chemelt.

items.title: Trajectories of Cognitive Functioning in Older Age Bipolar Disorder.
items.abstract: Objectives The prevalence of cognitive impairment is high in older age bipolar disorder (OABD). It remains unclear whether the course of cognitive functioning in these individuals follows a course of cognitive decline, whether this is different among subgroups, and if so, which factors are associated with cognitive decline. Methods Our clinical sample included 206 patients aged over 50 years from the Dutch Older Bipolar (DOBi) cohort with a total range of included measures of 306 months (1997-2022). Growth Mixture Modeling (GMM) was used to find homogeneous subgroups based on their longitudinal trajectories of the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores. Patients were categorized in classes based on similar trajectories, and these classes were compared based on their performance on nine cognitive tests using mixed models. Results Three classes could be identified through GMM, each demonstrating a modest, parallel decline in MMSE scores: one class showed consistently high cognitive performance; another with moderate cognitive functioning; and a third group with significant cognitive impairment. Multivariate analyses showed that an advanced age at baseline and an earlier onset of the disorder were predictive of a more impaired cognitive trajectory. Furthermore, nine supplementary cognitive assessments demonstrated pronounced disparities across these three groups, with the most substantial cognitive deficits in individuals with the most unfavorable MMSE trajectories. Discussion Our findings underscore the heterogeneous nature of cognitive aging in OABD, revealing a spectrum of cognitive longitudinal trajectories. Findings indicate that the MMSE is a valid screener in order to broadly predict cognitive functioning and its course in OABD. Identifying individuals who are particularly susceptible to cognitive decline is crucial for initiating tailored rehabilitation strategies.

items.title: Essential Oral Single Nutritional Therapy Products for Inherited Metabolic Diseases: Evidence and Consensus Assessment Using a Modified Delphi Method.
items.abstract: Nutritional therapy is critical in managing inherited metabolic diseases (IMDs), and includes specialized diets and single nutritional therapy products (sNTPs) such as vitamins, cofactors, and amino acids. Many sNTPs function as medicines, but are regulated as food (e.g., food supplements), which can limit access, reimbursement, and consistent supply. Essential medicines, as defined by World Health Organization (WHO), meet key healthcare needs and must be available, affordable, and quality-assured. Some sNTPs might meet this threshold, supporting their potential inclusion in the WHO essential medicines list. A modified Delphi process was conducted with a panel of 36 experts from 18 European countries to identify which sNTPs are essential for IMD treatment. Ninety-six sNTPs and their target IMDs were assessed using a literature-informed five-criteria framework, that included evaluation of the level of scientific evidence for usefulness and effectiveness. Overall, 31 sNTPs were deemed essential in the management of 55 IMDs, consisting of vitamins (n = 12), minerals (n = 4), amino acids (n = 6), sugars (n = 2), and other nutrients (n = 7). Evidence supporting their use ranged from levels 3 to 4 of the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine (OCEBM), reflecting the limited clinical trial data inherent to rare diseases. Seven of these are already included in the WHO essential medicines list. Recognition of the remaining 24 essential sNTPs could improve their availability and reimbursement, and in some cases, may warrant formal authorization as medicines. Subsequent research should focus on access inequities, cost barriers, and incorporate patient perspectives to optimize the use and impact of sNTPs in IMD management.

items.title: Bipolar Disorder and Perimenopause: An Update.
items.abstract: Objectives Perimenopause has been associated with mood worsening in some individuals, including increased depressive symptoms. Yet, the link between bipolar disorder (BD) and perimenopause remains understudied. This review aimed to provide an update on recent original studies and contextualize findings within the broader literature to guide future research and clinical practice. Methods A systematic search was conducted on Embase (January 1, 2018 to August 5, 2026) to identify studies on BD (I, II, or NOS/BD spectrum) that directly or indirectly examined perimenopause and BD. Pooled samples were included if they reported separate BD results. Results were narratively synthesized. Results Fourteen studies were identified from Australia (n = 4), Italy (n = 3), UK (n = 2), Taiwan (n = 1), South Korea (n = 1), Sweden (n = 1), USA (n = 1), and one study of international trials. There is converging evidence showing that perimenopause is a period of higher risk of first onset BD. Among individuals with existing BD, increased depression and heightened anxiety during perimenopause were the most consistent illness-course findings, whereas findings for hypo/mania were mixed. Evidence concerning psychotherapy or pharmacological treatment, including hormone replacement therapy, was limited or absent. Conclusions This review provides an updated perspective on BD and perimenopause, extending existing knowledge beyond mood symptoms and identifying several clinical and research gaps. Clinicians should consider the potential impact of perimenopause in BD management. Research using standardized menopause staging criteria (e.g., STRAW+10) is encouraged to inform mechanisms, illness trajectories, treatments, and to better support individuals with BD through perimenopause.

items.title: Mental Scene and Memory Construction and the Hippocampus.
items.abstract: A neurocomputational theory of scene and memory construction during memory recall, prospective thinking, and autobiographical memory is described. The theory describes the nature of the representation of scenes using spatial view cells in a continuous attractor network in the medial parahippocampal cortex, and how the location in the scene being represented can be shifted by self-motion eye position update even when the scene is not visible. The theory builds on the evidence for humans for a ventromedial visual cortical scene pathway via the prostriate cortex and ventromedial visual cortical regions to the medial parahippocampal scene (or place) area where scenes are represented. The approach builds on a theory about how visual features in scenes are used along this pathway to build a continuous attractor network representation of scenes in the medial parahippocampal cortex that represents the relative spatial locations of features or landmarks in the scene. The theory shows how episodic memory can be built in an attractor network in hippocampal CA3 that learns associations between the location in a scene ("where"), the object or person at that location in the scene ("what"), and the reward/affective value conveyed to the hippocampus from the orbitofrontal cortex in part via the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and posterior cingulate cortex. The theory of scene construction then shows how backprojections from hippocampal CA1 via the entorhinal cortex to the medial parahippocampal cortex can recall or construct the scene representation in the medial parahippocampal cortex, the parahippocampal scene (or place) area; and how whole memories including visual imagery of objects, rewards, and their locations in scenes can be constructed by iterative neocortical-hippocampal-neocortical processing.

items.title: Hookworm Parasitism Shapes Energy Status and Cardiovascular Disease Risk in Northeast Madagascar.
items.abstract: Objective Cardiometabolic diseases are rising in low- and middle-income countries, which also bear high burdens of helminth infection and malnutrition. Untangling the relationships among helminth infection, energy status, and cardiovascular disease is important for reducing these burdens. Methods We investigated the interacting risks and moderating variables associated with cardiometabolic health using demographic, health, and hookworm infection data from 874 participants in rural northeast Madagascar. Results We observed wide variation in body-mass index (BMI) and blood pressure, alongside high prevalences of two helminth infections: the human hookworm Necator americanus (53.6%) and the zoonotic hookworm Ancylostoma ceylanicum (20.4%). We hypothesized that hookworm infections would be associated with reduced BMI and lower blood pressure through energetic and immunomodulatory pathways. Yet, the two hookworm species showed different associations, with N. americanus infection negatively associated with BMI and A. ceylanicum infection positively associated with blood pressure. Wealthier individuals had higher BMI, but this positive effect was attenuated if they were infected with A. ceylanicum. Coinfection with both hookworms did not significantly modify these associations with BMI or blood pressure. Structural equation modeling indicated that N. americanus infection was associated with reduced blood pressure both directly and through its negative association with BMI, while A. ceylanicum infection was associated with increased blood pressure independent of BMI. Conclusions Our findings shed new light on the interacting burdens of malnutrition, parasitism, and chronic diseases with implications for public health, highlighting that these associations are dependent on parasite species.

items.title: Parent's and Service Provider's Perceptions of Family Involvement in Inclusive Early Childhood Education: Adaptation and Psychometric Validation of the Arabic Family Involvement Questionnaire.
items.abstract: Objectives This study aimed to adapt the Family Involvement Questionnaire (FIQ) into Arabic for use in the Saudi research context. The adaptation involved translating the instrument, producing the Arabic version (FIQ-A) and culturally modifying selected items. The study then examined the psychometric properties and suitability of the FIQ-A for exploring parents' and service providers' perceptions of family involvement in inclusive early childhood education settings in Saudi Arabia. Materials and methods The FIQ-A instrument created for this study was administered to participants from inclusive early childhood settings in Riyadh. The sample consisted of 100 parents and 35 service providers. The instrument measured three dimensions of family involvement: school-based involvement, home-based involvement and home-school conferencing. Descriptive statistics and reliability analyses were conducted to evaluate the psychometric properties of the scale and participants' perceptions of family involvement. Results Cronbach's alpha coefficients were α = 0.73 for school-based involvement, α = 0.89 for home-based involvement and α = 0.86 for home-school conferencing, demonstrating acceptable to high reliability across the three dimensions. Parents reported higher levels of home-based activities (M = 3.43 vs. 2.64) and home-school conferencing (M = 3.40 vs. 2.66) compared with school-based involvement (M = 3.07 vs. 2.56) than service providers (all p Conclusion The FIQ-A instrument demonstrated suitable psychometric properties, and the findings indicated that families were willing and prepared to engage in their children's education. Service providers were also ready to facilitate and support this engagement. Overall, these findings underscore the importance of strengthening multiple forms of family involvement to promote inclusive practices and support the participation of children with disabilities in high-quality early childhood education settings.

items.title: A Comparison of Two Species-Discriminatory SNP Sets for Taxonomic Assignment in Hybridizing European White Oaks (Quercus sect. Quercus).
items.abstract: Species identification is essential for conservation, forest management, and understanding ecological and evolutionary dynamics, such as adaptive introgression and maintenance of species boundaries in hybridizing taxa. Species-discriminatory marker sets have been shown to be more accurate than morphological identification, especially in hybridizing species complexes, and provide a more affordable alternative to genome-wide analyses. However, to our knowledge, no species complex exists for which several marker sets are available, let alone have been compared to each other. Moreover, it remains unclear how well marker sets can be applied to additional, closely related species. Here, we compared two independently developed SNP sets, one derived from amplicon sequencing and one from whole-genome sequencing, for three morphologically similar and hybridizing European white oak species sensu lato (Quercus robur, Q. petraea, and Q. pubescens). We applied the SNP sets to 560 samples, including samples of known pure ancestry, controlled crosses, natural populations, and four additional white oak species. Congruency between SNP sets was very high, but species assignment was slightly more accurate for the reference samples used in the development of the respective SNP set. Ancestry coefficients for first-generation hybrids were more precise with the SNP set based on whole-genome data. In a natural population, there was limited congruency between SNP sets in quantifying admixture. Notably, the SNP sets were able to identify up to two additional white oak species. Our study highlights the great potential of species-discriminatory SNP sets in science and practice, while demonstrating that ascertainment bias should not be neglected, and accurate introgression assessments may require genome-wide analyses.

items.title: Introduction and Spread of West Nile Virus in Lazio, Italy, 2025: Molecular Epidemiology and Genomic Characterization.
items.abstract: West Nile virus (WNV) is a flavivirus whose cycle involves mosquitoes and avian hosts that occasionally may infect horses and humans as "dead-end hosts." Human infection is mostly asymptomatic, sometimes leading to febrile or neuroinvasive disease. In 2025, Italy experienced its largest epidemic with an unprecedented geographic spread (79 provinces; 52% of cases in central Italy). Here we report whole‑genome sequencing and phylogeographic analysis of 39 WNV lineage 2 samples collected in Lazio and Campania regions between July and September 2025 from humans and animal samples. All 2025 strains belonged to a Southern Italian clade that diversified around 2020, with evidence of earlier circulation in 2024. All the 2025 genomes shared a substitution that lies in envelope protein domain III (K399R), potentially influencing interactions with the viral membrane. The same mutation was previously detected in Eastern European strains, leading to the hypothesis of introductions in Italy via migratory birds from these regions. Phylogeography identified strong viral dispersal routes within Central Italy supporting a pattern of short‑range spread and local overwintering. Overall, results highlight the roles of ecological conditions and cross‑border transmission dynamics in shaping the 2025 Italian epidemic, underscoring the need for integrated genomic/ecological surveillance.

items.title: Linking Population Genomics and Movement Ecology for Shark Conservation.
items.abstract: Climate change and overexploitation are increasingly threatening sharks, with pelagic species among the most affected. The complex ecology and life histories of these species, however, pose major challenges for conservation planning. Here, we examine how integrating genomics and movement ecology can better inform the conservation of highly migratory sharks. The growing availability of reference genomes and expanding population genomic datasets in sharks, coupled with advances in biologging, creates unprecedented opportunities to integrate these approaches and link long-term, population-level evolutionary processes with short-term individual, behavioural patterns. This mini review explores research applications that integrate both fields to overcome their individual limitations and strengthen the evidence and conclusions used to inform conservation. Then we discuss, based on previous studies, how this framework can address specific conservation objectives and lead to decision-ready outcomes, including the delineation of management units, the design of spatial and stock-specific fisheries management measures, and the assessment of species' vulnerability to climate change. We conclude by highlighting that the translation of this knowledge into practice requires engagement with the scientific and management bodies responsible for evaluating the evidence, advising decision-makers, and implementing shark conservation measures.

items.title: Anatomical Network Analyses of Pre- and Post-Metamorphic Cranial Systems Support the Adaptive Decoupling Hypothesis in Anura.
items.abstract: Complex life cycles characterized by distinct life phases connected by a metamorphosis raise the question whether traits of these distinct life phases can evolve independently or remain evolutionarily coupled. Because metamorphosis can include trait reorganization between life phases, the adaptive decoupling hypothesis proposes that larval and adult traits may evolve largely independent of each other. In anurans, the cranial system undergoes a major reorganization during metamorphosis, transitioning from a distinct cartilaginous larval cranium to an ossified adult cranium, yet this transformation has never been quantitatively characterized across species. We applied Anatomical Network Analysis (AnNA) to the cranial musculoskeletal systems of larval and adult anurans with different feeding and developmental modes. AnNA describes the topological organization of the cranium without the need for homologous landmarks, allowing comparisons between morphologically disparate systems. We calculated topological parameters describing integration and modularity, as well as connectivity modules (Q-modules) within each cranial network. As part of that analysis, expanded morphological descriptions of the cranial musculoskeletal system of larval and adult Smilisca phaeota were made. Larval and embryonic crania are topologically highly integrated and less modular, whereas adult crania are less integrated and organized into distinct modules. As a result, larval and adult life phases occupy distinct regions within a topological morphospace, whereby larvae and embryos of endotrophic anurans, despite lacking a free-living larval stage, cluster consistently within the larval topological space. Together, these findings support the adaptive decoupling hypothesis for the cranial system across anuran life phases.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Graph Methods for Microbiome Research: A Systematic Review.
items.abstract: The complexity of high-throughput sequencing data in microbiome research necessitates advanced analytical methods to decipher microbial community structures and interactions. Graph-based methods, which model taxa as nodes and their relationships as edges, have emerged as a powerful framework for this purpose. However, the rapid evolution of these techniques, from classical network analysis to modern graph representation learning, has created a fragmented and complex methodological landscape. This systematic review provides a comprehensive synthesis and structured overview of the field. We systematically review the literature and propose a three-part classification to categorize the primary contribution of each study: (1) novel methods for microbial network representation, (2) applications of classical graph analysis, and (3) the emerging use of graph representation learning for predictive modeling. We summarize the most frequent applications within each class, including keystone species identification, community clustering, and graph-based disease classification. Furthermore, we identify critical cross-cutting challenges, such as the lack of standardized tools and the need for improved model interpretability. By structuring the current landscape of graph-based methods, this review serves as a crucial guide for researchers to select appropriate models and highlights key gaps to direct future research.

items.title: The Genome and Population Structure of the Spruce Beetle, Dendroctonus rufipennis (Kirby, 1837), a Transcontinental Pest of North American Spruce.
items.abstract: The spruce bark beetle Dendroctonus rufipennis (Family: Curculionidae; Subfamily Scolytinae) is a major forest insect pest throughout the transcontinental range of spruce species (Picea spp.) in North America. Here, we present an annotated, near chromosome-level, genome assembly of 271 Mb, with 86% of the assembly contained in 16 pseudochromosomes and containing 17,778 predicted gene models. We also annotated 13 protein-coding genes, 2 rRNAs, and 22 tRNAs in its 19,637 bp mitochondrial genome. In addition, we present the annotated complete nuclear and mitochondrial genomes of an associated endoparasitic nematode, Contortylenchus sp. T'it'q'et (Order: Tylenchida; Family: Allantonematidae). Its nuclear genome assembly was 76.2 Mb, with 99.8% of the assembly contained in nine pseudochromosomes and containing 12,208 predicted gene models. We also annotated 12 protein-coding genes, 2 rRNAs, and 22 tRNAs in its extremely AT-rich, 15,509 bp mitochondrial genome. Population genomic analyses revealed broad consistencies with past microsatellite work, supporting the hypothesis of multiple range expansions from glacial refugia. Our analyses also identified alternate modes of population diversification which suggest that both neutral and non-neutral processes may be shaping current population genetic structure across the spruce beetle range.

items.title: Intraskeletal Pathway of the Trigeminal Nerve in Modern Bird Beak: 3D Comparative Anatomy Using the diceCT Method.
items.abstract: The morphology of the trigeminal nerve extending through the snout region in Archosauria has recently been the focus of extensive research, particularly in paleontology. However, the pathways of this nerve within cranial bones in extant birds have not been described in detail. Here, we describe trigeminal nerve pathways in the skull of nine avian species using a non-destructive soft-tissue imaging technique (diceCT) with a particular emphasis on osteological correlates, including intraskeletal neurovascular canals as well as foramina and grooves on the bony surfaces. In many species, a branch of the trigeminal nerve, the ophthalmic nerve, extends through the anterior premaxillary canal. Similarly, another branch of the trigeminal nerve, the maxillary nerve, passes through a bony canal in the maxillopalatine process at the posterior end of the snout in many species. However, apparently clade-specific unique pathways are also observed for the ophthalmic nerve around the external naris in Falconiformes and Psittaciformes and the maxillary nerve on the palatal surface in Anseriformes, the latter of which is likely associated with the specialized tactile sensation. Based on comparison with the condition in Crocodylia, the "reptilian-like" course of the maxillary nerve within the premaxilla is considered to have apomorphically been lost, whereas that of the ophthalmic nerve within the premaxilla has become extremely prominent in Aves. These changes in the intraskeletal nerve pathways in Aves have likely been associated with the enlargement of the premaxilla and the loss of teeth in the avialan lineage. The present observation of the trigeminal nerve pathway in Aves potentially contributes to the discussion of the homology of other associated soft-tissue structures and the presence of special sensory functions in fossil archosaurs.

items.title: Active Filtration of Airborne eDNA for Vertebrate Surveys in Tropical Caves.
items.abstract: Hidden from sunlight, caves are remarkable subterraneous ecosystems that host a wide range of animals, including unique species. Conventional cave biodiversity surveys can be physically challenging, disturb sensitive vertebrate communities, or require animal collection. Here we evaluate the use of metabarcoding of airborne environmental DNA (eDNA) as a non-invasive method for surveying cave vertebrates. We collected 55 samples by filtering air for 24 h at three light zones (outside, and in twilight and dark zones inside the cave) in three tropical caves in Amazonian Brazil. Using two metabarcoding primer sets targeting mammal and vertebrate DNA, we detected 123 wild vertebrate taxa encompassing mammals, birds, amphibians, and a reptile, of which 74 were identified to genus level. Genus richness in the twilight zone was significantly higher than outside the caves. Vertebrate diversity was also highest in the twilight zone, and community composition differed significantly between light zones and caves. Mammals and amphibians were mostly detected in the twilight and dark zones, whereas birds were more frequently detected outside the cave and in the twilight zone. While preliminary, our results show that caves with smaller entrances yielded more homogeneous communities in the twilight and dark zones. We detected eight of the 13 bat species and one of the four amphibian species recorded in previous surveys, while also detecting taxa not previously recorded in the caves, demonstrating complementarity with conventional surveys. As airborne eDNA requires minimal human presence in cave interiors, it reduces disturbance to sensitive fauna, lowers safety risks to surveyors, and offers a scalable method to complement conventional cave biodiversity surveys in tropical regions.

items.title: Comparative Physiological and Ecological Characterization of the Photosymbiotic Amoeba Mayorella viridis Across Symbiotic and Aposymbiotic States.
items.abstract: Symbiosis is a fundamental biological strategy that enables metabolic complementation between distinct organisms. The amoeba Mayorella viridis establishes a photosymbiotic relationship with the green alga Chlorella, yet the physiological basis of this association remains poorly understood. Here, we compared symbiotic (green) and aposymbiotic (white) strains to quantify phenotypic effects of the symbiotic state. Cell size did not differ when the cells were fed but was significantly reduced in the white strain under starvation, indicating that Chlorella contributes to host stability under nutrient limitation. Motility was unaffected by symbiosis. In contrast, photoresponses, including positive phototaxis and photophobic responses, were completely abolished in the white strain, demonstrating that symbiotic Chlorella is essential for host photoresponse. Growth and survival were significantly reduced in the white strain under both constant light and constant dark conditions, indicating that the symbiont enhances both proliferation and starvation tolerance. Notably, under dark and nutrient-limited conditions, intracellular Chlorella declined, suggesting digestion and utilization as an internal nutrient source. Photosymbiosis was re-established by reintroducing isolated Chlorella into aposymbiotic cells, restoring green phenotype and photoresponse. These findings establish a reversible system and clarify the physiological roles of photosymbiosis in M. viridis.

items.title: Carbon Catabolite Repression and Quorum Sensing Interplay in Marine Fish Spoilage: An Integrated Metabolic Perspective.
items.abstract: Bacterial quorum sensing (QS) systems pose a significant challenge to the preservation of protein-rich marine fish, as coordinated spoilage behaviors such as biofilm formation and volatile amine production are activated under specific metabolic conditions. Despite well-characterized spoilage organisms, the regulatory logic linking metabolic state to QS-driven collective behaviors remains incompletely understood. Thus, the goals of this review were to synthesize current knowledge on how carbon catabolite repression (CCR) gates QS-dependent spoilage programs in marine fish; examine the molecular mechanisms by which global regulators (cAMP-CRP, Crc/CrcZ, CcpA, (p)ppGpp-RpoS) interface with QS circuitry; and describe how this mechanistic understanding can be translated into anti-virulence preservation strategies that mislead metabolic sensors or disrupt quorum communication. In particular, this review focuses on the ecological manifestations of CCR-QS crosstalk in key spoilage genera and the latest progress in integrating metabolic modulators with QS inhibitors within stimuli-responsive smart packaging. Finally, current challenges limiting the systematic application of this metabolic perspective in the fish industry are discussed, including unresolved molecular interfaces in nonmodel spoilage organisms and methodological bottlenecks in spatially resolved analysis. It is important to note that while the proposed CCR-QS framework is strongly supported by direct mechanistic evidence in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, its molecular details remain largely unvalidated in most major marine fish specific spoilage organisms (SSOs). Nevertheless, this framework offers a testable conceptual scaffold that integrates nutrient-driven growth kinetics with QS-mediated social behavior, providing a mechanistic basis for designing next-generation precision preservation strategies.

items.title: Comparing Like With Like in Biological Invasion Risk Analysis.
items.abstract: Biological invasion decision-support methods are often compared under broad labels such as "risk assessment," even when they perform different functions. This Perspective argues that functional commensurability must be established before methods are compared. In biological invasion risk analysis, screening serves an initial risk identification function, flagging extant or horizon non-native species within a defined risk assessment area for prevention, surveillance, or more detailed evaluation. Comprehensive risk assessment examines entry or introduction, establishment, spread, and their ecological, economic, and socio-cultural consequences in greater detail. Risk management integrates risk with feasibility, cost, effectiveness, legal constraints, and stakeholder values. Impact classification and post-establishment population prioritization may contribute to these functions without being equivalent to them. Published comparisons show how conflating such functions can create false equivalence. The emerging Dispersal-Origin-Status-Impact (DOSI) literature provides an illustrative example through its comparisons with applications of the globally implemented Invasiveness Screening Kit (ISK) decision-support tools: population status and management priority are not the same quantities as prospective invasion risk screening, and species-based screening does not imply coarse spatial resolution. Forty-five peer-reviewed ISK-family studies report local or subnational screenings, including spatial resolutions comparable with or finer than DOSI applications. Valid comparisons require a shared decision objective, explicit spatial and temporal boundaries, independent evaluation evidence, and assessment of uncertainty and the consequences of error. These requirements permit methods to be evaluated for a common use, or combined within adaptive management, without treating disagreement between unlike outputs as evidence of superior performance.

items.title: Epidemiology and Haematological Alterations of Sheep Ked (Melophagus ovinus) Infestation and Farmers' Knowledge, Attitudes and Practices in Northwest Ethiopia.
items.abstract: Background Sheep ked (Melophagus ovinus) is an economically significant ectoparasite of sheep that adversely affects animal health, welfare, and productivity. However, epidemiological and haematological data on sheep ked infestation remain limited in Ethiopia. Objectives This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of sheep keds, identify factors associated with infestation, assess farmers' knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP), evaluate the association between infestation and packed cell volume (PCV), and characterize the morphometry and predilection sites of M. ovinus. Methods A cross-sectional study was condacted between September 2023 and June 2024 in the South Gondar Zone, Northwest Ethiopia. A total of 414 sheep were randomly selected and examined for sheep ked infestation. Data were analysed using multivariable logistic regression to identify factors associated with infestation, and PCV was compared between infested and non-infested groups using independent-samples t-test and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). items.title: Mapping the Evidence for Oropouche Virus to Inform Research Prioritisation.
items.abstract: Oropouche virus (OROV) infection has gained increasing public health attention due to the ongoing outbreaks in South and Central America. The World Health Organisation (WHO) lists OROV as a priority pathogen for epidemic and pandemic preparedness. This work aimed to identify and categorise the available evidence on OROV to inform research prioritisation. We conducted a rapid mapping review (search date: up to 5 June 2025) to identify primary studies on OROV and categorised these by area of research, study design, and geographic region using a pre-defined framework. Included studies were displayed in an interactive evidence gap map (EGM) to identify any evidence gaps. In total, 269 primary studies on OROV were included and mapped into the EGM. Of these, the majority of data and findings were reported from South America, Central America and the Caribbean, reflecting the geographical epidemiology of OROV. The majority of studies were observational and descriptive, based on specific outbreaks. Limited evidence was found on vector surveillance, viral pathogenesis, diagnostics and immune correlates of protection. No experimental studies on potential therapeutics or vaccines conducted in humans were identified. The findings from our mapping review and EGM highlight the utility of this methodology to rapidly identify gaps in scientific evidence for emerging or re-emerging pathogens with outbreak potential. The EGM can be used solely, or in conjunction with other prioritisation tools, in order to focus investment and research efforts towards priority topics.

items.title: Phylogeny and Morphology of Novel Labyrinthulomycetes in Nova Scotia, Canada.
items.abstract: Labyrinthulomycetes are ubiquitous marine decomposers and include the thraustochytrids, a lineage known for their extensive production of polyunsaturated fatty acids and biotechnology applications. Despite historical taxonomic confusion, environmental surveys have begun to expand the known diversity within labyrinthulomycetes. Here we present 18S ribosomal DNA sequences from 17 novel labyrinthulomycete strains established as cultures from natural samples taken from three locations in Nova Scotia, Canada. We also present light and transmission electron microscopic analysis for three of these isolates. The combination of phylogenetic and morphological analysis suggests that these isolates belong to three different genera: Thraustochytrium, Ulkenia and Oblongichytrium. Our results expand the known genetic diversity of labyrinthulomycetes in Atlantic Canadian waters, contributing new strains to understudied genera for future comparative genomic investigations, including Ulkenia and Oblongichytrium for which very few genomic resources are available.

items.title: High Burden of Goat Gastrointestinal Nematodes in South Ethiopia: Prevalence, Species Composition and Determinants of Infection.
items.abstract: Background In rural areas, goat farming is essential for maintaining livelihoods by ensuring income generation and enhancing agricultural resilience globally. However, the productivity of small ruminant systems is significantly affected by parasitic infections from gastrointestinal nematodes (GINs), particularly in regions where extensive production systems dominate. Objectives The objective of this study is to determine the prevalence and infection intensity of GIN parasites and associated risk factors in goats in the Humbo District of Southern Ethiopia. Methods A cross-sectional study examined faecal samples from 384 goats using a flotation test with the modified McMaster egg-counting technique, complemented by coproculture for nematode genera identification. Results The study revealed an overall GINs prevalence of 71.4% (95% CI: 66.6%-75.8%). Amongst the identified nematode parasites, Strongyle-type egg (STE) nematodes were the most common (45.3%), followed by mixed infections of STE and Strongyloides (14.6%), Strongyloides (10.15%) and Trichuris (1.3%) infections. Coproculture of pooled faecal samples (100 larvae counted) further identified Haemonchus (46%), Trichostrongylus (32%), Teladorsagia (12%), Oesophagostomum (5%), Bunostomum (3%) and Chabertia (2%) as the predominant genera. Multivariable logistic regression analysis indicated that younger goats, goats in poor body condition and those managed in lowland agroecological zones significantly influenced the occurrence of GINs infection (p Conclusion These findings underscore the substantial impact of GIN infections on goat health and productivity in the region and warrant the need for strengthened targeted parasite control strategies to reduce infection pressure and improve goat productivity in the study area.

items.title: Urban Infrastructures of Care: Buses as Resources for Recovery and Mental Wellbeing.
items.abstract: Although transport infrastructures are increasingly recognised as determinants of urban wellbeing, their role in trajectories of becoming well and becoming ill has received little empirical and theoretical attention, particularly in serious mental ill-health. This paper examines how bus infrastructures function as everyday resources and obstacles for people living with psychosis. Drawing on qualitative research with young people recovering from early psychosis in Lausanne, Switzerland, we examine the socio-material and affective dimensions of bus mobility through relational geographical perspectives on health and place, mobility studies and work on infrastructures of care. We show how buses can function as affective lifelines, anchors of autonomy and independence and gateways to formal and informal resources for wellbeing, supporting recovery and re-engagement with the city. Buses can also entail sensory overstimulation, proximity to others, perceived surveillance, anxiety and financial constraints. Our analysis highlights how mobility capacities are relationally constituted through encounters with urban infrastructures: buses can cultivate or undermine capacities to engage with the city. We argue that buses should therefore be understood not simply as transport services or conduits to therapeutic resources, but as ordinary infrastructures of care and enabling places through which recovery is enacted in urban life.

items.title: Integrated Reproductive and Cytogenetic Assessment of Infertility in a Captive Jaguar (Panthera onca).
items.abstract: Background Ex situ conservation of threatened felid species requires a thorough understanding of reproductive biology and realistic evaluation of assisted reproductive techniques (ART). In jaguars (Panthera onca), however, knowledge of reproductive limitations in captivity remains scarce. Objectives On the basis of a comprehensive single-timepoint assessment, this study applied an integrated clinical, endocrinological, semen analysis and cytogenetic approach to investigate persistent infertility in a captive jaguar breeding pair recommended for reproduction within the European Association of Zoos and Aquaria (EAZA) programme. Methods Both animals underwent comprehensive reproductive and health assessments, including genital examination, ultrasonography, haematological and hormonal profiling. Semen quality was evaluated following electroejaculation, and cytogenetic screening was performed to detect potential chromosomal abnormalities using conventional staining, banding techniques and fluorescence in situ hybridization. Results Cytogenetic analyses revealed a standard felid karyotype (2n = 38) in both individuals, with no evidence of aneuploidy or structural chromosomal rearrangements. Clinical and endocrinological assessments of the female did not identify abnormalities likely to impair fertility. In contrast, semen evaluation of the male revealed markedly reduced ejaculate volume, low sperm concentration, low sperm motility and a high proportion of morphologically abnormal spermatozoa, consistent with severe teratozoospermia. Conclusions Taken together, these findings indicate that although genetic and general clinical contraindications for reproduction were absent, semen quality represents a critical limiting factor for successful natural breeding. Under the observed reproductive profile, ART feasibility requires functional validation through sperm selection and competence assays. This study highlights the value of combining cytogenetic and reproductive assessments to support evidence-based decision-making in captive breeding programmes and provides novel cytogenetic data for the jaguar.

items.title: Deep learning reveals persistent individual signatures in bat echolocation calls of the greater leaf-nosed bat.
items.abstract: Intraspecific variation is a prerequisite for natural selection and can manifest in various phenotypic traits, including vocal signals. However, classifying individuals based on their vocalizations, or acoustic individual identification (AIID), remains a significant challenge. This is particularly true for species that use rapidly varying echolocation calls for orientation. Here, we demonstrate that deep learning can overcome the limitations of traditional methods and reveal persistent individual signatures within bat echolocation calls. We recorded 17 584 echolocation calls from 34 individuals of the greater leaf-nosed bat ( Hipposideros armiger ) under controlled laboratory conditions, with 19 individuals recorded repeatedly over three months. We show that a convolutional neural network (CNN) significantly outperforms a traditional method, achieving an average identification accuracy of 84% for single calls and 91% for call sequences. In contrast, the traditional discriminant functional analysis method achieved accuracies of only 39% and 47%, respectively. By systematically altering the temporal structure of echolocation calls in input sequences, we found that temporal patterning enhances individual classification accuracy, suggesting it contributes to the encoding of individual-specific information. This study reveals that echolocation calls of H. armiger can contain stable, individual identity information that was previously undetectable. Our findings highlight the potential of deep learning for non-invasive AIID and provide a methodological basis for future studies aiming to monitor animals in more dynamic environments.

items.title: Spatial Diversity of Marine Protists Along the Northern Norway Fjords During the Sub-Arctic Summer.
items.abstract: Polar coastal waters are highly complex and productive ecosystems that experience increasingly higher average water temperatures, shallower and stronger stratification, and higher glacier-melting rates. Yet, the environmental complexity and high microbial diversity within fjords pose challenges to understanding the impacts of these changes and the ecological processes driving them. Here, we studied protists and prokaryote communities, their distribution, and functional ecology along the northern Norwegian coast in summer 2019 using SSU rRNA gene metabarcoding. Physicochemical data provided insights into the main drivers for differences in plankton communities. We found significant differences in alpha and beta diversity among the different fjords and between the western (Vesterålen, Balsfjorden, and Lyngenfjord) and northern areas (Porsangerfjord, Laksefjord, and Tanafjord). Temperature, salinity, and phosphate are the main drivers for community composition differences, positively correlating with the western fjords and negatively with the northern ones. Metabarcoding analyses revealed dinoflagellates, cryptophytes, and ochrophytes as the most abundant groups on the north Norwegian coast and confirmed the bloom of the ichthyotoxic haptophyte Chrysochromulina leadbeateri in Balsfjorden. Our comprehensive spatial study of communities and key contributors across different fjords set a baseline for future environmental monitoring of these unique and productive ecosystems, which are subject to rapid environmental changes.

items.title: A thermally processed cafeteria diet reproducibly mimics early metabolic syndrome through obesity, insulin resistance, and inflammatory activation in Wistar rats.
items.abstract: The obesogenic nutrient composition and processing characteristics of ultra-processed foods may contribute to metabolic dysfunction. The present study evaluated a standardized cafeteria diet, alone or combined with low-dose streptozotocin (STZ), in male Wistar rats. Animals (n = 32) were allocated to Healthy Control, STZ (35 mg/kg), Cafeteria Diet (CAF), and CAF + STZ groups. The diet contained standard chow, condensed milk, refined sugar, hydrogenated fat, soybean oil, and chocolate-filled biscuits, homogenized and thermally processed at 180°C. After 102 days, anthropometric, metabolic, inflammatory, gene expression, microbiota, and histopathological parameters were assessed. CAF induced a marked obesogenic phenotype, with increased body weight (+172.3%) and abdominal circumference (+38.7%; P < 0.01). CAF showed hyperglycemia (median glucose, 403 mg/dl) and higher HOMA-IR than Healthy Control (P < 0.01); CAF + STZ also showed increased HOMA-IR (P < 0.05). CAF increased IL-1β and IL-6 (P < 0.05), triglycerides, adipocyte hypertrophy (P < 0.01), and adipose leptin expression (P < 0.05), while reducing muscle Slc2a4/GLUT4 expression (P < 0.01). Liver, kidney, and pancreatic histopathological scores did not differ significantly. Gut microbiota showed marked compositional imbalance and low taxonomic evenness, with Firmicutes (99.83%), Ligilactobacillus (99.36%), and Lactobacillaceae (99.52%) predominating, while Enterobacteriaceae represented 0.14%. Despite no reduction in Shannon or Simpson indices, extreme Ligilactobacillus dominance indicated a restricted and uneven community. Overall, the cafeteria diet reproduced obesity-associated metabolic dysfunction, characterized by hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, inflammation, adipocyte hypertrophy, altered glucose and leptin expression, and substantial microbiota restructuring.

items.title: The Brocken tree limit: treeline, summit syndrome or forest advance?
items.abstract: Climatic treelines mark the low-temperature limit of upright tree growth, yet visible upper tree limits do not necessarily coincide with this thermal boundary. The treeless summit plateau of Mt. Brocken (1,141 m a.s.l.), northern Germany, has repeatedly been interpreted as a climatic treeline. However, visible upper tree limits may also reflect summit syndrome, i.e. exposure-driven suppression of tree stature near mountain summits, as well as historical land use or ongoing management rather than temperature limitation. Here, we reassess the Brocken tree limit using long-term climate records, root-zone temperature measurements, wind data, and recent growth observations of Picea abies. Growing-season temperatures consistently exceeded thermal thresholds commonly associated with global treelines, with mean root-zone temperatures around 8°C in 2025. Growing-season soil temperature well predicted air temperature at the monthly scale, supporting the use of soil temperature measurements as a proxy for thermal conditions at the tree limit: an approach of general utility for logger-based treeline assessment. Long-term air-temperature records likewise remained above commonly reported treeline thresholds and showed significant warming since the 1980s. Spruce individuals surrounding the plateau exhibited vigorous recent height growth, while juvenile trees were observed establishing directly on the plateau. We conclude that the Brocken plateau does not represent a classical temperature-limited treeline but rather an upper tree limit shaped by wind, snow and ice loading and anthropogenic influences (summit syndrome). As such, Mt. Brocken provides a useful model system for distinguishing climatic treelines from exposure- and management-maintained upper tree limits in low-elevation temperate mountains.

items.title: Differential impacts of anthropogenic disturbances on forest structure, diversity, and composition in subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forests
items.abstract: Anthropogenic land-use change creates contrasting forest–matrix interfaces, yet comparative evidence of how these interfaces affect forest structure and plant diversity across vegetation strata remains limited. We used a paired-site design comprising 35 sites and 70 plots in a subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forest region of central China. Disturbed plots adjacent to Roads, Buildings, Mining, Tourism, and Farming were compared with relatively Undisturbed plots located farther from the corresponding disturbance boundaries. Stand structure and plot-level α-diversity were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models with site as a random effect. Community composition was evaluated using paired PERMANOVA, and total Jaccard β-diversity was partitioned into turnover and nestedness-resultant components using paired bootstrap and permutation procedures. Vegetation responses differed among disturbance types and forest layers. Mining reduced stand density, basal area, horizontal and vertical richness, and tree-layer species richness, Shannon diversity, and Simpson diversity. Roads increased stand density but reduced basal area, whereas Tourism, Buildings, and Farming reduced stand density. Farming increased herb-layer species richness, while Tourism reduced shrub-layer evenness. Community composition differed between Disturbed and Undisturbed plots in the shrub and herb layers but not in the tree layer. Total Jaccard dissimilarity increased in the tree layer but decreased in the shrub and herb layers. Turnover decreased only in the herb layer, whereas nestedness-resultant dissimilarity did not differ significantly in any layer. These findings demonstrate that vegetation responses at forest-disturbance interfaces are disturbance- and stratum-dependent. Integrating stand structure, α-diversity, community composition, and β-diversity provides a more complete basis for context-specific monitoring and management of adjacent forest remnants than any single indicator alone.

items.title: Synzoochory by scatter-hoarding rodents in a seasonally dry forest of Madagascar
items.abstract: Seed dispersal by scatter-hoarding rodents (synzoochory) is an important mechanism contributing to tree species diversity. Madagascar has a low diversity of frugivorous seed dispersers due to the island’s biogeographical history and lacks native large-bodied terrestrial dispersers. Consequently, relatively small-bodied animals may play important roles as seed dispersers, yet there are limited evaluations of synzoochorous rodents. To address this research gap, we conducted seed-tracking experiments to evaluate the quantitative and qualitative seed dispersal effectiveness of scatter-hoarding rodents in the tropical dry forest of Ankarafantsika National Park, northwestern Madagascar. Our use of a thread-marking method combined with fluorescent paint enabled us to recover more than 93% of removed Anacolosa pervilleana seeds, including those dispersed more than 20 m away. Although two rodent species (Macrotarsomys ingens and Eliurus myoxinus) removed A. pervilleana seeds, M. ingens removed 64.4% of the tagged seeds identified in the video analysis. These rodent species removed 59.1% of placed seeds and dispersed 40.3%; however, only 7.3% of seeds survived for 2 months. The dispersal distances were short (mean = 4.5 m), and most seeds were dispersed within 10 m. Rodents tended to disperse seeds in microhabitats with low understory coverage, where seed survival over the following 2 months was lower than in microhabitats with high understory coverage. These results suggest that scatter-hoarding rodents can serve as seed dispersers, with high quantitative but relatively low qualitative effectiveness. This study highlights the importance of considering rodent-mediated seed dispersal when assessing plant regeneration in Madagascar’s forests.
