items.title: Rare processes in ultrahigh-energy tau-lepton transport
items.abstract: Abstract In cosmic neutrino observatories, charged-lepton transport is a key input for interpreting observables and reconstructing neutrino events. Charged leptons propagating through matter undergo several energy loss processes, such as electron pair production and photonuclear interaction. In this work, we investigate several rare processes in tau-lepton transport, focusing primarily on muon pair production, $\tau N \to \tau \mu^+\mu^- N$, and Primakoff neutral-pion production, $\tau N \to \tau \pi^0 N$. At EeV energies, we find that the energy loss contributions from muon pair and Primakoff pion production are only $0.6\%$ and $0.2\%$, respectively, of that from electron pair production. Nevertheless, dimuon production may be relevant to tau neutrino searches in underwater and under-ice Cherenkov telescopes. The interaction length for dimuon emission by an EeV tau is only $6~{\rm km}$ in standard rock. Such events may be identified through the lateral separation of dimuon tracks or through a kebab topology if tau decays in the detector. In addition, we also emphasize that hard photonuclear scatterings during tau transport become increasingly important at the energy scales relevant for lunar neutrino searches like SKA-Low. items.title: Orbital Migration of Interacting Stellar Mass Black Holes in Disks around Supermassive Black Holes. III. Mass Distribution of Hierarchical Mergers
items.abstract: Abstract Active galactic nucleus (AGN) disks are a promising location for the formation of binary black holes (BBHs) that will merge on relatively short timescales and be detected by LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA (LVK). To compare the mass function (MF) of black holes (BHs) undergoing hierarchical mergers in AGN disks to the inferred MFs from LVK observations, we perform 360 simulations with an N -body code augmented to include an analytic model for migration torques and other gas forces. We focus on the region surrounding migration traps in AGN disks where migration torques cancel out and BHs converge. We find that regardless of changes in the initial MF and BBH merger criteria, frequent mergers deplete the number of BHs with masses ≲10 M ⊙ and fill the upper mass gap with a roughly uniform distribution from 40–100 M ⊙ , with a slight overabundance around ≈70 M ⊙ from resonant orbiters. We also find an average merger rate of ∼6 Gpc −3 yr −1 for migration-trap-aided BBH mergers in our AGN disk model. ∼40%of these mergers have uneven mass ratios and 16% have a primary mass ∈[50−100] M ⊙ . Therefore, AGN disks could easily be the source of BBH mergers observed by LVK that are difficult to produce through traditional stellar evolution channels. Our simulations also form a separate higher-mass intermediate mass black hole (IMBH) population >200 M ⊙ after ∼2 Myr. Future gravitational wave detectors can use observations of this IMBH population to constrain models of AGN accretion disks.

items.title: Estimation of systematic error from bulk deformation of end test mass induced by photon calibrator for LIGO post-O5 gravitational wave projects
items.abstract: Abstract We studied bulk deformation of the end test masses (ETMs) of gravitational wave (GW) detectors caused by calibration devices named Photon Calibrator (Pcal). This bulk deformation is one of the source of calibration error since it induces non-linear displacement from the ideal pendulum motion of the ETM. Particularly, it is the dominant error source above 1500 Hz which is crucial to the studies of neutron star mergers. The displacement also depends on beam offsets of the main interferometer (IFO) beam and Pcal beams. We conceptually described frequency dependent effect of bulk deformation and evaluated it in several cases of the beam offset with finite-element analysis (FEA) software, for ETM models of Advanced LIGO (aLIGO), KAGRA, Advanced Virgo (AdVirgo), and LIGO A#.

items.title: Deep radio characterization of the supernova remnant G343.1-00.7
items.abstract: Supernova remnants (SNRs) are extended radio sources whose morphology and evolution are shaped by the interaction of strong shocks with the surrounding medium. Radio morphological and spectral studies are essential for investigating their local physical properties and particle acceleration mechanisms. We conducted a detailed radio morphological analysis of the SNR G343.1-00.7 and accurately determined its radio continuum spectral properties, both integrated and spatially resolved. We combined the 0.944 GHz Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathﬁnder (ASKAP) image from the Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) survey with 0.088–0.200 GHz MWA-GLEAM data to characterize the integrated radio spectrum of G343.1-00.7 and perform its first sensitive spatially resolved spectral analysis. We derive an integrated spectral index of α=-0.50 for G343.1-00.7, confirming the previously reported value with significantly improved accuracy. We redefine the radio morphology of the remnant, providing the first morphological and spectral evidence that the filamentary structures overlapping the nearby G343.147-00.44 are physically associated with the SNR. Local brightness-brightness analysis further reveals flatter-spectrum filaments along the southeastern shell, consistent with a possible thermal bremsstrahlung contribution from radiative or partially radiative shocks. By comparison with and CO data, we identify atomic and molecular gas components kinematically consistent with the SNR distance, although no clear morphological evidence of interaction is found. The gas distribution around the however, suggests the presence of an expanding shell partially embedded within its parent molecular cloud. Overall, theoretical models based on our radio characterization place G343.1-00.7 between the late Sedov phase and the early pressure-driven phase of its evolution, suggesting that different regions may be at different evolutionary stages. Our results demonstrate the potential of high-resolution ASKAP observations for characterizing the morphology and spatially resolved spectral properties of SNRs, particularly for poorly studied remnants in complex Galactic environments.

items.title: Enhancing the Interpretability of Radial Velocity Analysis Using Leave-one-out Cross Validation
items.abstract: Abstract Radial velocity (RV) observations are reaching increasingly high precision, enabling the targeting of low-amplitude signals. Assessing results obtained at the limits of our capabilities requires understanding the relationship between data, models and inference. Leave-one-out cross validation (LOO-CV) has become an increasingly popular tool for interpretable model criticism in astronomical data analysis. In this work, we demonstrate how LOO-CV can provide insight into the RV analysis of exoplanetary systems through three case studies. We first investigate the anomalously high mass of HD 119130 b inferred from CARMENES RVs, later revised significantly downward after follow-up observations with other instruments. We show that this high mass was strongly driven by two individual measurements, whose removal significantly reduces the tension between data sets. Next, we use LOO-CV as a model selection tool for the GJ 4276 system. Here, LOO-CV prefers an eccentric single-planet model over a two-planet model, and identifies the orbital phases at which follow-up observations would best discriminate between them. Finally, we extend LOO-CV to models with correlated noise, applying it to the GJ 357 system, whose RVs are modeled with a Gaussian process. We find no predictive support for a fourth planetary signal that is moderately favored by the Bayesian evidence, strengthening the interpretation of a three-planet architecture previously reported in the literature. We provide practical guidance for implementing LOO-CV in RV analysis, together with an online tutorial. Such methods will become ever more important as future RV surveys push the limits of planet detection and characterization.

items.title: High-resolution Spectropolarimetric Observations of the Optical Filaments surrounding NGC 1275 with ESPaDOnS
items.abstract: Abstract We analyze archival high-spectral-resolution ESPaDOnS spectropolarimetric observations ( R = λ /Δ λ = 68000) of three targeted locations within the filamentary nebula surrounding NGC 1275. We present here the analysis of the main filaments' emission lines, namely, [N ii ] λ 6584, H α , and [N ii ] λ 6548, across our three pointings displaying clear detectable emission, with one also showing an additional [S ii ] λ 6716 and [S ii ] λ 6731 emission line doublet. Using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm and thanks to the exceptionally high spectral resolution of the observations, we resolve for the first time each of the emission lines within one of the pointings into a set of three emission components with a remarkable velocity dispersion contrast ( σ 1 ∼ 25 km s −1 , σ 2 ∼ 90 km s −1 , and σ 3 ∼ 208 km s −1 ). We also perform flux ratios of the three detected emission components, which reveal differences in electron density and ionization sources. Consequently, the ESPaDOnS observations appear to reveal for the first time the overlap of an outer quiescent filament and a central turbulent filament likely affected by the active galactic nucleus (AGN) activity at a distance of ∼6 . ″ 8 (∼2.5 kpc) from the central brightest cluster galaxy (BCG). Finally, ESPaDOnS polarimetric data of one of the pointing allow us to confirm an average linear polarization degree of ∼0.15%–0.14% and an angle of polarization of 5 . ° 3 ± 25 . ° 7 for the optical emission of the filaments, as well as polarization dips associated with the H α emission line and its multiple emission components. We interpret these features and measurements as tentative polarization due to dust scattering.

items.title: Gamma-ray calorimetry of Seyfert winds
items.abstract: Two stacking analyses based on Large Area Telescope (LAT) data have detected GeV emission from local radio-quiet Seyferts. One was selected via an X-ray ultra-fast outflow (UFO) and one is hard-X-ray-bright. Similar luminosities are attributed to different mechanisms: wind-driven shocks and the accretion-disk corona. Fermi We investigated how efficiently Seyfert outflows convert mechanical power into GeV photons, whether the two detections require distinct mechanisms, and how Seyferts compare with low-ionization nuclear emission-line regions (LINERs). We performed no new reduction of -LAT data but homogenized published measurements to 0.1--100 GeV, placed local mechanical accelerators on one L_γ-- Fermi diagram, and expressed η=L_γ/ as a fraction (̊ho) of the fiducial complete-calorimetry efficiency η_ inverting ̊ho for the ambient density required by pp losses. Winds from Seyfert active galactic nuclei (AGNs) have ̊ho=0.020^ +0.018 _ -0.011 for an acceleration efficiency of 0.1, a factor of simeq13.5 below starburst superwinds (̊ho=0.26^ +0.37 _ -0.16 ). The difference exceeds a factor of three with probability 0.95 and is independent of acceleration parameters common to both classes; it is conditional on the wind kinetic powers, collapsing only if every wind sits at its minimum launch radius. The implied densities, sim10 and sim10^2 cm -3 $, are consistency values, as density, shock radius, and speed are degenerate. The two stacking detections agree within a factor of 1.75 in γ-ray output per unit Eddington luminosity, but the 95 percent interval, 0.26--$24, is too wide to distinguish between them. A third stack, of 186 low-luminosity AGNs, extends the comparison 1.5 dex lower, ordered by AGN power. The GeV detectability of a non-jetted AGN is set by the product of mechanical power and calorimetric fraction. LINER outflows lack the power. For the adopted wind energetics, UFO-selected Seyfert winds fall short in calorimetry. Starburst superwinds succeed in both.

items.title: Multiline Spectropolarimetric Evidence for Photospheric Reconnection in Ellerman Bombs from DKIST
items.abstract: Abstract Ellerman bombs (EBs) are compact, transient brightenings observed in the wings of Balmer lines and are believed to result from magnetic reconnection in the lower solar atmosphere. However, their signatures have rarely been observed simultaneously in multiple spectral lines sensitive to the lower atmosphere. We present novel high-resolution multiline spectropolarimetric observations of EBs obtained with the Visible Spectro-Polarimeter (ViSP) on the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST). Simultaneous observations reveal remarkable H β wing enhancements extending up to ∼4 Å from the line core and intensity enhancements in the Na i D1 and Fe i 6302 lines. Using multiline non-LTE inversion of the Na i and Fe i lines, we infer localized photospheric heating of up to Δ T ∼ 800 K, accompanied by weak upflows and downflows at EB locations. Comparing with synthetic observables from Bifrost radiative-MHD simulations, we find that synthetic spectra reproduce the observed H β and Na i D wing enhancements and yield atmospheric stratification broadly consistent with those inferred from the non-LTE inversion. This study provides strong evidence that EBs are driven by photospheric magnetic reconnection below the temperature-minimum region, and places new constraints on the realistic EB models and small-scale energy release in the lower solar atmosphere.

items.title: The MIni-Halos in MIni-Clusters (MIMIC) project. New insights into the origin of mini-halos from a LOFAR, uGMRT, and MeerKAT study of diffuse radio emission in Abell 496 and ZwCl 235
items.abstract: This work is aimed at investigating the presence of diffuse radio emission in low-mass (M_ 500 łeq3 M_⊙) relaxed galaxy clusters. 14 We present a pilot study for the MIMIC (MIni-halos in MIni-Clusters) project, focusing on Abell 496 and ZwCl 235, using LOFAR (54 MHz, 144 MHz), uGMRT (400 MHz, 650 MHz), and MeerKAT (1.28 GHz) data, as well as X-ray data. Chandra We detected diffuse radio emission in the central ∼100 kpc of both Abell 496 and ZwCl 235, spatially confined within the sloshing-induced cold fronts seen in X-ray images. The diffuse sources satisfy the classification criteria for radio mini-halos and represent the least powerful known to date, with 1.4 GHz radio powers of (2.2 W/Hz in Abell 496 and (1.3 W/Hz in ZwCl 235. The mini-halos have steep spectra (-1.9łeq In particular, in Abell 496, we find an outward steepening of the spectral index. In both clusters, the radio and X-ray surface brightness are correlated over the diffuse source extent, with sublinear or nearly linear slopes depending on frequency. Separately, we present the properties of two extended ($>200$ kpc) tailed radio galaxies in both clusters. The steep spectra, sublinear radio–X-ray correlations, and confinement within cold fronts suggest that contribution from fossil plasma advected from the central radio galaxy and plausible turbulent reacceleration are at play in Abell 496 and ZwCl 235. These two systems allow us to extend mini-halo scaling relations toward the low-power regime. We confirm a strong correlation between the mini-halo radio power and the cool core X-ray luminosity, with P_ 1.4 ∝ L_ X,70 ^ 1.5 . We find, for the first time, tentative indications that mini-halos with steeper radio spectra could preferentially be associated with lower core X-ray luminosities and lower radio power. We speculate that mini-halos may originate from a combination of hadronic and leptonic reacceleration mechanisms, whose relative importance varies with the properties of the host cluster: higher core X-ray luminosities at a given mass (i.e., reflecting higher gas densities) might make the contribution of hadronic interactions more substantial.

items.title: Development of Numerical Program on 2-Dimensional Inviscid Burgers Equation in Finite Volume Method with UPWIND and TVD Scheme
items.abstract: This paper presents the development and validation of a numerical solver for the two-dimensional steady-state inviscid Burgers equation using the Finite Volume Method (FVM). The Burgers equation serves as a fundamental model for studying nonlinear wave propagation and shock formation in hyperbolic conservation laws. Two numerical schemes are implemented and compared: the first-order Upwind scheme and high-resolution Total Variation Diminishing (TVD) schemes with various flux limiters including Min-Mod, Van Leer, Superbee, QUICK, and UMIST. The numerical solutions are validated against an exact analytical solution derived using the method of characteristics. Results demonstrate that while the Upwind scheme is robust and stable, it exhibits significant numerical diffusion that smears shock discontinuities. In contrast, TVD schemes achieve sharper shock resolution while maintaining monotonicity. The upwind scheme spreads the shock over 3.86 cells, whereas the limiters confine it to between 1.73 and 1.91 cells, reduce the L1 error by 60 to 67 per cent and reproduce the total variation of the exact solution exactly. Superbee gives the sharpest shock and QUICK the lowest L2 error, while Min-Mod is the most diffusive of the limiters; the most compressive limiters, however, only reach a steady state once the CFL number is reduced. A refinement study over nine grids gives observed orders of accuracy of 0.86 in L1 and 0.52 in L2 with a non-convergent maximum error, which is the behaviour expected of a first-order monotone scheme applied to a discontinuous solution.

items.title: Phi-Resonant E8 Roots Quantize Gravitational Wave Frequencies — E8 Intelligence Research
items.abstract: Mapping the 240 E8 root vectors onto a discrete harmonic grid tuned to the 132 Hz base frequency yields a set of resonant frequencies that are integer multiples of 132 Hz. The φ‑scaled spacing of these resonances creates a self‑similar hierarchy where each successive mode is φ times the previous, echoing the golden‑ratio eigenvalue pattern seen in the Dirac operator. This φ‑modulated E8 spectrum predicts quantized gravitational wave mode amplitudes that correspond to the mass spectrum of elementary particles when expressed in hertz. Thus, E8 geometry provides a natural mechanism linking particle physics with low‑frequency spacetime vibrations, offering a testable bridge between quantum field theory and gravitational wave astronomy. items.title: Ensemble transport modelling of solar energetic particle events
items.abstract: Variations in the acceleration and transport conditions may account for the large inter-event variation noticed in observed solar energetic particle (SEP) events. As an initial attempt to quantify this variability, we examine the sensitivity of the solutions from a 2D SEP transport model to different initializations. An ensemble modeling approach is used to initiate the model with different input parameters, related to the acceleration and transport of these particles. We show that, at Earth’s position, seemingly small changes in the acceleration and transport parameters can lead to significant variations in the SEP peak intensity, onset delay, and peak delay. We posit that this might explain much of the observed SEP variability. While the methodology used in this work is a basic, first proof-of-concept, approach, we suggest that a similar, but refined, approach might be a viable method that could even be implemented in (near) real-time physics-based predictive models to illustrate the associated uncertainty in simulation results.

items.title: Galaxy Clusters from the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys. IV. Alignment of Member Galaxy Orientations at z < 0.5
items.abstract: Abstract Using DESI photometric catalog data, we systematically analyze the spatial alignment of star-forming galaxies (SFGs) and quiescent galaxies (QGs) in clusters. The results reveal that, in both brightest central galaxy (BCG) alignment (BA) and satellite alignment (SA), the alignment signals of SFGs and QGs exhibit opposite trends in several aspects. For the BA signal, SFGs show stronger alignment in cluster outskirts, whereas QGs exhibit stronger alignment in inner regions. For the SA signal, both SFGs and QGs exhibit nearly isotropic signals in outer regions, while in inner regions they show opposite signals. In addition, the BA signal depends on cluster richness and QG fraction, and is more pronounced in mature clusters. Specifically, QGs show a stronger BA signal overall, which increases with luminosity and axis ratio, whereas SFGs show a weaker BA signal with no significant dependence on these parameters. The BA signal also exhibits a strong dependence on satellite galaxy color, which is independent of morphology. We confirm this by analyzing the BA signal in two populations: red disk and blue elliptical galaxies. However, neither BA nor SA shows a significant dependence on redshift at z < 0.5. In summary, these findings reflect how galaxy transport along cosmic filaments drives cluster evolution: early stage SFGs fall into clusters along filaments, and during cluster relaxation their spatial orientations are reshaped by gravitational potentials and tidal forces, weakening BA signal and enhancing SA signal. In contrast, QGs, as early cluster members, exhibit a more pronounced anisotropic distribution and maintain relatively stable spatial orientations.

items.title: A chemical inventory of the disk around the class 0 protostar L1527 IRS with ALMA
items.abstract: Planet formation starts in disks that are still embedded within their natal envelopes. Here, we compile an extensive inventory of the chemical composition of the disk and envelope ( < 3500 au) around the Class 0 protostar L1527 IRS. Using all publicly available ALMA (Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array) data, we report the detection of 40 molecules, including isotopologues. Of these, 23 are different molecular species and 29 are reported here for the first time toward L1527 in ALMA observations. CH 3 OH is the only complex organic molecule detected, while the hydrocarbon CH 3 CCH is the largest molecule detected. Overall, only a few programs are sensitive enough to detect emission unambiguously originating from the disk based on the kinematics. Nitrogen-bearing molecules are predominantly detected on more extended scales, while hydrocarbons show a distinct tail roughly along the southeastern outflow cavity wall, probably due to a stronger UV field in the eastern outflow lobe. The L1527 IRS protostellar system is not rich in sulfur-bearing molecules, with only strong emission observed for CS and SO. Overall, the envelope appears dominated by a carbon-rich chemistry, which seems to transition into an oxygen-rich chemistry in the disk. We calculate column densities of all detected species, providing a starting point to quantify the chemical diversity among young disks and the chemical evolution of the planet-forming material.

items.title: The Making of Earth: From the first particle to a finished planet, element by element
items.abstract: Every atom in Earth was made somewhere else, at a particular time, by a particular process, and then sorted into its present place by a second sequence of events that took a few hundred million years. This paper tells both stories in order. The first runs over nine billion years: protons and neutrons in the first microseconds, hydrogen, helium and lithium in the first twenty minutes, the first atoms at 373,000 years, the first carbon, oxygen and iron in the first stars a hundred million years later, and then nine billion years of stellar generations in the Milky Way that built up the oxygen, magnesium, silicon and calcium of rock, the iron and nickel of the core, and the gold, platinum, uranium and thorium of the trace inventory. The second story begins 4,567.3 million years ago, when the first solids condensed from the cooling gas around the young Sun. It follows the condensation sequence that set which elements a rocky planet could hold, the growth of planetesimals heated by aluminium-26, the descent of iron into the core within about thirty million years, the Moon-forming impact, a magma ocean and steam atmosphere, the first oceans and continental crust by 4.4 billion years ago, the late addition of gold, platinum, water, carbon and nitrogen, the start of the geodynamo, and the radioactive heat engine that still drives the planet. A timeline (Figure 1, Table 2) and an element ledger (Table 3) record what arrived when and where it now resides. The arc is the history of the universe from creation to crunch in the Euler Cosmos, measured by the phase θₜ = H₀t, which runs from 0 at creation through 0.881 now to about 3.95 at the crunch. On the arc, Earth’s material is gathered by θₜ ≈ 0.59, and the planet is finished in outline by θₜ ≈ 0.62, before the first trace of life. Every number in the paper is imported from nuclear physics, astronomy, cosmochemistry and geology. The contribution is the ordering: a single continuous record from the first particle to a planet ready for chemistry.

items.title: EXPRESS: Targeting the Neurovascular Interface: Endothelial Optogenetics as a New Frontier for Brain Circuit Interrogation.
items.abstract: The advent of optogenetics has revolutionized neuroscience by enabling precise manipulation of neural circuits, solidifying a neuron-centric view of brain function. This perspective has increasingly expanded to encompass non-neuronal cells, with the optogenetic control of astrocytes, microglia, and pericytes revealing their active roles in information processing. Yet the vascular endothelium long regarded as a passive conduit has remained largely unexplored through this lens. Here we discuss the emerging field of endothelial optogenetics, which seeks to isolate the cell-autonomous signaling capacity of brain endothelial cells, distinct from their hemodynamic functions. We explore the hypothesis that targeted optical stimulation of these cells may evoke calcium-dependent release of angiocrine factors, establishing a vasculature-to-parenchyma signaling axis that directly modulates neuronal activity and behavior. This approach not only challenges the traditional neurovascular coupling paradigm but also offers transformative potential for reinterpreting neuroimaging data and developing novel therapies for neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. By elevating the endothelium to the status of an active computational element, endothelial optogenetics promises to reshape our understanding of the brain as an integrated hemo-neural system.

items.title: Serotonin signaling enhances phagocytosis by brain macrophages through Htr2b and alleviates brain injury after stroke.
items.abstract: Brain myeloid cells, including infiltrating monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) and microglia, play critical roles in ischemic brain injury, clearing debris and shaping neuroinflammation and neurological outcomes. Yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, using single-cell RNA sequencing and fate mapping with an MDM-specific Ms4a3 creERT2 -Ai14 mouse line, we identified serotonin receptor Htr2b + MDMs as a crucial cell population involved in resolving neuroinflammation within the ischemic penumbra. Htr2b + MDMs significantly accumulate in the peri-infarct region and exhibit enhanced phagocytosis and inflammation-resolving gene signatures. Mechanistically, Htr2b activation promotes nuclear translocation of Tfe3, a key lysosomal regulator, enhancing lysosomal biogenesis and supporting phagocytic activity. MDM-specific Htr2b ablation impairs debris clearance, exacerbates neuroinflammation and ischemic injury, whereas pharmacological agonism or Tfe3 activation restores lysosomal biogenesis in brain MDMs and improves post-stroke outcomes. Thus we demonstrate a previously unrecognized Htr2b + MDM subset that integrates serotonin signaling to license intrinsic phagocytic function, alleviating ischemic brain injury.

items.title: Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator for fly walking.
items.abstract: Animal locomotion relies on rhythmic body movements driven by central pattern generators (CPGs): neural circuits that produce oscillating output without oscillating input. However, the circuit structure of a CPG for walking is not known in any animal 1,2 . To identify the cells and synapses that underlie rhythmic leg movement in walking flies, we developed dynamic simulations of the Drosophila ventral nerve cord connectomes 3-6 . A computational activation screen of descending neurons from the central brain identified DNg100-a known command neuron for walking-as the strongest driver of rhythmic leg motor activity. Simulated network pruning isolated a minimal rhythm-generating circuit consisting of one inhibitory and two excitatory interneurons; this three-neuron circuit was necessary and sufficient for motor rhythms across all six legs and in four connectome datasets. Simulations also predicted that a separate descending pathway (DNb08) drives rhythmic leg movements, which we confirmed experimentally using optogenetics in behaving flies. Our results reveal the cellular identity and synaptic structure of a putative CPG circuit for walking and other rhythmic leg movements in flies.

items.title: Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature.
items.abstract: Cognitive reappraisal refers to changing how one thinks about a situation to alter its emotional impact. It is central to well-being 1 and engages prefrontal regulatory circuits 2 , prompting the assumption that their activity reflects a person's capacity to regulate emotions 3-5 . Yet evidence for this assumption remains inconclusive and has not been established at scale. Here we analysed 40 task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) datasets in a preregistered consortium with 2,175 participants and show that three widely used indicators of reappraisal capacity-trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation-do not converge on a common core. Moreover, none of the three indicators showed the expected association with canonical prefrontal regulatory circuits. Trait questionnaires showed no detectable neural associations across the brain and task-based affective ratings were instead associated with responses in the amygdala and sensorimotor cortices. At the process level, canonical control circuits were engaged during both emotion generation and reappraisal, challenging their presumed specificity for emotion regulation. These findings caution against using activation in putatively regulatory brain regions to infer how well a person regulates emotions, with implications for neural biomarkers, interventions and psychoeducation that link emotion regulation difficulties to specific regional brain deficits.

items.title: Pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 as a therapy against solid and blood cancers.
items.abstract: The N7-methylguanosine (m 7 G) modification is one of the most prevalent tRNA modifications, mainly catalysed by the METTL1-WDR4 protein complex 1-4 . The m 7 G methyltransferase METTL1 has been linked to oncogenic transformation and the maintenance of several aggressive malignancies; however, the clinical implications of therapeutically targeting a tRNA-modifying enzyme have not been established. Here we present the development and characterization of STM9005, a highly selective and potent first-in-class tRNA methyltransferase inhibitor of METTL1. Treatment of numerous cancer cell models (including leukaemia, melanoma, pancreatic carcinoma, oesophageal cancer and small cell lung carcinoma) with STM9005 blocks cell growth, causes differentiation changes and dysregulates cell cycle progression. These cellular effects were accompanied by a selective decrease in m 7 G on a subset of tRNAs and a reduction in their expression levels, which impacted the translation of oncogenic mRNAs. We show that pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 in vivo impairs tumour growth and significantly prolongs survival in multiple mouse cancer models of different tissue origin. Collectively, our results provide a strong proof of concept that targeting of tRNA methylation is a promising avenue of anti-cancer therapy and illustrate that catalytic inhibition of METTL1 represents a therapeutic strategy against a number of aggressive malignancies.

items.title: Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury.
items.abstract: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most devastating gastrointestinal emergency in preterm infants, frequently causing mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment 1,2 . Although the gut microbiota has been implicated in NEC pathogenesis 3-5 , the microbial factors driving NEC and the following brain pathology remain unclear. Here we identify Clostridium perfringens pathobionts containing Delta toxin in the gut microbiome of individuals with severe and fatal NEC. Clinically, infected infants show worse outcomes, including aberrant systemic inflammation, severe neurological damage and coagulopathy. We establish a mouse model in which Delta-toxin-positive C. perfringens infection, or Delta toxin exposure alone, recapitulates clinical features of NEC, including intestinal necrosis and acute cerebral injury. Mechanistically, Delta toxin preferentially targets macrophages, potently activating inflammasome signalling and pyroptosis, triggering a rapid inflammatory cascade that compromises blood-brain barrier integrity and drives neuroinflammation. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify the tetraspanin CD9 as the host receptor for Delta toxin. Using systemic, myeloid-specific and intestinal-epithelial-specific Cd9-knockout mice, we show that systemic and myeloid Cd9 ablation protects mice against toxin-induced lethality, blood-brain barrier dysfunction and multiorgan injury, whereas epithelial Cd9 deletion shows partial protection, implicating macrophage targeting as a primary driver of C. perfringens CD9-dependent pathogenesis. Furthermore, a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody confers protection against disease progression. These findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a specific-toxin-mediated disorder and validate the Delta toxin-CD9 axis as a therapeutic target for this subset.

items.title: An engineered, compact Cas12m variant for multiplexed gene activation in vivo.
items.abstract: Achieving coordinated CRISPR-based transactivation (CRISPRa) regulation in vivo remains challenging, as the requisite genetic elements frequently exceed the packaging capacity of AAV vectors. Here we report the identification and engineering of the Cas12m protein family, a naturally nuclease-dead CRISPR system that possesses intrinsic self-processing activity for its precursor crRNA. We develop an optimized variant, denCas12m, and leverage it in the smCRISPRa platform. We show that a single transcriptional unit encoding a multi-gRNA array can be processed into individual functional guides within a target cell, enabling efficient synergistic activation of a single gene through multiple sites or simultaneous activation of distinct endogenous genes from a single all-in-one AAV vector. We demonstrate phenotypic rescue in mouse models of Duchenne muscular dystrophy and Scn1a haploinsufficiency. Furthermore, a single all-in-one AAV vector supports the simultaneous activation of multiple distinct endogenous genes in mice, with a single vector delivering up to eight crRNAs for activation of six different genes, demonstrating the platform's high-order multiplexing.

items.title: Learning from Error Predictions Rather Than Prediction Errors: A Perspective on Self-Supervised Learning in the Brain.
items.abstract: Humans learn by doing and observing but also by imagining the result of simulated actions in their mind. When learning from executed or observed actions, traditional theories posit that behavior improves by minimizing the difference between (1) the perceived outcome derived from sensory feedback and (2) the desired outcome (performance error) or the outcome predicted by an internal model (prediction error, PE). Supporting these theories, decades of electrophysiological studies have documented the role of the dopaminergic system and cerebellum in generating activity patterns compatible with the hypothesized error signals. In comparison, our understanding of the neural basis underlying the ability to learn from simulated actions is far more limited. Here, I argue that this form of self-supervised learning is best described in terms of a quantity known as the predicted performance error (PPE), theorized more than 30 years ago and yet largely overlooked ever since. Complementary to PEs, PPEs reflect "error predictions" between predicted and desired outcomes. Unlike PEs, however, PPEs exist even in the absence of sensory feedback and can in principle serve to evaluate actions without executing them, based on an efference copy of the underlying motor plan. I review evidence supporting the computation of PPEs in the brain and propose a network implementation based on a cortico-basal ganglia loop interacting at multiple timescales with prefrontal, parietal, and hippocampal areas. I then connect PPEs to recent discoveries on motor planning and formulate novel predictions linking PPEs to various high-level brain functions such as metacognition, problem-solving, and deception.

items.title: GradLint: a fast, open-source Rust tool for b-vector flip detection, gradient-scheme QC, and auto-repair in diffusion MRI.
items.abstract: Background Diffusion MRI (dMRI) infers white-matter tracts using stored gradient tables. If a table is flipped or permuted relative to the image coordinates during conversion or transfer, downstream tractography is silently corrupted. New method GradLint is a fast, open-source tool that detects gradient flips, audits acquisition schemes, and repairs corrupted tables. It evaluates all 48 signed-permutation candidate conventions from a single DTI fit using an analytic matrix transformation, ranking them with an anatomy-anchored, directional-stepping fiber-coherence index. Results On 1106 corrupted cases (HCP, single-site, and clinical datasets), GradLint ranked the correct convention first in every case and retained antipode-aware agreement with the field reference dwigradcheck. At the default 2% relative-margin threshold, --apply-repair yielded 1022 correct FLAG repairs; 84 L5 WARN cases required additional --force-repair authorization. Without authorization, corrections were withheld. It successfully resolved acquisition obliquity in voxel space. The frame-aware writer verified correctness on 190 subjects. With eight threads per tool, the median within-subject speed-up was 12.90-23.25× across the three timing groups; with automatic/default threading it was 5.27-8.91×. GradLint's eight-thread median check times were 2.85-14.07s. Comparison with existing methods Unlike tools that repeat expensive tracking or DTI fitting for every candidate, GradLint obtains all candidate eigenvector fields analytically from one fit. It integrates a scheme quality-control audit, outputs machine-readable provenance, returns exit codes for CI/CD integration, and generates optional DTI principal-direction glyph figures. Conclusions GradLint is a fast, open-source Rust tool that acts as a quality-control gate, guarding dMRI preprocessing pipelines against silent orientation errors.

items.title: SCN2B Drives Depression-like Phenotypes in Mice by Suppressing BDNF Signaling via Its Intracellular Domain NICD.
items.abstract: The rising global burden of depression necessitates novel mechanistic insights and therapeutic targets. Voltage-gated sodium channel β2-subunit (Navβ2, coded by SCN2B) has been implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders, yet its role in depression remains unexplored. Here, we identify SCN2B as a previously unrecognized driver of depression-like pathophysiology. Using SCN2B-overexpressing (SCN2B-OV) mice across different ages (1, 12, and 20 months) and CRISPR- engineered Navβ2V173A,V175K mice with selective reduction of the Navβ2 intracellular domain (NICD), we combined behavioral phenotyping, electrophysiology, neurotransmitter profiling, and molecular analyses, with chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) as an environmental challenge. SCN2B-OV mice exhibited accelerated depression-like phenotypes, including anhedonia (sucrose preference 52.42% reduction, P<0.05), behavioral despair (forced swim test immobility 67.42% increase, P<0.05), and cognitive deficits (Y-maze alternation 50.90% reduction, P<0.05), independent of natural aging. Electrophysiologically, SCN2B overexpression induced a striking prefrontal-hippocampal imbalance: prefrontal cortex (PFC) became hyperexcitable (glutamate release increased by 64.7%; sEPSC amplitude increased 2.05-fold, P<0.05), whereas the hippocampus showed synaptic suppression (GABA release reduced by 32.65%; sIPSC frequency reduced by 66.67%, P<0.05). Mechanistically, SCN2B overexpression suppressed BDNF/TrkB/PI3K/AKT signaling axis (BDNF reduced by 53.17%; p-TrkB reduced by 63.62%, P<0.05), accompanied by decreased synaptic proteins (PSD95 43.45%, synapsin I 40.31%, P<0.05). Remarkably, NICD-reduced Navβ2V173A,V175K mice were fully resistant to CUMS-induced behavioral and neurotransmitter deficits, establishing NICD as a critical mediator of stress vulnerability. Collectively, these findings unravel a causal pathway in which SCN2B overexpression drives NICD-dependent suppression of BDNF signaling, leading to region-specific excitatory/inhibitory imbalance, synaptic disintegration, and depression-like phenotypes. Targeting Navβ2 proteolysis to block NICD generation may thus represent a novel therapeutic strategy for mood disorders.

items.title: Elimination profile of dexamethasone in dried blood spots (DBS) following single and multiple oral administration and proposal of the minimum reporting level to distinguish forbidden from allowed administrations in sports drug testing.
items.abstract: Glucocorticoids (GC), such as dexamethasone (DEX), are prohibited in sports competitions when administered by systemic routes including oral, injectable, and rectal administrations. Since they remain permitted by other therapeutic routes, Minimum Reporting Levels (MRLs) are required to detect misuse in sports. Although antidoping analyses are mainly performed in urine, increasing interest has recently focused on alternative matrices such as dried blood spots (DBS). In this study, the suitability of DBS for the detection of DEX and the evaluation of its elimination profile was investigated. A liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry method was developed for the quantification of DEX and its main metabolite, 6β-hydroxy-DEX, in DBS. The method showed good linearity, sensitivity, precision, and accuracy, with no significant matrix effects. It was applied to samples collected after oral administration of DEX in healthy male participants following single-dose (4 mg, n=8) and multiple-dose (2 × 2 mg/day for 5 days, n=8) regimens. DEX and its metabolite reached the highest concentrations within the first 4 h post-administration and were generally detectable up to 24 h, without evidence of accumulation after repeated dosing. Cortisol suppression was observed in all participants, confirming the systemic effect of oral DEX administration. Plasma samples collected at the same time points showed similar concentration profiles, suggesting homogeneous distribution of DEX between plasma and red blood cells. Based on the DBS-to-plasma ratio obtained and literature plasma data, an MRL of 2 ng/mL in DBS was proposed to identify prohibited systemic DEX administration during sports competitions.

items.title: Neuroinformatics in Pakistan: building a national framework for data-driven Neuroscience and Neurotechnology.
items.abstract: Neuroinformatics represents a rapidly evolving interdisciplinary field that integrates Neuroscience, computational science, artificial intelligence, and data engineering to acquire, manage, analyze, and interpret increasingly complex brain data. Advances in Neuroimaging, electrophysiology, multimodal data integration, and computational Neuroscience have made robust Neuroinformatics infrastructure essential for modern data-driven Neuroscience, precision medicine, and intelligent clinical decision support. This Perspective examines the emerging Neuroinformatics landscape in Pakistan, examining institutional research capacity, computational infrastructure, educational and training initiatives, funding mechanisms, clinical informatics, and emerging Neurotechnology and industrial activities. Global developments in Neuroinformatics and Neurotechnology are also examined to contextualize Pakistan's current position and identify opportunities for strategic integration into the international Neuroscience ecosystem. Major barriers are critically evaluated, including fragmented neurological data resources, limited high-performance computing capacity, shortages of interdisciplinary expertise, regulatory and ethical challenges, inadequate interoperability, and barriers to sustained academic-clinical-industrial collaboration. Building on this evidence-informed assessment, this Perspective proposes a national strategy centered on interoperable Neurodata repositories, shared computational infrastructure, interdisciplinary workforce development, responsible data governance, strengthened research-industry partnerships, and international collaboration. Collectively, these priorities provide a practical roadmap for transforming existing computational and Neuroscience capabilities into a coordinated national Neuroinformatics ecosystem. Strategic investment in these areas could strengthen neurological research, accelerate data-driven clinical innovation, and position Pakistan as a more active contributor to the global Neuroinformatics and Neurotechnology landscape.

items.title: Altered Neural Oscillatory Coupling Reveals Cognitive Control Deficits with Hierarchical Characteristics and Emotional Specificity in Major Depressive Disorder.
items.abstract: Background Cognitive control deficits are a prevalent feature of major depressive disorder (MDD) and are influenced by emotional contexts. However, it remains unclear whether these deficits specifically exist at particular hierarchical levels of cognitive control and whether they are selectively exacerbated under distinct emotional contexts. Furthermore, the neural mechanisms underlying such deficits and their association with depressive symptoms remain to be further elucidated. Methods To fill these gaps, two experiments were conducted. In Experiment 1, 54 MDDs and 41 healthy controls (HCs) performed emotional and non-emotional hierarchical cognitive control tasks. Hierarchical demands were manipulated using low- and high-abstraction rules. Based on hierarchy- and emotion-specific deficits identified in Experiment 1, Experiment 2 (34 MDDs; 28 HCs) introduced rule memory set-size manipulation to test whether the deficit generalized to other hierarchical cognitive control subprocesses. Electroencephalography and eye-tracking were simultaneously recorded. Phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) quantified cross-frequency interactions subserving cognitive control. Results Delta-beta PAC was selectively reduced in MDDs compared with HCs during high-abstraction conditions under negative emotional contexts, but not in low-abstraction conditions or other contexts. Under the same conditions, MDDs also failed to show the typical memory-related increase in theta-gamma PAC. Moreover, emotion regulation scores significantly mediated the pathway from PAC abnormalities to depressive severity. Conclusions Our findings indicate that altered neural oscillatory coupling reveals cognitive control deficits in MDD that exhibit both hierarchical characteristics and emotional specificity. These neural abnormalities may contribute to depressive severity through maladaptive emotion regulation strategies, providing a novel biological account of the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying MDD.

items.title: Dyadic fNIRS Hyperscanning: Experimental Paradigms and What They Reveal About Interbrain Synchrony.
items.abstract: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) hyperscanning enables the simultaneous measurement of the brain activities of various individuals performing shared or interactive tasks and estimating their interbrain synchrony (IBS). IBS is believed to reflect different mechanisms, including social bonding or mutual prediction, and to be modulated by various factors, such as familiarity or the experimental paradigm. In this systematic review, we assessed fNIRS hyperscanning studies conducted until January 2026, focusing on the experimental protocols and their relation to reported IBS findings. Specifically, we aimed to understand task dependence of IBS results and how they differ between different kinds of dyad compositions. Additionally, we investigated other parameters, including IBS metrics and the association between IBS and psychological, behavioral, and physiological measures. We reviewed a total of 206 studies, revealing a predominance of joint action task paradigms. Our findings suggest that IBS is modulated by the characteristics of dyad composition. IBS is usually higher in dyads with closer bonds, and varies with gender, although a universal pattern could not be identified. Furthermore, the study protocols employed also seem to have an influence on IBS, as participants who engage in face-to-face interactions frequently show higher IBS than those who do not. We also observed that IBS is often associated with behavioral and psychological outcomes, while the association with physiological outcomes is scarcely studied. Future research should consistently include details about dyad familiarity and sex pairings, expand to underrepresented dyads, and investigate IBS across diverse paradigms and contexts in association with other metrics.

items.title: Geometric inference of cross-species transcriptome correspondence.
items.abstract: Sequence homology reveals evolutionary gene correspondences, but identifying functionally corresponding genes within specific cell types or during cell fate specification remains non-trivial. Here, frameworks that translate insights from model organisms into other species would accelerate wet-lab studies, so we develop Species-OT, a cross-species transcriptome analysis framework using Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport, which quantitatively compares the geometry of transcriptome distributions. Given a pair of bulk or single-cell RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) datasets, Species-OT returns a gene-to-gene correspondence capturing probabilistic alignments of regulatory roles and a transcriptomic distance quantifying overall divergence. Applied pairwise, Species-OT yields a transcriptomic discrepancy array and a hierarchical clustering tree analogous to a phylogenetic tree. We validate Species-OT using bulk RNA-seq data for cell fate specification from pluripotent stem cells in mice, monkeys, and humans and single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) data from pluripotent stem cells of six mammalian species. Species-OT identifies gene correspondences within cell fate specification, while transcriptomic discrepancies recapitulate expected species relationships.

items.title: Organoids and organs-on-a-chip as new approach methodologies at the convergence of cell biology and bioengineering.
items.abstract: The rapid growth of new approach methodologies (NAMs), including organoids and organs-on-a-chip (OOCs), has revealed a need for interdisciplinary dialogue between cell biologists and bioengineers to develop human models that can best complement therapeutic development. Stem cell-derived and bioengineered human tissue models are redefining how we understand human physiology and pathophysiology, offering control that traditional preclinical models cannot provide. By recapitulating complex tissue microenvironments, multi-organ interactions, and patient-specific biology, these systems are bridging long-standing gaps in the drug development and clinical application pipelines. Here, we synthesize advances in organoids, OOCs, and other bioengineered technologies for translational medicine to identify remaining gaps, including challenges in reproducibility, validation, and regulatory acceptance. Emerging opportunities at the intersection of synthetic biology, multi-omics, machine learning, and genetic engineering are positioning NAMs not merely as improved experimental tools but as foundational platforms for accelerating therapeutic discovery and enabling personalized medicine at scale.

items.title: The effects of cannabis legalization on psychological and physical impairment in individuals who use cannabis frequently.
items.abstract: We investigated the relationship between the use of cannabis available after legalization and adverse effects in individuals diagnosed with Cannabis Use Disorder (CUD). We utilized an existing longitudinal study of high-risk individuals (364 high-risk participants in treatment for substance use disorder (SUD) in adolescence and 407 of their siblings) that were assessed twice before January 2014 (when recreational cannabis dispensaries first opened in Colorado) and once after 2014. We hypothesized that participants who met DSM criteria for CUD after 2014, when high THC concentration cannabis products became more readily available, would demonstrate more adverse physical and psychological symptoms and endorse more DSM criteria compared to those meeting DSM criteria for CUD before 2014. In general, we did not find evidence for significant mean differences in impairment after 2014. Contrary to expectation, we found that high-risk participants with CUD endorsed significantly more DSM criteria before 2014 than after 2014. Exploratory trajectory analyses identified a small subgroup of high-risk participants (21.5%) and siblings (20.1%) exhibiting an increase in the number of CUD criteria endorsed who experienced significantly more psychological and physical symptoms after 2014. It is possible that increased THC potency products have had less effect on individuals in this high-risk sample, many of whom have been daily users for many years and have substantial tolerance for THC. Similar studies of individuals who use cannabis recreationally and less frequently are necessary.

items.title: Modeling reaction-diffusion processes in simplified to complex astroglial branchlet geometries using different simulation tools.
items.abstract: Computational modeling of spatial biochemical processes in neuroscience is increasingly important as advances in experimental and imaging techniques provide detailed insights into cellular organization. Reaction-diffusion models are commonly used to study the diffusion and interactions of ions and molecules within neuronal cells, and multiple open-access simulation platforms have been developed to support such analysis. However, a comprehensive analysis of commonly used simulation tools, including MCell, STEPS, NeuroRD, and NEURON, remains lacking, particularly for realistic glial cell geometries, as these tools were originally developed for neurons. Here, we present a systematic analysis of these four simulation environments by implementing equivalent calcium diffusion and calcium-calmodulin reaction-diffusion models across a range of spatial domains. These include simplified geometries (cylinders and rectangular cuboids) as well as biologically realistic astroglial morphologies derived from electron microscopy data, including mouse Bergmann glia and mouse and human cortical astrocytes. Using matched kinetic parameters and diffusion constants, we examine simulation outputs and morphological variations across platforms under comparable conditions. We find that all tools produce overall consistent results for the systems considered, indicating that each can reliably capture diffusion and reaction-diffusion dynamics in simplified and complex geometries. At the same time, we show that the structural heterogeneity of branchlets from human astrocytes and mouse Bergmann glia gives rise to distinct calcium signaling, demonstrating that fine-scale morphology critically shapes astroglial dynamics and must be accurately captured by simulation frameworks. In addition, notable differences emerge in geometry representation, implementation strategies, computational aspects, and usability of the tools. By highlighting key trade-offs between geometric fidelity, flexibility, and computational cost in modeling intracellular biochemical processes, these findings provide practical guidance for selecting appropriate simulation tools. More broadly, our results support the use of reaction-diffusion modeling in morphologically realistic astrocytic environments and contribute to enabling mechanistic studies of localized signaling events at synaptic and perisynaptic sites.

items.title: Presynaptic filopodia form kinapses and promote convective membrane flow to sustain synchronous neurotransmitter release.
items.abstract: Synaptic plasticity is the principal mechanism by which neural circuits compute and adapt. Presynaptic plasticity is traditionally regarded as a transient adaptation of the synaptic vesicle fusion and recycling machinery, whereas the role of structural remodeling of synaptic boutons remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate a mechanical coupling between presynaptic structural remodeling and synaptic efficacy. We find that dynamic presynaptic filopodia emerge during active synaptic transmission and deform synaptic boutons while forming transient contacts with postsynaptic structures, which we term neuronal kinapses. Filopodia formation is activity dependent and occurs in intact circuits and human brain. Mechanistically, filopodial growth induces convective in-plane membrane flow toward the filopodium, accelerating release site clearance, a process associated with sustained release probability during repeated synaptic vesicle fusion. As a result, filopodia formation favors an increase in synchronous over asynchronous neurotransmitter release. These results indicate that presynaptic structural remodeling can alter the spatial organization of neurotransmission and, through the membrane flow it generates, modulate its temporal precision.

items.title: Trans-synaptic interaction of orphan GPCR GPR88 and adhesion GPCR BAI3 through C1ql1 maintains synapse integrity.
items.abstract: GPR88 is an orphan GPCR with genetic variants associated with multiple neuropsychiatric conditions. GPR88 exhibits enriched expression in the striatum, olfactory tubercle, and inferior olive. Despite these functional associations, its endogenous ligand and its downstream molecular pathways remain unresolved. Here, we found that climbing fiber (CF)-localized GPR88 regulates CF-Purkinje cell synapses in the cerebellum and associative learning behaviors. The results support the CF-secreted protein C1ql1 as the ligand of GPR88 and further revealed that C1ql1 activates biased Gq signaling to enhance CF synapses. Last, we demonstrated that GPR88 anchors C1ql1 and, via C1ql1, forms a tripartite complex with the postsynaptic adhesion GPCR BAI3 in vitro. These findings resolve the orphan status of GPR88 and likely reveal a mechanism by which a secreted protein links two GPCRs to fine-tune synaptic signaling at pre- and postsynaptic sites.

items.title: Ultrasound neuromodulation hypotheses on the directionality of effects and community resource.
items.abstract: Low-intensity transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) is a promising non-invasive technique for brain stimulation and focal neuromodulation. Research with humans and animal models has raised the possibility that TUS can be biased towards enhancing or suppressing neural function. Here, we first collate a set of hypotheses on the directionality of TUS effects and conduct an initial meta-analysis on available healthy human participant TUS studies reporting stimulation parameters and outcomes (n = 47 studies, 52 experiments). In initial exploratory analyses with univariate tests, we find that parameters, such as the intensity and continuity of stimulation (duty cycle, DC) show statistical trends towards likely TUS neural enhancement or suppression of function. Machine-learning analyses were limited by the currently small sample size. Given that human TUS sample sizes are expected to increase, predictability on the directionality of TUS effects could improve if a database is available. Therefore, we establish an inTUS database and resource for the systematic reporting of TUS parameters and outcomes to assist in greater precision in TUS use for brain stimulation and neuromodulation. The paper concludes with a selective review of human clinical TUS studies illustrating how hypotheses on the directionality of TUS effects could be developed for empirical testing in the intended clinical application, not limited to the examples provided.

items.title: Facing far forward: Mental health in large-scale combat operations.
items.abstract: Large-Scale Combat Operations (LSCO) present unprecedented challenges to the provision of medical and mental health care on the battlefield. Characterized by restricted mobility, contested logistics, disrupted communication, drone attacks, subterranean environments and the necessity for prolonged field care, the LSCO environment will severely disrupt traditional models of combat and operational stress control (COSC) that rely on far-forward specialty providers and fixed facilities. This article introduces a special issue of Military Psychology dedicated to reviewing mental health in LSCO. By outlining the anticipated psychological demands of future near-peer conflicts, the goal of this special issue is to facilitate a shared and comprehensive understanding of possible threats and lay the groundwork for a way ahead to manage mental health in LSCO. Specifically, to maintain warfighter readiness and operational effectiveness, foundational COSC principles - Proximity, Immediacy, Expectancy, and Simplicity - must be reimagined. We highlight possible shifts in conceptualizing mental health care, including relying on leader-led interventions, peer-to-peer support and the training of non-specialty medical personnel (e.g. medics and corpsmen) to manage acute combat stress reactions using evidence-informed, rapid-intervention protocols. Ultimately, the goal is to synthesize current research, lessons learned from global operations, and conceptual frameworks to establish priorities for mental health training, intervention development, and policy in preparation for managing mental health in LSCO environments.

items.title: Brace for impact: A roadmap for the future of mental health in large-scale combat operations.
items.abstract: Large-scale combat operations (LSCO) are expected to present critical challenges to military units in terms of austere conditions, the potential for misinformation, specific LSCO-related threats, and the limitations of access to traditional medical care. As part of a special issue of Military Psychology dedicated to the topic of mental health in LSCO, 25 articles address these challenges. Articles cover key threats such as mass casualty events, drone warfare, and threats to the community. Articles also identify how traditional military mental health support may need to be adapted to take prolonged field care into account, with a focus on mental health support becoming the responsibility of individuals, informal peers, trained peers, and leaders. Furthermore, the articles address special topics such as the impact of LSCO on medical personnel burnout, attitudes toward novel solutions such as mindfulness, and training models for integrating mental skills into simulations and field-based exercises. Collectively, these articles inform the development of a schematic model of LSCO Mental Health. In addition, future research topics provide direction for assessing, preventing, and intervening with mental health health and cognitive strain in the LSCO context. By bringing this array of articles together, the field can prepare more effectively to meet the psychological demands of the LSCO battlespace.

items.title: Orexin and pupillary modulation for hunger control.
items.abstract: Fasting-based interventions improve metabolic health and are also explored as adjuncts in other clinical settings, but hunger remains a barrier to adherence. Fasting activates AgRP/NPY neurons (ANs), a hunger-promoting population whose inhibition reduces eating in hungry animals. Here we identify hypocretin/orexin neurons (HONs), classically associated with arousal, as rapid suppressors of AN activity. HON ablation increased AN population activity, whereas HON optostimulation rapidly suppressed it. Combined recordings of AN activity and pupil size-a direct arousal metric not previously linked to AN dynamics-revealed that HONs contributed to pupil dilation-associated AN suppression. In fasted mice, sensory stimulation rapidly recruited this pupil-HON pathway, and suppressed AN activity and eating. These findings reveal an arousal-hunger pathway through which self-initiated pupil dilations, or dilations driven by salient environmental events, interrupt fasting-induced hunger signals. They also suggest a framework for noninvasive, sensory-, and pupillometry-guided approaches to hunger control during fasting.

items.title: Forniceal deep brain stimulation improves memory in Rett syndrome mice by promoting the maturation of newborn hippocampal neurons.
items.abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is associated with an increase in hippocampal neurogenesis and memory benefits, but the causal mechanism is unclear. Here, we use a mouse model of Rett syndrome, a severe learning disability syndrome caused by MECP2 loss of function, to find that DBS promotes the maturation and integration of newborn dentate granule cells (DGCs) into the neural circuit. Suppressing hippocampal neurogenesis prevented DBS from improving learning and memory. Newborn methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MeCP2)-deficient DGCs in Rett syndrome mice showed attenuated development and synaptic dysfunction, but DBS rescued DGC dendritic arborization, synaptogenesis, and long-term synaptic plasticity. DBS achieves this, at least in part, by increasing the protein level and shifting the phosphorylation of potassium chloride cotransporter 2, thereby restoring the conversion of GABAergic signaling from depolarization to hyperpolarization, a process that is otherwise delayed by MeCP2 deficiency. This study pinpoints one mechanism by which chronic DBS promotes neuronal maturation and enhances memory.

items.title: Lysine crotonylation acts as an epigenetic switch for glutamate neurotransmission and spatial memory.
items.abstract: Histone posttranslational modifications, particularly lysine acetylation (Kac), are critical epigenetic regulators of transcriptional programs underlying long-term memory consolidation. Beyond Kac, several other non-acetyl acylations have been identified with the ability to regulate transcription; however, their role in memory consolidation remains unknown. Here, we identify histone lysine crotonylation (Kcr) as a molecular switch for long-term memory and glutamatergic neurotransmission. We find that spatial learning induces distinct spatiotemporal patterns of Kcr across hippocampal subregions. Through genetic manipulations, we show that reducing hippocampal Kcr levels impairs memory, while increasing Kcr levels by means of crotonate administration enhances long-term memory. Single-nuclei transcriptome and chromatin accessibility analyses reveal that crotonate facilitates activation of genes regulating glutamate signaling. Cell-cell communication analysis further suggests a strengthening of glutamatergic signaling within hippocampal excitatory neurons following crotonate administration. Real-time fluorescence imaging with genetically encoded sensors functionally validates our multiomics and computational findings-demonstrating the role of Kcr in regulating presynaptic glutamate release and neuronal activity. In summary, our findings elucidate a key mechanism underlying long-term memory consolidation and excitatory neurotransmission, linking epigenetic events to synaptic function and behavior.

items.title: Colours of the mind: A qualitative study exploring the relationship between neurodivergence and creativity.
items.abstract: The neurodiversity movement advocates for a societal framework that recognises neurodivergence as a difference, rather than a disorder. Despite the advocacy efforts, neurodivergent people still face issues with their physical and mental health at higher rates than the general population. Some scholars argue that these disproportionate rates originate from stress resulting from discrimination and societal stigma faced by neurodivergent people. This study aims to challenge these societal views through exploring one of the reported strengths of being neurodivergent: creativity. This study aims to explore why neurodivergent populations may be creative. To research this complex relationship between being neurodivergence and creativity a qualitative study was conducted. Ten neurodivergent adults who had studied or were currently studying a creative degree were interviewed on Zoom, exploring their beliefs about this relationship. An inductive thematic analysis was then carried out. The analysis gave rise to three themes: (1) The Construct of Creativity, (2) Resilience, & (3) Empowerment. These themes provided hypotheses for understanding the connection between neurodivergence and creativity. The results provided two hypotheses. The 'innate trait hypothesis' posits that traits thought to be intrinsic to neurodivergence may be beneficial in fostering creativity. The innate traits that arose were divergent thinking, monotropism and communication differences. The 'social isolation hypothesis' posits that the discrimination that neurodivergent people face leads to profound isolation and in some cases mental health challenges. Neurodivergent people may then use creativity as a method for regulating their emotions, providing solace from distress. Moreover, the isolation they experience provides an opportunity for introspection, which fuels creativity. Our results highlight that some neurodivergent traits, when placed within a creative context, can become strengths. This highlights the possibility that the pathologisation of neurodivergent traits is not just damaging but also invalid, with the reality being much more nuanced.

items.title: When Fakes Feel Real: Behavioral and Neural Mechanisms of Deepfake Hyperrealism in Younger and Older Adults.
items.abstract: Deepfakes are designed to mimic real people and constitute an emerging exploitation threat. They are potent methods of fraud as humans detect deepfake images at near or below chance levels, and deepfakes are frequently perceived as more real even than real images (deepfake hyperrealism). Anterior insula (aINS) function is implicated in processing salient, untrustworthy cues suggesting that low aINS recruitment during deepfake perception may underlie experiences of deepfake hyperrealism. Further, aging may confer increased experiences of deepfake hyperrealism, given increased susceptibility to deception and reduced aINS sensitivity to deceptive stimuli with age. Here, 156 participants (62 younger: 18-37 years, 94 older: 60-89 years) evaluated the realness of real and deepfake face images while undergoing fMRI. Behavioral results revealed deepfake hyperrealism in both age groups, with these effects more pronounced in older adults. Our imaging results indicated lower aINS activation was associated with higher realness ratings and aINS activity was also lower for deepfake than real images in both younger and older adults. These findings provide additional support for deepfake hyperrealism in perception, underscoring the threat of deepfakes as a method of exploitation across adulthood. Results also support that muted aINS response to deepfakes constitutes a neuromechanism in deception vulnerability.

items.title: Susceptibility to task-irrelevant auditory distractors in relation to visual working memory in children with and without attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder.
items.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder associated with increased distractibility. Previous research has reported that susceptibility to task-irrelevant visual distraction is linked with visual working memory (WM) capacity in adults. Here, we examined how neural susceptibility to task-irrelevant auditory distractors related to visual WM capacity in children with and without ADHD. Across two experiments, electroencephalography (EEG) signals were recorded from 146 Chinese children aged 7-15 (63 with ADHD, 23% girls; collected in 2022-2024), during which they performed visual tasks of varying difficulty with auditory distractors. The mismatch negativity (MMN) amplitude was measured as neural susceptibility to auditory distractors, and a K-score was calculated to assess visual WM capacity. In typically developing (TD) children, those with higher visual WM capacity showed less susceptibility to auditory distractors under high audiovisual competition (r = 0.494), whereas this relation reversed under low competition (r = -0.319). Conversely, in children with ADHD, lower visual WM capacity predicted higher susceptibility under both high (r = 0.442) and low competition (r = 0.326). These findings indicate that susceptibility to task-irrelevant auditory distraction is related to visual WM capacity in children, but the patterns differ between typical and atypical neurodevelopment and are modulated by audiovisual competition.

items.title: Naturalistic Movie Viewing Reveals a Distributed Network Supporting Audiovisual Speech Processing
items.abstract: Traditional paradigms in cognitive neuroscience often fail to capture the richness of real-world experiences. To bridge this gap, researchers increasingly use naturalistic stimuli such as movies, which provide complex, multisensory input. Speech perception is a prime example of such complexity: it is inherently multisensory, involving the integration of auditory cues, lip movements, and facial expressions. Prior studies suggest that the left posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) and superior temporal gyrus (STG) play a critical role in this integration. However, most studies of audiovisual speech have relied on simplified or artificial stimuli, limiting ecological validity. To address these gaps, we analyzed fMRI data from human participants watching two full-length films (500 Days of Summer, Citizenfour) to assess the consistency of multisensory speech processes across distinct genres and narratives. We manually annotated word onset times and modality (audiovisual vs. auditory-only). Across two movies and 38 participants we observed consistent speech-related activation in the pSTS and STG across speech types. Compared to auditory-only speech, audiovisual speech recruited a broad left-lateralized network including the angular gyrus, posterior temporal cortex, temporal pole, and inferior frontal gyrus, along with the right cerebellum. These findings were also consistently present in single-subject data. Importantly, most of the regions observed in our analyses have been implicated in multisensory function in the nonhuman primate literature despite receiving relatively little focus in human neuroimaging. Together our results demonstrate that speech processing during naturalistic viewing recruits a distributed network extending substantially beyond regions traditionally emphasized in audiovisual speech research.

items.title: Towards a scalable effective connectivity estimation in fMRI
items.abstract: Characterizing directed connections between brain regions is fundamental for understanding the brain’s network organization and how it supports cognitive processes. However, a reliable methodology allowing assessment of effective connectivity (EC) at the whole-brain level and across high-resolution parcellations has remained elusive. This limitation reflects a trade-off between model detail and scalability. Mechanistic approaches such as Dynamic Causal Modeling (DCM) provide a principled description of directed interactions but become impractical for large parcellations, whereas scalable methods based on linear-system inversion often fail to reliably recover key features of the underlying effective connectivity. Here, using data from the Human Connectome Project S1200 release, we show that the multivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (mOU) approach for EC estimation can be adapted to yield EC estimates that are in broad agreement with those of an advanced DCM, at least when the spatial variability of the hemodynamic response falls within the physiological range characteristic of the healthy adult brain. Furthermore, thanks to its low computational cost, mOU can be easily scaled up to large neuroimaging cohorts and high-resolution parcellations. High-resolution, mOU-based EC outperforms functional connectivity for single-subject connectome fingerprinting. In addition, it enables a high-resolution characterization of the brain’s hierarchical organization and modular architecture by identifying directed interactions within and between communities and revealing driver and receiver regions. Overall, our methodology provides a reliable and scalable EC estimation pipeline of wide applicability to cognitive and network neuroscience.

items.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Dementia: From Network Degeneration to Compassionate and Skilled Care
items.abstract: Dementia is a progressive syndrome characterized by neurodegeneration across distributed brain networks that results in cognitive, behavioral, and functional declines. Conventional psychoeducation provides disease facts and resources but often lacks the mechanistic grounding needed to translate knowledge into durable caregiver skills. Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) extends traditional approaches by offering brain-based explanations of symptoms and caregiving challenges, paired with learning principles optimized for stressed learners. This chapter proposes a dementia-specific NIPE framework grounded in network-level neuroscience and cognitive reserve, specifying core content domains across the disease course, delivery structures, and mechanism of efficacy. The chapter synthesizes evidence for effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, cultural adaptation, clinician training, and outcome measurement, presenting NIPE as a pragmatic approach to strengthening person-centered dementia care.
